(p-209) Surat al-A'raf

(Makkiyyah, except for eight verses from His saying ﴿And ask them﴾ to His saying ﴿And when We raised the mountain﴾; and its verses are two hundred and six.)

﴿Alif. Lam. Mim. Sad.﴾ Either it is recited in the enumerative manner (al-ta'did) according to one of the two aspects mentioned at the opening of Surat al-Baqarah, in which case it has no place in i'rab (grammatical analysis), or it is the name of the surah, in which case its place is nominative (marfu') as the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), the estimate being: "This is al-Mas" (ha dha al-Mas); that is, it is named by it. The demonstrative is masculine although the named thing is feminine, because the pointing is made to it insofar as it is named by the mentioned name, not insofar as it is named as a surah. The demonstrative was valid even though it had not been previously mentioned, because by virtue of its being about to be mentioned, it has become like something present and witnessed.

The Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 7, verse 2:

As for His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Kitab﴾ (a Book). According to the first aspect, it is the predicate of an omitted subject, which is what the enumeration of the letters indicates, as if it were said: "What is composed of the kind of these letters," meaning by it: "The surah is a Book..." etc. Or it is a demonstrative noun, pointed to with it, as a descent to the status of the composed (text) from Him, because the presence of what is composed from it is like the presence of the composer himself; that is: "This is a Book..." etc.

According to the second aspect, it is a predicate after a predicate, brought after the explanation of its being named with a wondrous name, which indicates its strangeness in itself, in order to make clear the greatness of its station, by explaining that it is a single one of the divine Books, possessing the perfections specific to them.

It has also been permitted that it be a predicate, with al-Mas being the subject; that is, "The one named al-Mas is a Book." You have already known what is in this, that what is made a title for the subject should be, before that, known as attributed to it by the addressee; and since there is no prior familiarity with the naming, its proper function is to inform of it.

﴿Unzila ilayka﴾ (it was sent down to you); that is, from Him, Exalted is He. The verb is built in the passive voice, in keeping with the manner of majesty, and as an indication of dispensing with explicitly mentioning the agent, due to the extreme clarity of its being determined. This is the secret in leaving out mention of the source of the sending down, as in His saying, may His remembrance be exalted: ﴿Proclaim what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾ and its parallels.

The clause is a qualifier of Kitab, honouring it and the one to whom it was sent down. Making it a predicate of it, in the sense of "a Book of great importance sent down to you," is contrary to the basic principle.

﴿So let there be no constriction in your breast﴾; that is, doubt, as in His, Exalted is He, saying: ﴿But if you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you﴾. Except that He expressed it by what accompanies it of constriction, for the doubter is overcome by tightness of the breast, just as the one who is certain is overcome by its expansion and widening, in exaggeration of the purification of his sanctity, upon him be blessings and peace, from attributing doubt to him, even in the form of a prohibition, for it is among the inner states whose occurrence in him ﷺ is impossible.

As for what may occur of attributing it to him in the form of a prohibition, it is in the manner of stirring up and inflaming, and of exaggerating in deterrence and warning, by creating the impression that this is of such ugliness and evil that one is forbidden from it, even one from whom it cannot possibly issue at all (p-210), so how much more so one from whom it could issue. The tanwin is for diminishing.

The preposition in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿from it﴾ is connected to constriction; it is said: "He was constricted from it," that is, his breast was straitened by it. Or it is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a qualifier of it; that is, a constriction existing from it, meaning: let there not be in you any doubt regarding its truth, or regarding its being a Book sent down to you from His presence, Exalted is He.

So the fa' according to the first is for the sequence of the prohibition, or for the consequence drawn from the content of the sentence, since that necessitates the total absence of doubt concerning what was mentioned and the attainment of certainty about it with certainty.

As for the second, it is for the sequence of what was mentioned upon the informing of that, not upon itself; so reflect.

And the directing of the prohibition at the constriction, while the intended meaning is his, upon him be blessings and peace, being prohibited from it, is either because of the exaggeration already mentioned in declaring him far removed, upon him be blessings and peace, from doubt concerning what was mentioned, for prohibition from a thing gives the impression of the possibility of the prohibited thing issuing from the one prohibited; or for the sake of exaggeration in the prohibition, for the occurrence of doubt in his breast, upon him be blessings and peace, is a cause for his being characterised by it, upon him be blessings and peace.

The prohibition of a cause is a prohibition of the effect by way of demonstrative argument, and a negation of it from its root altogether, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And let not the hatred of a people...﴾ the verse. This is not of the kind of "Let me not see you here," for there the prohibition is directed at the effect, with the intention of prohibiting the cause, so the outcome is the prohibition of him, upon him be blessings and peace, from engaging in what produces constriction; so reflect.

It has been said: the constriction is in its literal sense; that is, let there not be in you constriction of breast from conveying it, for fear that they will deny you and that you will fall short in discharging its right. For he, upon him be blessings and peace, used to fear his people's denial of him and their turning away from him, so his breast would be constricted from carrying out the task and would not be expanded for it. So God, Exalted is He, granted him security and forbade him from being concerned. Then the fa' is at that point for the sequence upon the content of the sentence, or upon the informing of it, for each of them necessitates proceeding to convey and the removal of fear with certainty, though its second necessitating is by means of the first.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That you may warn thereby﴾; that is, by the Book sent down, it is connected to "was sent down," and what lies between them is a parenthetical insertion placed between them, establishing what precedes it, preparing for what follows, and definitively excluding the notion that the locus of doubt is the sending down for the purpose of warning.

It has been said: it is connected to the prohibition, for the absence of doubt regarding its being sent down from His presence, Exalted is He, necessitates warning by it with certainty, and likewise the absence of fear of them, or knowledge that he is granted success in discharging its right, necessitates boldness in doing so.

You know well that the first explanation is not feasible, because giving the reason for the prohibition of doubt by what was mentioned of warning and reminding, together with the impression that it is possible for it to issue from him, upon him be blessings and peace, indicates that the prohibited thing is not harmful in itself, but rather because of its leading to the loss of warning and reminding; at the very least it signals that this is the greater part of its harm, and there is no doubt about its corruption.

As for the second explanation, the reason given can only be warning, not reminding the believers, since there is no trace of fear in it that could be made the goal of its absence.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And a reminder for the believers﴾, it is in the position of the accusative by an implied verb, coordinated with "that you may warn"; that is, and that you may remind the believers with a reminder; or in the genitive by coordination with the locus of "an tundhira"; that is, for warning and reminding.

It has been said: it is in the nominative, coordinated with "Kitab," or a predicate of an omitted subject; and the restriction of reminding to the believers is to indicate that warning is specific to the disbelievers; that is, "that you may warn thereby the polytheists and remind the believers." And warning is placed first because it is more important according to the context.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 3:

﴿Follow what has been sent down to you﴾ is a resumptive statement (kalam mustaʼnaf), addressed to all who are responsible (mukallafun) by way of generalization (talwin). They were commanded to follow what the Prophet ﷺ had been commanded to convey before them, by way of warning and reminding. Making it "sent down to them" is through its being sent down to him, peace and blessings be upon him. It follows the mention of what corrects them, namely warning and reminding, to emphasize the obligation of following it.

His saying, exalted is He: (p-211) ﴿from your Lord﴾ is connected to "sent down," with min (from) denoting the starting point of the action, used metaphorically. Alternatively, it is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause (hal) of the relative pronoun (al-mawsul), or of its pronoun in the relative clause (al-silah). In mentioning the attribute of lordship (rububiyyah) together with its attachment to the pronoun of the addressees, there is an added kindness toward them, an encouragement for them to comply with what they have been commanded, and an emphasis on its obligation.

Taking "what has been sent down" here to be general, encompassing the verbal and practical Sunnah, is far-fetched. Yes, its ruling encompasses both by way of implication (dalalah), not by way of direct expression (ibarah).

Since following what Allah, exalted is He, has sent down is following Him, exalted is He, the command was followed by a prohibition against following other than Him. It is said: ﴿And do not follow, instead of Him﴾, that is: instead of your Lord, who has sent down to you what guides you to the truth. Its position is accusative (nasb), as it is a circumstantial clause (hal) of the subject of the imperative verb fa-fʻal; that is: do not follow, going beyond Allah, exalted is He.

﴿Protectors﴾ from among the jinn and mankind, by your accepting from them what they cast to you by way of whispering and seduction of falsehoods, so that they may lead you astray from the truth and drive you toward innovations and deviant desires.

Or, "from" (min) protectors, with the preposition placed before it because the word is indefinite; had it been placed after it, it would have been a qualifier of it. That is: protectors that are other than Him, exalted is He. It was also said: the pronoun refers to the relative pronoun, with an omitted noun before "protectors," meaning: do not follow, instead of what has been sent down, the falsehoods of protectors. As if it were said: do not follow, instead of the religion of your Lord, the religion of protectors. It has been read as (wa-la tabtaghu), "and do not seek," as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion﴾.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Little is it that you remember﴾, with one of the two tas omitted and the dhal lightened. It has also been read with the dhal doubled, by assimilating the voiceless ta into the voiced dhal. It has also been read (yatadhakkarun), "they remember," in the third person form.

"Qalilan" (little) is in the accusative, either governed by what follows it, as an attribute of an omitted verbal noun placed before it for restriction, or of an omitted time expression of the same kind. "Ma" is an added particle (zaʼidah) to emphasize the paucity; that is: you remember with little remembrance, or for a little time, not much, in that you are not affected by it and do not act upon its requirement, and you abandon the religion of Allah, exalted is He, and follow other than it.

It is also permissible that paucity is intended to mean non-existence, as was said regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So little do they believe﴾. The clause is a concluding parenthetical addition (i'tiraḍ tadhyili), brought to censure the condition of the addressees. The shift to the third person in the last reading serves to indicate that the badness of their condition, in not complying with the command and the prohibition, requires turning the address away from them and relating their offenses to others by way of exaggeration. Or, it is accusative as a circumstantial clause of the subject of "do not follow," with "ma" being a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah) raised by it; that is: do not follow, instead of Him, protectors, little is your remembrance. However, the prohibition is not directed at the restricted element alone, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do not approach the prayer while you are intoxicated﴾, but at both the restricted element and the restriction together. Its specification by mention is for added censure of their condition, by their combining between being deniers.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 4:

﴿How many a town We have destroyed!﴾ This begins the warning to them about what befell the earlier nations, because of their turning away from following Allah the Exalted and their persistence in following the religion of their protectors (awliya'). "Kam" (how many) is an informative particle indicating multitude, in a position of nominative case as the subject (mubtada'), as in your saying: "Zayd, I struck him," where the predicate (khabar) is the sentence that follows it.

"Min qaryatin" (of a town) is a specification (tamyiz). The pronoun in "ahlaknaha" (We destroyed it) refers to the meaning of "kam"; that is: many of the towns We have destroyed. Alternatively, it is in a position of accusative case with "ahlaknaha" as its governing verb, as in the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We have created everything according to a measure﴾. The meaning of destroying them is the intention to destroy them, as in the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿When you stand up for prayer﴾; that is, We intended to destroy them.

﴿Then Our punishment came to them⦆; that is, it came to its people.

﴿Our punishment⦆; that is, Our chastisement.

﴿By night⦆: "bayatan" is a verbal noun used in the sense of the active participle, occupying the place of a circumstantial state (hal); that is, while they were spending the night, like the people of Lot.

﴿Or while they were resting at midday⦆ is coordinated with it; that is, or while they were taking a midday rest: from "qaylula," the middle of the day, like the people of Shu'ayb. The conjunctive waw was dropped from the circumstantial clause coordinated with its sister, to avoid the accumulation of two conjunctions, since the waw of the circumstantial clause is a conjunctive particle borrowed for linking, not a substitute for the pronoun, as in: "Zayd came to me, he is a horseman," which is not eloquent. The specification of these two states for punishment is because the descent of calamity while people are heedless and at ease is more dreadful, and its narration to listeners is more effective in restraining and deterring them from being deceived by the means of security and comfort. The describing of all of them with the two states of night-time and midday rest, although some of those destroyed were far removed from them, especially the midday rest, is to indicate their complete heedlessness and sense of security.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 5:

﴿So their call was not﴾; that is, their supplication and their appeal to their Lord, or what they used to claim of their religion and profess of their creed.

﴿when Our punishment came upon them﴾ — "ba's" meaning Our chastisement — and they witnessed its signs.

﴿except that they said﴾ — all together.

﴿"Indeed, we were wrongdoers."﴾ That is, it was nothing but their confession of their wrongdoing in what they had been upon, and their testimony to its falsehood, out of regret over it, remorse, and a hope for deliverance; but "hayhat" (too late), and there was no longer a time for salvation.

This is the commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 6:

﴿So We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent﴾ is an explanation of their otherworldly punishment, following the explanation of their worldly punishment. The difference is that it has also touched on explaining the starting states of all the accountable people, because this is more effective in inspiring awe. The *fa'* (فاءُ) here is for the sequencing (*tartib*) of the otherworldly states after the worldly ones in mention, according to the order in which they occur in existence (*wujudan*). That is: We will surely question all the nations, saying: ﴿What did you answer the messengers?﴾

﴿And We will surely question the messengers﴾ about what they were answered. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿On the Day when Allah will gather the messengers and say, "What was your answer?"﴾. The purpose of the questioning is the rebuke and reproach of the disbelievers. The questioning negated by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And the criminals will not be asked about their sins﴾ is the questioning of *istilam* (seeking information). Or the first is at the station of reckoning, and the second is at the station of punishment.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 7:

﴿So We will surely relate to them﴾; that is: to the Messengers, when they say: ﴿We have no knowledge. Indeed, You are the Knower of the unseen﴾; or to them and to those to whom they were sent, all together, what they used to do.

﴿With knowledge﴾; that is: knowing their outward and inward states, or with Our knowledge of them.

﴿And We were not absent﴾ from them in any state of their affairs, so that anything of their deeds and conditions would be hidden from Us. The sentence is a concluding affirmation (tadhyil) confirming what precedes it.

The Weighing (al-wazn): that is, the weighing of deeds, and distinguishing between their heavy and light, good and bad. It is in the nominative case as a subject (mubtada').

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿that day﴾ is its predicate (khabar).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿the truth﴾ is its attribute (sifah); that is: the true weighing is established on the day when questioning and recounting take place. It was also said: it is the predicate of an omitted subject, as if it were said: what is that weighing? Then it was said: the truth, that is: the just, upright justice.

It has been read as (al-qist) [the equity]. Scholars differed over the manner of the weighing. The majority hold that it is the records of deeds that are weighed, by a balance that has a pointer and two pans, which all creatures look at, to show the equilibrium and to cut off excuses, just as He asks them about their deeds, and their tongues and limbs acknowledge them, and the prophets, angels and witnesses testify against them, and just as they are recorded in their books, so that they read them at the place of reckoning. This is supported by what is related: a man is brought to the balance, and ninety-nine registers are unrolled for him as far as the eye can see, then a card (bitaqah) containing the two testimonies (kalimatan al-shahadah) is brought out for him, and the registers are placed in one pan and the card in the other pan, so the registers rise up light and the card grows heavy.

It was also said: persons are weighed, on the basis of what has been related from him, upon him be blessings and peace: "Indeed a great, fat man will come on the Day of Resurrection who will not weigh the wing of a gnat in the sight of God." 

It was also said: "weighing" is an expression for upright judgment and just decision. This was said by Mujahid, al-A'mash, and al-Dahhak, and many of the later scholars chose it, on the basis that the use of the word "weighing" in this sense is common in the language and custom by way of metonymy. They said: the balance is only intended as a means of knowing the measures of a thing, and the measures of the deeds of servants cannot be displayed by it, since they are accidents that have passed away, and even if they remained they would not accept weighing.

It was also said: the outward deeds in this world appear in accidental forms, which in the next world emerge in substantial forms corresponding to them in beauty and ugliness, so that sins and disobediences take on bodily form there and appear in the form of fire. On this interpretation is understood His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed Hell encompasses the disbelievers﴾, and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those who devour the property of orphans unjustly only devour fire into their bellies﴾. Likewise is His saying, upon him be blessings and peace, concerning one who drinks from vessels of gold and silver: "He only gulps into his belly the fire of Hell." There is no remoteness in this, do you not see that knowledge appears in the world of images in the form of milk, as is not hidden from one who has experience of the conditions of the five presences (al-hadarat al-khams).

It has been related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: that good deeds are brought in beautiful forms and evil deeds in ugly forms, and they are placed in the balance. If it is said: the accountable person on the Day of Resurrection is either a believer that He is Wise and exalted above injustice, so the judgment of God regarding the modes and quantities of the deeds suffices him; or a denier of this, who then does not concede that the preponderance of some deeds over others is due to properties returning to the essences of those deeds, but rather ascribes it to God's manifesting it to him in that manner. What then is the benefit of the weighing? It is answered: the state becomes manifest on that day, and all things appear in their realities as they are, with their attributes and conditions in themselves, of beauty, ugliness and otherwise, and they strip off the borrowed forms through which they appeared in the world. So no one among those who witness them retains any doubt that they are the very same things that existed in the world, and that each of them has appeared in this realm in its true form, entailing its attributes, and it does not occur to him that it is otherwise. And God knows best.

﴿Then those whose balances are heavy﴾: this is an elaboration of the rulings that follow from the weighing. "Mawazin" (balances) is either the plural of "mizan" or the plural of "mawzun" (that which is weighed), with the meaning of that which has weight and measure, namely the good deeds, since the heaviness of one entails the heaviness of the other. That is: whoever's balances are heavy, by which his good deeds are weighed, or his deeds that have measure and weight. It is related from al-Hasan al-Basri: it is right that a balance in which good deeds are placed should become heavy, and it is right that a balance in which evil deeds are placed should become light.

﴿Those﴾ is a pointer to the relative clause (al-mawsul) with regard to its being characterized by the heaviness of the balance; the plural is with regard to its meaning, just as the plural of "mawazin" is for that reason. As for the pronoun in "mawazinuhu" (his balances), it refers to the singular form, with regard to its wording. The sense of distance in it (the demonstrative "ulaika") indicates the loftiness of their rank and the remoteness of their station in excellence and honour.

﴿they are the successful﴾: the ones who attain salvation and reward. "Hum" (they) is either a separating pronoun (damir al-fasl), which separates the predicate from the attribute and emphasizes the attribution and conveys the restriction of the predicated to the subject; or it is a subject whose predicate is "al-muflihun," and the clause is the predicate of "ulaika." The definiteness of "al-muflihun" serves to indicate that they are the people whom you have learned to be successful in the Hereafter, or it is a pointer to what every person knows of the reality of the successful and their characteristics.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 9:

﴿And as for those whose scales are light﴾; i.e., the scales of their deeds, or their deeds that have no weight and no regard paid to them, which are their evil deeds.

﴿Then those﴾: a reference to them in view of their being characterized by that ugly attribute. The plural form and the sense of distance are for what has passed just before in its like, and it is the subject (mubtada'), whose predicate (khabar) is (p-214) ﴿who have lost their souls﴾; i.e., they wasted the sound natural disposition (fitrah) upon which they were created, which had been reinforced by the clear signs.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿because they used to wrong Our signs﴾, the phrase is connected to "lost" (khasira). Ma is a verbal-masdar particle (masdariyyah), and "by Our signs" is connected to "wrong" (yazlimun), on the basis of implying the meaning of denial (takdhib). It was placed before the verb for the sake of observing the rhyme endings (fawasil). The combination of the past and the present verb forms serves to indicate the continuity of wrongdoing in the world. That is: "Then those" who are described by lightness of scales, "who have lost their souls" because of their continuous denial of Our signs, being wrongdoers.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 10:

﴿And We have certainly established you upon the earth﴾. When God, glorified is He, commanded the people of Makkah to follow what was sent down to them, and forbade them to follow anything else, and made clear to them the evil outcome of that, namely destruction in this world and everlasting punishment in the Hereafter, He reminded them of the manifold blessings He had bestowed upon them, which call for gratitude, in order to encourage them to comply with the command and the prohibition after having frightened them. That is: We have made for you in it a place of settlement and a dwelling, or We have given you dominion over it and empowered you to dispose of it.

﴿And We have made for you therein means of livelihood﴾. Ma'ayish (means of livelihood) is the plural of ma'ishah (livelihood), which is that by which one sustains life, such as food and drink and other things, or that by which one attains such things. The correct reading of it is with a pure yā' (ma'ayish, without hamzah). Ibn 'Amir reported it with a hamzah, assimilating it to ṣaḥā'if and madā'in.

Al-ja'l (making) here carries the sense of bringing into being and originating: that is, We have brought into existence and originated, for your welfare and benefit in it, means by which you live. Each of the two adverbial phrases (fīhā and lakum) is connected to it, or to an implied verb that occurs as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) of its indefinite object; for had it been placed after it, it would have been a qualifier of it. Placing the two before the object, although their proper place is after it, is for the reason already mentioned more than once: the concern with what is placed first and the arousing of eagerness for what comes later. For when the mind is kept waiting for what should have come first to be delayed, especially when the front-placed element signals a benefit to the listener, it remains anticipating the arrival of the delayed element, so that upon its arrival it settles in with especially firm embedding.

As for placing the lām (lakum) before fī (fīhā), it is because it is the element that signals the benefit mentioned, so attention to its matter is more complete and the hastening to mention it is more important.

That said, it has been said that al-ja'l is transitive to two objects, the second of which is one of the two adverbial phrases, on the basis that it is a stable predicate placed before the first; and the other adverbial phrase is either a loose element connected to al-ja'l, or to the implied verb that serves as a circumstantial clause of the first object, as already mentioned.

You are aware that there is no worthwhile benefit in reporting that the means of livelihood have been made to be obtained by them, or to be obtained in the earth.

And His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿Little is it that you give thanks﴾; that is: for that blessing. It is a concluding remark (tadhyīl) brought to explain the bad condition of those addressed and to warn them. The rest of the discussion of it is the same as what has passed in the explanation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Little is it that you remember﴾.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 11:**

﴿And We certainly created you, then We fashioned you﴾ is a reminder of a great blessing, overflowing upon Adam, peace be upon him, and flowing on to his offspring, which obliges them to give thanks. Its placement after the reminder of the blessing that came before it, namely the blessing of establishment (tamkin, the settling of people) on the earth, is either because the latter overflows directly upon those addressed, whereas this one reaches them through an intermediary, or it is to indicate that each of them is an independent blessing that requires thanks in its own right. For attention to the sequence of occurrence may lead to the mistaken assumption that everything counts as a single blessing, as was mentioned in the story of the cow.

The opening of the two clauses with the oath and the particle of affirmation serves to show the utmost concern with their content. The creating and fashioning are attributed to those addressed, although what is meant by them is the creating of Adam and his fashioning, definitively, in order to give the occasion of bestowing favour its due and to emphasise the obligation of gratitude upon them. This is by way of allusion to the fact that they have a share in his creation, peace be upon him, and in his fashioning, since these two are not among the distinctive features confined to him, peace be upon him, such as the prostration of the angels to him, peace be upon him. Rather, they are among matters that pass on to all his offspring, since everything is created within his creation, formed after his pattern and made in his likeness. Thus it is as though they were the very one to whom his creation and fashioning were attached. That is: We created your father Adam from clay, not yet fashioned, then We fashioned him in the most excellent fashioning and the finest form, which passed on to all of you.

﴿Then We said to the angels: Prostrate to Adam﴾ is explicit that this came after his creation, peace be upon him, and after his proportioning and the breathing of the spirit into him, that is, a command that was carried out, distinct from the conditional command which came earlier in His words, exalted is He: ﴿So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My spirit, fall down before him in prostration﴾. This is what is meant by what is related in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And when We said to the angels: Prostrate to Adam…﴾, the verse in surah al-Baqarah, surah Bani Isra'il, surah al-Kahf and surah Ta-Ha, without any reference to its time.

The word "then" (thumma) here requires a delay after the fashioning, without any indication of what took place between the two. We have already explained in surah al-Baqarah that this was the manifestation of Adam's excellence, after the dialogue preceded by the announcement of his vicegerency (istikhlaf), as expressed in His words, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels: Indeed I am placing in the earth a khalifah (vicegerent)﴾, through to His words: ﴿and what you used to conceal﴾.

That too is among the matters to which the conditional command, concerning the proportioning and breathing of the spirit, was attached. The fact that it is not mentioned when the account is related does not require that it was not mentioned when the related event occurred, just as the non-mention of the conditional command when relating the executed command does not necessitate that it did not precede it. For relating one speech in different styles as required by context is not uncommon in the noble Qur'an. Thus it may be that He first conveyed to the angels, peace be upon them, all that the executed command depends on in summary, by saying for example: "I am creating a human from clay, and I am making him a vicegerent on the earth. When I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My spirit, and his excellence has become clear to you, then fall down before him in prostration." So He created him and proportioned him, breathed into him of His spirit, and then they said what they said at that point. Or the report of the vicegerency was conveyed to them after the stated conditions were fulfilled, by saying immediately after the breathing of the spirit: "I am placing this one as a vicegerent on the earth." Thereupon they mentioned concerning him, peace be upon him, what they mentioned. Then God, exalted is He, strengthened him with the teaching of the names, so they witnessed from him, peace be upon him, what they witnessed. At that point the executed command came, out of concern for the matter of what was commanded and as a notice of its time.

Some of the matters mentioned have been related in some places and others in other places, relying on what is mentioned in each place to avoid what is omitted in another place. What lifts the veil of confusion from sound insight is that what is in surah (Sad) from His words, exalted is He: ﴿When your Lord said to the angels﴾, and the verses that follow, is a substitution (badal, apposition) for His words before it: ﴿when they dispute﴾, from His words: ﴿I had no knowledge of the Exalted Assembly (al-mala' al-a'la) when they were disputing﴾. That is: by their speech during their dispute.

There is no doubt that what is meant by the Exalted Assembly are the angels, Adam and Iblis, peace be upon them, as the majority of the exegetes have agreed. By their dispute is meant what took place among them about the matter of the vicegerency, of contention, of which part was what came from him, peace be upon him, concerning the announcing of the names.

By the principle of substitution (badaliyyah), the aforementioned dispute occurred within what was explained in detail concerning the conditional command, what was attached to it of creating, proportioning and breathing the spirit into him, what followed from it of the prostration of the angels, the obstinacy and cursing of Iblis, his expulsion from among the angels, and what took place after that of deeds and words. Since the full dispute did not end with the prostration of the angels and Iblis's arrogant refusal and his being driven away from their midst, as you have come to know, because he was one of the disputants, just as it did not take place before the creation necessarily. Therefore it occurred after the breathing of the spirit and before the prostration, by one of the two ways mentioned. And God, exalted is He, knows best.

﴿So they prostrated﴾; that is, the angels, peace be upon them, after the command, without hesitation.

﴿Except Iblis﴾: an exception that is connected (istithna' muttasil), because he was a single jinn, submerged among thousands of angels, characterised by their attributes, so that they overpowered him in it and prostrated; then he was excepted as one of them. Or because among the angels there is a kind who reproduce, called the jinn, as was mentioned in surah al-Baqarah.

So His words, exalted is He: ﴿he was not among those who prostrated﴾, that is, among those who prostrated to Adam, is a resumptive statement (kalam mustanaf) explaining the manner of the non-prostration implied by the exception. For non-prostration may be for the purpose of deliberation, after which prostration occurs; and from this it is known that it never occurred at all. It has been said: the exception is disconnected (munqati'), and then it would be connected to what follows it; that is: but Iblis was not among those who prostrated.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 12:

﴿Said﴾ is a resumptive statement (isti'naf), framed as an answer to a question arising from the narration of his not prostrating, as if it were said: "What did Allah, exalted is He, say then?" It is from this that the shift to the third person (iltifat ila al-ghayba) becomes apparent, since there is no reason to frame the question in the form of direct address. There is another benefit in this, namely the indication that the narrated matter does not concern the addressees, as in the narration of the creation and the shaping (of Adam).

﴿What prevented you from prostrating?﴾ That is: from prostrating, as occurs in surah Sad (38). The "la" (not) is an emphatic supplement (za'ida mu'akkida) reinforcing the meaning of the verb it precedes, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so that the People of the Book may not know﴾ (57:29), alerting that the thing for which he is rebuked is the abandoning of prostration. It has also been said: the one prevented from something is diverted to its opposite, so the meaning is: "What turned you away so that you did not prostrate?"

﴿When I commanded you﴾. It has been said: this contains evidence that an absolute command implies obligation and immediacy. In surah al-Hijr: ﴿O Iblis, what is the matter with you that you are not among those who prostrate?﴾ (15:32), and in surah Sad: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating to what I created with My two hands?﴾ (38:75).

The variation of expressions in the narration indicates that the accursed one combined three disobediences in a single act: violating the command, separating himself from the community, and refusing to be counted among those brought near, together with arrogance and belittling Adam, peace be upon him. He was rebuked then for each of these, but in the narration in each place only what is mentioned there is stated, relying on what is mentioned in another place, and indicating that each of them is sufficient for the rebuke and for showing the falsehood of what he committed. The narration of the rebuke was omitted altogether in surah al-Baqarah, surah Bani Isra'il, surah al-Kahf and surah Ta-Ha.

﴿Said﴾ is a resumptive statement as before, based on a question arising from the narration of the rebuke, as if it were said: "What did the accursed one say at that?" So it was said: "He said."

﴿I am better than him﴾, deviating from matching his answer to the question by saying "I was prevented by such and such," and instead claiming for himself, by way of resumption, something whose implication for his refusal to prostrate, in his own view, is clear, and indicating that one whose nature is this does not fittingly prostrate to one lower than himself, so how could he fittingly be commanded to do so? This is what the words in surah al-Hijr point to: ﴿I was not going to prostrate to a human whom You created from clay of black, moulded mud﴾ (15:33). He was the first to lay the foundations of the edifice of arrogance, and to invent the doctrine of good and evil as rational (ʿaqli) categories.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You created me from fire and You created him from clay﴾ is a justification (ta'lil) for what he claimed of his superiority over him. The accursed one erred, in that he restricted the excellence to what pertains to the matter and the element, and overlooked what pertains to the agent, as indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating to what I created with My two hands?﴾, that is, without intermediary, in a manner of special care for him; and what pertains to the form, as alerted by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and I breathed into him of My spirit﴾ (15:29); and what pertains to the final purpose, which is the crux of the matter. For this reason the angels were commanded to prostrate to him, peace be upon him, when it became evident to them that he was more knowledgeable than them regarding what the matter of the caliphate on earth revolves around, and that he had attributes not belonging to anyone else. In the verse there is evidence of generation and corruption (al-kawn wa al-fasad), and that the devils are existing bodies. Perhaps the attribution of the creation of humans to clay and of the devils to fire is by considering the predominant component.

Abu al-Su'ud, Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim, on surah 7, verse 13:

﴿He said﴾: this is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), as explained before.

The fa' (fa) in His words, exalted is He, ﴿Then descend from it﴾ indicates that the command follows from what became apparent from the accursed one (la'een): his opposition to the command, his giving false reasons (ta'lil) for it with falsehoods (abatil), and his persistence in that. That is: ﴿descend from it﴾, meaning from the Garden (Jannah). The pronoun is given before the Garden is mentioned because it was well known that he was one of its inhabitants.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both, said: they were in 'Adn, not in the Garden of Eternity (Jannat al-Khuld). It was also said: he was among the honoured ranks of the angels (malaikah al-mu'azzazin), for leaving their company is a descent, and what a descent it is. In Surah al-Hijr: ﴿Then go out from it﴾.

As for what has been said, that the intended meaning is descent from the heaven, it is refuted by the fact that his whispering to Adam, peace be upon him, took place after this expulsion. So it must be understood in one of the two senses definitively, and his whispering in the first sense would be by way of calling out from the gate of the Garden, as narrated from al-Hasan al-Basri.

His words, exalted is He, ﴿It is not for you﴾: that is, it is not proper for you, nor does it befit you, nor does it suit your station.

﴿To be arrogant therein﴾: that is, in the Garden, or among the ranks of the angels. This is a reason (ta'lil) for the command to descend, for the impropriety of being arrogant therein is a cause for the stated command, since it is the place of the obedient and humble. There is no indication in this that arrogance is permitted elsewhere. In it there is a warning that arrogance does not befit the people of the Garden, and that Allah, exalted is He, expelled him only because of his arrogance, not merely because of his disobedience.

His words, exalted is He, ﴿So go out﴾: an emphasis on the command to descend, branching from its cause.

His words, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed you are among the debased﴾: a reason for the command to leave, indicating that it is because of his arrogance; that is, among the humiliated and those of abasement before Allah, exalted is He, and before His friends, because of your arrogance.

It is reported from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: "Whoever humbles himself for Allah, Allah raises his wisdom (hikmah)," and he said: "Lift yourself up, may Allah lift up your [low] state (na'sh)." And whoever is arrogant and transgresses his bounds, Allah presses him down to the earth.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 14:

﴿Qāla﴾ (He said) is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), as has been explained before, constructed in answer to a question arising from what precedes it. It is as if it were said: "What did the accursed one say after hearing this emphatic expulsion?" So it was said: "He said."

﴿Anẓirnī﴾ (Grant me respite); that is: give me a delay and do not cause me to die.

﴿Ilā yawmi yub'athūn﴾ (Until the day they are resurrected); that is: Adam and his offspring, for recompense after their annihilation, and this is the time of the second blast (al-nafkha al-thāniya). The accursed one intended by this to find a breathing space in misleading them, to take his revenge upon them, and to escape death, since it becomes impossible after the resurrection.

﴿He said﴾ is a resumptive statement, as has been explained before.

﴿Indeed, you are among those given respite﴾. The answer comes in a nominal sentence, and it covers what the others asked for, in a way that suggests the questioner is following them in this. It is explicit that this is an announcement of the respite that was decreed for them from eternity, not a fresh granting of a particular respite in answer to his supplication. And his request for respite was a request to delay death, since through it he would become one of them, not a request to delay punishment, as has been said. That is: you are among those whose terms were deferred from eternity, as the creative wisdom requires, until the time of the end, excepting what God the Exalted has excluded from the creatures, namely the first blast, until the time of resurrection, which is what is asked about.

The timing has been omitted for brevity, relying on what occurred in Surat al-Hijr and Surat Sad, just as mention of the call has been omitted.

The fa' (then) in the request for respite and in the granting of it is based on what was mentioned in those two surahs in His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿My Lord, then give me respite until the day they are raised﴾ ﴿He said, "Then indeed you are among those given respite"﴾ ﴿until the day of the known time﴾. In granting him respite there is a trial for the servants and an opportunity for reward.

If you say: there is no doubt that the speech reported from one who utters it has, at the time of its utterance, a specific situation that requires it to come in a particular form of arrangement, such that if any part of that is neglected, the speech falls entirely from the rank of eloquence. So a single speech reported in various forms, if the situation requires it to come in one specific form among those forms that occur in reporting, then that form is the one that fits what the situation requires and reaches the rank of eloquence, to the exclusion of the other forms. Once this is established, we say: it is not hidden that the respite-request of the accursed one was issued from him only once and no more. So if his station required the display of humility, and the ordering of the request for respite upon what befell him of curse and expulsion, in the manner of seeking restoration in return for breaking, as is evident from his saying "My Lord, then give me respite," as was related of him in the two surahs, then what is related here would be far from matching what the situation requires, let alone ascending to the heights of inimitability. We say: the station of his request for respite does require what was mentioned, namely the display of humility and the ordering of the request for respite upon the deprivation indicated by the expulsion and stoning. Likewise, the station of the granting of respite requires ordering the announcement of the respite upon the request for it. The speech was arranged on this in those two surahs, and each of the two stations, that of the reporting and that of what is reported, was given its full due.

As for here, since the station of reporting required merely the announcement of the request for respite and the granting of it, the reporting was delivered in a manner of brevity and conciseness, without addressing how each of them occurred in the course of address and dialogue. If you say: then that would not be a transmission of the speech as it is, nor would it match what the station requires. We say: what must be observed in transmitting speech is only its original meaning and the very content it conveys. As for the manner in which it conveys that, this is by no means something that must be observed in transmission; rather, it may or may not be observed, according to what the station requires.

Stripping the speech of these manners does not harm its original content. Rather, in transmitting it, manners and particulars may be observed that the speaker himself did not observe at all, and that does not impair the transmitted text being the original meaning. Do you not see that all the statements transmitted in the Noble Qur'an are reported with manners and considerations that the one who uttered them could not necessarily have been able to observe, for otherwise it would have been possible for an inimitable speech to issue from a human being, in case what is reported was speech.

As for its failure to match what the situation requires, its source is heedlessness toward what must be fully supplied of the situational requirements. For the decisive matter is the station of reporting. As for the station in which the reported speech occurred, if its requirement agrees with the requirement of the station of reporting, each of the two stations is given its due, as in Surat al-Hijr and Surat Sad. For since the station of reporting in those two surahs required expanding the speech and detailing it according to the manners in which it occurred, the rights of both stations were observed together.

As for in this noble surah, since the station of reporting required brevity, its side was observed. Do you not see that when the addressed denier is one who understands only the original meaning, it is obligatory for the speaker to strip his speech of emphasis and the other special features and qualities that the situation requires, and to address him in the manner suited to him. Yet, despite that, he must intend an additional meaning that another eloquent hearer would understand, namely the stripping of it from those features, in observance of the requirement of the addressee's state of understanding. By this his speech rises above the rank of the cries of animals, as has been verified in its proper place. So if observing the station of reporting is obligatory even when it leads to stripping speech of features and qualities entirely, then what is your opinion on the obligation of observing it along with adorning the speech with other qualities by which it rises to the rank of inimitability? Especially when the right of the station of what is reported has been fulfilled in the two noble surahs, and this brevity was founded upon that and relied upon it.

**(p-219)** ﴿He said﴾: this is a resumptive sentence (istinaf), like those before it.

﴿So because You have sent me astray﴾: the *ba'* (ba', the preposition) here is for oath (qasam, swearing an oath), as in His saying, ﴿By Your might, I will surely mislead them all﴾. His sending him astray (ighwa'uhu ta'ala iyyahu) is one of the effects of His power, and one of the rulings of His dominion, so the swearing by either of them amounts to the same thing. It may be that the accursed one swore by both of them together, and so one report mentions his oath by one of them and another report by the other.

The *fa'* (fa', the particle of consequence) indicates that the content of the sentence follows from the granting of respite (al-in-zar). The *ma* is verbal-masdarial (masdariyyah), meaning: "So I swear by Your sending me astray, ﴿that I will surely sit in wait for them﴾." Alternatively, the *ba'* expresses causation (sababiyyah), with the *ba'* attached to the deleted verb of oath, not to His saying, ﴿I will surely sit in wait for them﴾ as in the first reading, because the *lam* prevents that. The meaning is: "Because of Your sending me astray, for their sake, I swear by Your might that I will surely sit in wait for Adam and his descendants, lying in ambush for them, as highwaymen sit in wait for travelers on the road to rob them."

﴿Your straight path﴾: the path that leads to Paradise, which is the religion of Islam. Thus "sitting" (qu'ud) is a figurative usage (majaz) that branches out from an allusion (kinayah). Its accusative case is adverbial of place (zarfiyyah), as in the line of poetry:

*"As the fox hurries along the road."*

It is also said that it is accusative by the removal of the preposition, its estimated form being "on Your path," as in your saying: "Zayd was struck on the back and the belly."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 17:

﴿Then I will surely come to them from before them and from behind them and from their right and from their left﴾; that is, from the four directions from which an enemy customarily attacks, like his intent to beguile and mislead them from whatever direction is made easy by an enemy's approach from the four directions. For this reason, He did not mention above and below.

And from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "From before them" means from the direction of the Hereafter; "from behind them" means from the direction of this world; "from their right and from their left" means from the direction of their good deeds and their bad deeds.

It has also been said: "From before them" means from where they know and are able to guard against it; "from behind them" means from where they neither know nor are able [to guard]; "from their right and from their left" means from where it is easy for them to know and guard against it, but they did not do so due to their lack of vigilance and caution; and from where that is not easy for them. The verb was made to govern the first two with the preposition of origin (min), because it comes toward them from those two directions; and the other two with the preposition of passing beside ('an), because the one who comes from those two sides is like one who turns aside and passes by them, going across their width. A parallel to this is: "I sat to the side of his right (jalastu 'an yamînihi)."

﴿And You will not find most of them grateful﴾; that is, obedient. He said this as a guess, based on the words of the Most High: ﴿And Iblis did confirm his assumption about them﴾, because he saw in them the beginning of evil as manifold and the beginning of good as single. It has also been said: he heard it from the angels, peace be upon them.

"﴿Said﴾ — a resumptive (istinaf) clause, as has occurred many times before.

﴿Get out from it﴾; i.e., from the Garden, or from the heaven, or from among the angels.

﴿Disgraced﴾; i.e., disgraced, from dhamma-hu (ذَأمَهُ): when one blames him. It is also read as "madhuman" (مَذُومًا), like "masul" in "masul" [mas'ul], or like "makul" in "makil," from dhama-hu, yadhimu-hu, dhaiman.

﴿Banished﴾: expelled.

﴿Whoever follows you among them﴾: the lam (لَام) here is a preparatory lam (al-lam al-muwatti'ah) for the oath and its answer.

﴿I will surely fill Hell with you all﴾: this stands in place of the answer of the conditional clause. It is also read "liman tabi'aka" (لِمَن تَبِعَكَ) with a kasra on the lam, in which case it is the predicate of "la-amla'anna" [the lam here marks the oath], meaning: this threat is for whoever follows you; or it is a reason for "ukhruj." "La-amla'anna" is then the answer to an omitted oath. The meaning of "minkum" (مِنكم) is: from you (sing.) and from them, by giving precedence to the addressee (taghlib al-mukhatab)."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 19:

﴿And O Adam﴾; that is: "and We said," as occurred in Surat al-Baqarah. (p-220) The opening of the speech with the vocative (nida') serves to alert the listener to the importance of receiving what is commanded, and the address is specifically directed to him, peace be upon him, to indicate his primacy in receiving the revelation and in carrying out what is commanded.

﴿Dwell, you and your spouse, in the Garden﴾: this is from sakan (dwelling), which is an expression for remaining, settling and residing, not from sukun (stillness), which is the opposite of motion. And "anta" (you) is a pronoun emphasized to make the hidden pronoun in "uskun" (dwell) valid as the object of the conjunction (ma'tuf) upon it.

The fa' (so) in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So eat from wherever you wish of it﴾ serves to explain the intended meaning of His saying in Surat al-Baqarah, ﴿And eat from it in abundance wherever you wish﴾, namely that this was a joint permission together with an ordering (of sequence). His saying ﴿from wherever you wish﴾ means: "from it, wherever you wish." "Raghadan" (in abundance) is not mentioned here, relying on what was mentioned there. The address is directed to both of them to generalize the honour and to indicate their equality in carrying out what is commanded, since Hawwa' is an example for him, peace be upon him, with regard to eating, unlike dwelling, where she follows him.

Because the prohibition is explicitly attached to the tree in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And do not approach this tree﴾, it was also read as "hadhi" (this), which is the original form, its diminutive being "dhiyya," and the ha' is a substitute for the ya'.

﴿And you will be among the wrongdoers﴾: it is either jazm (apocopated) by way of conjunction (ma'tuf), or nasb (accusative) as an answer (jawab) to the preceding command.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 20:**

﴿So Satan whispered to them﴾; that is, he performed whispering (waswasa) for their sake, or he spoke to them a hidden, repeated, successive speech. Whispering (waswasa) originally means a hidden sound, such as the faint murmur and rustling, and from it comes "the ornament whispered" (waswasa al-hilyu). Its manner has already been explained in Surat al-Baqara.

﴿That he might reveal to them﴾; that is, that he might make manifest to them. The lam here indicates consequence (al-lam li-l-'aqiba), or it indicates purpose (al-lam li-l-gharad), on the basis that he intended by his whispering that it would distress them by the exposure of their two private parts (sawatayhima). For this reason they were referred to by the word "private parts" (sau'a). In this is evidence that uncovering the private parts in privacy and in front of a spouse, without need, is ugly and detestable in human nature.

﴿What was concealed from them of their private parts﴾: what was covered and hidden from them of their nakedness (awra), and they did not see it on themselves nor one of them on the other. The waw, being pronounced, was not changed into a hamza in the well-known reading, as it was changed in "Uwaysil," the diminutive of Wasil, because the second letter is a long vowel (mudda). It has also been read as "sawatihima" with the hamza omitted and its vowel transferred to the waw, and with it converted into a waw and the resulting quiescent waw assimilated into it.

﴿And he said﴾: a conjunction upon "whispered," by way of explanation (bayan).

﴿"Your Lord has forbidden you from this tree"﴾; that is, from eating it.

﴿"Only lest you become two angels"﴾; that is, only out of aversion to your becoming two angels.

﴿"Or become of the eternal ones"﴾, those who do not die, or who abide forever in Paradise. There is no indication in this of the superiority of the angels, peace be upon them, since it is known that realities do not change. Their desire was only that there should be attained for them the attributes of the angels, namely the innate perfections and independence from food and drink. That is far from indicating superiority in the disputed sense.

Translation:

﴿And he swore to them, "Indeed, I am to you among the sincere advisors."﴾ That is: he swore to them. The form (qāsama, "to swear to one another / to share an oath") is of mutual striving (al-mughālaba), for emphasis (lil-mubālagha). It is also said: they both swore to him that they accepted (his counsel). And it is also said: they said to him, "Will you swear by Allah that you are indeed among the sincere advisors?" and he swore to them, so that this was made a mutual swearing (muqāsama).

(p-221) ﴿So he brought them down﴾: He lowered them to the eating from the tree. This indicates that He caused them to descend by that act from a lofty rank, since *tadliya* and *idla'* both mean sending something down from above to below.

﴿by deception﴾: by what He deceived them with through the oath. They assumed that no one swears by Allah falsely, or they were engaged in deception.

﴿When they tasted the tree, their private parts became apparent to them﴾: that is, when they found its taste and began eating from it, punishment and the ill consequence of disobedience seized them. Their clothing fell away from them, and their nakedness became visible to them. Scholars differ over whether the tree was the ear of grain, the grapevine, or something else, and over whether the clothing was light or nails.

﴿and they began to patch﴾: *Ṭafiqa* (طَفِقَ) is one of the verbs of beginning and continuing (*af'al al-shuru'*), like *akhadha*, *ja'ala*, *anshaʾa*, *ʿallaqa*, *habba* and *inbarā*. That is, they started to mend and stick one leaf upon another.

﴿over themselves from the leaves of the Garden﴾: It is said that these were fig leaves. It is also read *yakhṣifāni* from *akhṣafa*, meaning "they patch themselves"; and *yukhaṣṣifāni* from *takhṣīf*. The root of *yakhṣifāni* is *yakhtaṣifāni*.

﴿And their Lord called out to them﴾: the Owner of their affair, by way of reproach and rebuke.

﴿Did I not forbid you﴾: this explains the calling, so it has no place in the grammatical analysis (*i'rab*), or it is the object of an omitted verb: that is, He said, or saying: Did I not forbid you...

﴿from that tree﴾: the demonstrative carries the sense of distance, because it refers to the tree which they were forbidden to approach.

﴿And did I not say to you﴾: conjoined with "did I not forbid you"; that is, did I not say to you...

﴿Indeed Satan is a clear enemy to you﴾: this is reproach and rebuke for being deceived by the words of the enemy, just as the first was reproach for opposing the prohibition. It is said that this shows that an unqualified prohibition implies prohibition in the strict sense. *Lakum* is linked to *ʿaduww* because it contains the sense of a verb, or it is linked to an omitted element that is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from *ʿaduww*. This view is not reported here, but it is reported in Surat Ta-Ha with His words: ﴿Indeed this is an enemy to you and to your wife...﴾ up to the end of the verse.

It is narrated that He, exalted is He, said to Adam: "Did I not give you among the trees of the Garden an alternative to this tree?" He said: "Yes, by Your might, but I did not think that any of Your creation would swear by You falsely." He said: "By My might, I will surely bring you down to the earth, and then you will not obtain a living except with toil." So he was brought down, and he was taught the craft of iron. He was commanded to till the land, so he tilled, irrigated and harvested, threshed and winnowed, and kneaded and baked.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 23:

﴿They said: "Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves"﴾; that is, we harmed them by disobedience and by exposing ourselves to being expelled from the Garden.

﴿And if You do not forgive us﴾ that,

﴿and have mercy on us, we will surely be among the losers﴾. This is evidence that minor sins are punished if they are not forgiven. The Mu'tazilah said: it is not permissible to punish for them when major sins are avoided. For this reason they interpreted their saying ﴿that﴾ as referring to the habits of the muqarrabun (those brought near), who magnify minor misdeeds and belittle great good deeds.

﴿Said﴾ — a resumptive statement (istiʼnaf), as has been mentioned many times before.

﴿Go down﴾ — an address to Adam, Eve and their progeny, or to the two of them and Iblis. The command was repeated for him (Iblis) as a follower of the two of them, to make known that they are companions forever. Or it is reported what He said to them separately, as in His saying: ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things﴾. Here the acceptance of their repentance is not mentioned, relying on what is mentioned in the other places.

﴿Some of you are enemies to others﴾ — a circumstantial clause (jumlah ḥāliyyah) from the subject of "go down"; that is: hostile to one another.

﴿And for you on the earth is a dwelling place﴾ — that is: settled residence, or a place of settlement.

﴿And provision﴾ — that is: enjoyment and benefit.

﴿For a time﴾ — this is the time of the end of your terms (ājāl).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 25:

﴿He said﴾ The resumption (istinaf, a sentence that begins a new statement without grammatical connection to what precedes it) is repeated. It is either to signal that what follows is not connected to what came before, as in His saying, ﴿He said: "What is your business, O messengers?"﴾ after His saying, ﴿He said: "Who despairs of the mercy of his Lord except the astray?"﴾ (p-222), and His saying, ﴿He said: "Have you considered this one whom You have honored above me?"﴾ after His saying, ﴿He said: "Shall I prostrate to one whom You created from clay?"﴾.

Or it is to show the importance given to the content of what follows, His saying, ﴿Therein you will live, therein you will die, and from it you will be brought forth﴾. That is, it is for the requital, as in His saying, ﴿From it We created you, into it We will return you, and from it We will bring you forth once more﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 26:

﴿O children of Adam!﴾ This is an address to all of mankind, and the reason for addressing them with this title is not hidden.

﴿We have sent down to you clothing﴾; that is, We created it for you through heavenly arrangements and causes descending from them. A parallel to this is ﴿And He sent down for you of the cattle...﴾ and so on, and His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And We sent down iron﴾.

﴿Covering your private parts﴾, which Iblis intended to expose from your two parents, until they were compelled to stick leaves together, while you are free of needing that.

It is narrated that the Arabs used to circumambulate the House naked, saying: "We will not circumambulate in garments in which we have disobeyed God, the Exalted." So this was revealed. Perhaps the mention of the story of Adam, peace be upon him, at that point is to signal that the exposure of nakedness was the first evil that befell humanity from the side of Satan, and that he misled them in this just as he misled their two parents.

﴿And as finery﴾, and clothing with which you adorn yourselves. Al-rīsh (plumage, finery) means beauty; it was also said to mean wealth, and from it comes the expression "tarayyasha al-rajul," meaning he became wealthy. It is also read as ﴿ri'āsh﴾, which is the plural of rīsh, like sha'b and sha'āb.

﴿And the clothing of righteousness﴾; that is, the fear of God, the Exalted. It was also said to mean faith, it was said to mean good bearing, and it was said to mean armour for war.

Its nominative case is due to it being the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is the clause ﴿that is better﴾; or it is a predicate with "that" as its attribute, as if it were said: "And the clothing of righteousness, to which reference is made, is better." It is also read as ﴿wa-libāsa al-taqwā﴾ in the accusative, coordinated with ﴿libāsan﴾.

﴿That﴾; that is, the sending down of clothing.

﴿Is among the signs of God﴾, indicating His great bounty and His all-encompassing mercy.

﴿That perhaps they may take heed﴾, so that they recognise His blessing, or so that they admonish themselves and thereby refrain from vile deeds.

﴿O children of Adam﴾: The repetition of the address signals the great care taken with the content it introduces. As for the reason they are addressed with this title, it is not hidden.

﴿Let not Satan tempt you﴾: That is, let him not bring you into temptation and trial by preventing you from entering Paradise.

﴿as he caused your parents to leave Paradise﴾: This is an adjective (*na't*) modifying an elided verbal noun (*masdar*). That is, "Let him not tempt you with a temptation like the expulsion of your parents." It is also permissible to take the implied sense as: "Let him not drive you out by his temptation an expulsion like his expulsion of your parents." Although the prohibition is directed at Satan, in reality it is directed at the addressees, as in your saying, "Let me not see you here." This has been verified many times before.

﴿stripping them of their clothing to show them their private parts﴾: This is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring either to your parents or to the subject of "caused to leave." The attribution of the stripping to him is causative (*li-l-tasbib*). The use of the present tense is to bring the scene vividly to mind.

As for His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, he and his tribe see you from where you cannot see them﴾: That is, his soldiers and offspring. This is a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*) giving the reason for the prohibition and emphasizing the warning against him.

﴿from where you cannot see them﴾: "Min" indicates the starting point of the seeing, and "haythu" is an adverb of place denoting the location where seeing is absent. The clause "you cannot see them" stands in the genitive position by the adverb's annexation to it. Their seeing us from where we do not see them does not necessitate the impossibility of our seeing them absolutely, nor the impossibility of their taking forms visible to us.

﴿Indeed, We made the devils﴾: His tribe is counted among them, so the plural is used.

"Those who do not believe": That is, We made them, by the affinity We established between them, or by sending them upon them and empowering them to mislead them and to drive them toward what they have made attractive to them, "allies," that is, companions imposed upon them. The sentence is another reason for the prohibition and a further emphasis on the warning following a warning.

﴿وَإذا فَعَلُوا فاحِشَةً﴾ is an independent sentence (*jumlah mubtada'ah*) with no place in *i'rab* (grammatical analysis, the case-endings and syntactic function of words). It has also been permitted to treat it as coordinated (*'atf*) with the relative clause (*silah*, the clause that completes a relative). *Al-fahishah* is an act that is extremely ugly. The *ta'* (ة) is there either because the word is treated as modifying a feminine noun, or because it marks the transfer of the word from being an adjective (*wasfiyyah*) to being a noun (*ismiyyah*). What is meant by it is the worship of idols and the uncovering of the private parts during the circumambulation (*tawaf*) and similar practices.

﴿قالُوا﴾ is an answer to those who forbade them from it.

﴿وَجَدْنا عَلَيْها آباءَنا واللَّهُ أمَرَنا بِها﴾ They argue with two claims: the imitation (*taqlid*) of their fathers, and the fabrication of lies against God, glory be to Him. Perhaps the placing of the preceding element first is to signal, on their part, that their fathers were only doing it by God's command to do it. Furthermore, the pronoun in ﴿أمَرَنا﴾ refers to them and to their fathers.

Then the reason for turning away from the first claim in refuting their statement becomes clear, in the words of the Exalted: ﴿قُلْ إنَّ اللَّهَ لا يَأْمُرُ بِالفَحْشاءِ﴾ [Say: Indeed God does not command immorality]. His habitual practice, exalted is He, is to command good deeds and to urge the pursuit of praiseworthy qualities. There is no indication in this that the ugliness of an act, in the sense that blame attaches to it in this world and punishment in the next, is rational (*'aqli*, known by reason alone). The meaning of *al-fahishah* is what the sound natural disposition (*tab'*) recoils from and what upright reason considers deficient.

It was also said: these two are answers to two sequential questions, as if it was said, when they had done it: "Why did you do it?" They said: "We found our fathers doing it." It was then said: "Why did your fathers do it?" They said: "God commanded us to do it." On both interpretations, imitation is prohibited when evidence contrary to it has been established, not absolutely.

﴿أتَقُولُونَ عَلى اللَّهِ ما لا تَعْلَمُونَ﴾ is part of the speech that was commanded. The interrogative particle *hamzah* (*al-hamzah*) serves to deny the act that has occurred and to declare it ugly. The denial and rebuke are directed at their saying, about God, what they do not know to have come from Him, exalted is He, even though some of them know that it did not come from Him. This is an exaggeration in denying that form of speech. For the attribution to Him, exalted is He, of what is not known to have come from Him is reprehensible when it is an abomination, so the attribution to Him, mighty and majestic, of what is known not to have come from Him is even more ugly and more deserving of denial.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 29:

﴿Say: My Lord has commanded justice.﴾ This is an explanation of what is commanded, following the negation of the matters whose command was attributed to Him, Exalted is He, among the things that are forbidden. Al-qist (justice) is al-'adl (equity), and it is the middle course of every thing, keeping away from the two extremes of excess (ifrat) and neglect (tafrit).

﴿And set your faces upright﴾, that is, turn toward His worship, being upright, not deviating toward anything else; or, set your faces upright toward the qiblah.

﴿At every place of prostration﴾, that is, at every time of prostration or place of prostration, which is the prayer; or in any mosque at which the prayer has come upon you, and do not delay it until you return to your mosques.

﴿And call upon Him﴾, that is, worship Him.

﴿Making your religion sincerely His﴾; that is, the obedience, for your return is to Him in the Hereafter.

﴿As He originated you﴾; that is, He brought you into being at first.

﴿You will return﴾ to Him by His bringing you back, so that He may recompense you for your deeds. The return was likened to the origination only to affirm its possibility and His power over it. It has been said: as He originated you from dust, you will return to it. It has been said: barefoot, naked, uncircumcised, you will return to Him. It has been said: as He originated you believing and disbelieving, He will restore you.(p-224)

﴿A group He guided﴾, by enabling them to have faith.

﴿And a group upon whom misguidance was justly decreed﴾, in accordance with the preceding decree (al-qada' al-sabiq), which follows the will (al-mashi'ah) that is grounded in consummate wisdoms. Its being in the accusative (intisabuhu) is due to an implied verb that the following clause explains; that is, "and He forsook a group."

﴿Indeed, they took the devils as allies besides Allah﴾ is a causal explanation of His forsaking them, or a confirmation of their misguidance.

﴿And they think that they are guided﴾ indicates that the disbelieving one who errs and the stubborn one are equal in deserving blame. The distinction between them may be taken to refer to the one who is negligent in reflection (al-muqassir fi al-nazar).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 31:

﴿O Children of Adam, take your adornment﴾; i.e., your clothing, to cover your nakedness.

﴿at every place of worship﴾; i.e., at circumambulation (tawaf) or prayer. It is part of the Sunnah that a man take his best appearance for prayer. And in it is evidence for the obligation of covering the nakedness (sitr al-'awrah) in prayer.

﴿And eat and drink﴾ of what is good for you. It is narrated that the Banu 'Amir, during their days of Hajj, would not eat food except in small quantities (qut), and would not eat fat, glorifying their Hajj by doing so. The Muslims then intended to do the same, and this verse was revealed.

﴿And do not be excessive﴾ by forbidding what is lawful, or by transgressing into what is unlawful, or by overindulgence in food and greed for it. And it is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: "Eat what you wish, so long as two qualities do not mislead you: extravagance (israf) and vanity (makhilah)." And 'Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn Waqid said: "Allah gathered medicine (al-tibb) into half a verse, when He said: ﴿And eat and drink, and do not be excessive﴾."

﴿Indeed, He does not love the excessive﴾; i.e., He does not approve of their conduct.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 32:**

﴿Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah﴾ from clothing and whatever one beautifies oneself with.

﴿which He has brought forth for His servants﴾ from plants, such as cotton and flax; from animals, such as silk and wool; and from metals, such as coats of mail.

﴿and the good things of provision﴾; that is, the pleasant things of food and drink. This indicates that the basic principle regarding foods, clothing, and all kinds of adornment is permissibility (al-ibahah), because the interrogation in "مِن" (man, "who") is a denial (istifham inkari, an interrogation expressing rejection).

﴿Say: They are for those who believed in the life of this world﴾ primarily, while the disbelievers, though they share in them, do so only secondarily (bi-al-tabi', by way of subordination).

﴿purely for them on the Day of Resurrection﴾, with none of others sharing in them. Its case-ending (intisab) is that of the circumstantial accusative (al-haliyyah, a grammatical state of the subject), and it has been read in the nominative (bi-al-raf'), in which case it is a predicate (khabar) following another predicate.

﴿Thus do We detail the signs for a people who know﴾; that is, in the same manner as this detailing, We detail all the rulings for a people who know the subtle and refined meanings contained within them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 33:

﴿Say: My Lord has only forbidden indecencies, what is apparent of them and what is concealed﴾; i.e., those sins whose ugliness is extreme. It has also been said: those of them that relate to the private parts.

﴿what is apparent of them and what is concealed﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "indecencies"; i.e., their open and their secret forms.

﴿and sin﴾; i.e., that which entails sin. This is a generalization after a specification. It has also been said: it is the drinking of wine.

﴿and transgression﴾; i.e., injustice or arrogance. It is mentioned separately for the sake of emphasis (mubalagha) in deterring from it.

﴿without right﴾ is connected to "transgression" and emphasizes its meaning.

﴿and that you associate with Allah that for which He has sent down no authority﴾ is a mockery of the polytheists and an alert to the prohibition of following what no proof supports.

﴿and that you say about Allah what you do not know﴾ by deviating (ilhad) concerning His attributes and fabricating against Him, such as their saying: "Allah commanded us to do it." The directing of the prohibition to their saying about Him, exalted is He, what they do not know to have occurred, and not to what they know not to have occurred, has already had its secret explained.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 34:

﴿And for every nation﴾ of the destroyed nations.

﴿A term (ajal)﴾: a specific, fixed span of time appointed for their destruction.
