﴿So when their term comes﴾: if the pronoun is taken to refer to the nations implied by "every nation," then the explicit mention of "term" as a genitive-modified noun serves to convey the intended meaning, which is that every nation reaches its own particular term and that it comes to them. This is achieved through the term acquiring generality by means of the annexation, which conveys the sense of plurality, as if it were said: "When their terms come to them, such that each of those nations has its own particular term come to it."

And if "for every nation" is taken as referring specifically to each nation, as is the apparent meaning, then the explicit noun in place of the pronoun is for the sake of added emphasis, and the annexation to the pronoun serves to convey the most complete specification; that is: when its own particular term comes to it.

﴿They will not delay﴾ from that term.

﴿An hour﴾: that is, a small portion of time. It is an expression for extreme brevity of time. That is: they will not be delayed at all. The form of the verb (istif'al) indicates their helplessness and deprivation of that, despite their seeking it.

﴿Nor will they advance﴾: that is, nor will they go ahead of it. This is conjoined to "they will not delay," but not to indicate the negation of advancing while it is possible in itself as delay is; rather it is for the sake of emphasizing the negation of delay by placing it in the category of what is rationally impossible, as in His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿And repentance is not for those who commit evil deeds until, when death approaches one of them, he says, "Indeed, I have repented now," nor for those who die while they are disbelievers﴾. For whoever dies as a disbeliever, while it is clear that he has no repentance at all, has been placed in the category of non-acceptance alongside one who postpones it until the presence of death, signifying that the existence of repentance at that time and its non-existence are entirely equal.

It was said: the intended meaning of "coming" is "approaching," such that it is possible to advance in some respect, like the coming of the day that was appointed for their destruction, in which there is an hour. But this is not the case. And the mention of the negation of postponement first is because the primary purpose is to state that they will not escape the punishment.

As for what is in His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿No nation precedes its term, nor do they delay﴾, with the precedence of "precede" being mentioned first, that is because the purpose there is to explain the secret of delaying their destruction despite their deserving it, as indicated by His saying: ﴿Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves, and let hope divert them; they will soon know﴾. Therefore, the more important matter there is to explain the negation of precedence.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 35:

﴿O Children of Adam﴾: a shift in address (talwin al-khitab), directed to all of mankind, out of concern for the matter contained within its scope.

﴿If there come to you﴾: here "in" (in, the conditional particle) has "ma" (ma) added to it to emphasize the meaning of the condition. For this reason the verb after it is required to take the heavy nun or the light nun. This also serves as a reminder that the sending of messengers is something permissible (jaiz), not something rationally obligatory (wajib 'aqlan).

﴿messengers from among you﴾: the prepositional phrase "min" (from) is connected to an omitted element that is a qualifier (sifa) of "messengers"; that is, they are of your own kind (ka'inun min jinsikum).

And His words: ﴿who recite to you My signs﴾ are another qualifier of "messengers"; that is, they make clear to you My rulings and My laws.

And His words, exalted is He: ﴿So whoever fears God and makes amends, there shall be no fear for them, nor shall they grieve﴾ are a conditional sentence that stands as the response (jawab) to the condition (al-shart); that is, whoever among you fears (ittaqa) rejecting (al-takdhib) and makes his deeds right (aslaha 'amalahu), then there is no fear... etc. (p-226)

Likewise is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who denied Our signs and turned arrogantly away from them, those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.﴾ That is, "And those among you who denied Our signs." The mention of *al-ittiqa'* (guarding oneself against wrongdoing, taqwa) in the first clause indicates that the basis of *al-falah* (success) is not merely the absence of denial, but *al-ittiqa'* and *al-ijtinab* (keeping away) from it. The insertion of the *fa'* (the particle "then") in the first response clause but not the second is for emphasis in the promise and leniency in the threat.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 37:

﴿Who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah or denies His signs?﴾; that is: he who attributes to Him what He has not said, or denies what He has said; that is, he is more unjust than every unjust person. Its verification has been discussed repeatedly before.

﴿Those﴾ is a reference to the relative pronoun (al-mawsul), and the plural is used in view of its meaning, just as the singular of the two verbs is used in view of its wording. The sense of distance in it is to indicate their persistence in evil condition; that is: those described with what was mentioned of fabrication and denial.

﴿Their share from the Book will reach them﴾; that is, of what has been written for them of provisions and lifespans. It has also been said: "the Book" is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh); that is, what has been recorded for them in it.

In either case, "min" (from) is the partitive/initial min (min al-ibtida'iyyah), related to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause (hal) describing "their share"; that is: their share reaching them being from the Book. It has also been said: their share is of the punishment, and of blackness of the face, and of blueness of the eyes.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them: "Blackness of the face is written for one who fabricates against Allah." He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection you will see those who lied against Allah, their faces blackened﴾.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Until, when Our messengers come to them﴾; that is: the Angel of Death and his assistants.

﴿Taking their souls﴾; that is: while they are taking their souls. This supports the first view. For although "hatta" (until) is the particle with which speech begins, it is nonetheless a limit (ghayah) for what precedes it. So their share must be of what they enjoy until the time of their death; that is: their share from the Book reaches them until the angels of death come to them. When they come, ﴿they will say﴾ to them:

﴿Where is what you used to invoke besides Allah?﴾; that is: where are the deities you used to worship in the worldly life? The "ma" was written conjoined with "ayna" in the Qur'anic script, though by rule it should be separated, because it is a relative pronoun.

﴿They will say﴾: a resumptive clause (isti'naf) occurring as an answer to a question arising from the narration of the messengers' question, as if it were said: "What did they say at that time?" So it was said: "They said."

﴿They have gone astray from us﴾; that is: they have vanished from us; that is, we do not know their whereabouts.

﴿And they will bear witness against themselves﴾ is coordinated with "they said"; that is: they will acknowledge against themselves.

﴿That they were﴾; that is: in the worldly life.

﴿Disbelievers﴾: worshipping what does not deserve worship at all, since they witnessed its condition and its misguidance. Perhaps by the time of the coming of the messengers and the state of death is meant the extended period from the beginning of the coming and the taking of souls until its end on the Day of Recompense; based on the certainty of the coming, and the taking of souls throughout all that time as a continuing state, even if their occurrence is only at its beginning. Or it is intended to show the extreme swiftness of the occurrence of the Resurrection and recompense, as if both were present at the beginning of the taking of souls, as indicated by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever dies, his resurrection has come." Otherwise, this question and answer and what follows from them, including the command to enter the Fire, and what took place among its people of mutual cursing and blaming, necessarily occur after the Resurrection.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 38:

﴿He will say﴾; i.e., Allah, Mighty and Majestic, on the Day of Resurrection, either directly or through the intermediary of an angel.

﴿Enter among nations that have passed away before you﴾; i.e., being among a company of nations, accompanying them.

﴿of jinn and humans﴾ meaning: the disbelievers of the earlier nations, of both kinds.

﴿into the Fire﴾ is connected to His saying: "enter."

﴿Every time a nation enters﴾ from the earlier and later nations therein.

﴿it curses its sister﴾ who went astray by following it.

﴿until, when they have all overtaken one another therein﴾; i.e., they catch up with one another and follow one another into the Fire.

﴿The last of them will say﴾ in entering or in rank, and they are the followers.

﴿about the first of them﴾; i.e., concerning them, since the address is to Allah the Exalted, not to them.

﴿Our Lord, these are the ones who misled us﴾; they set down misguidance for us, so we followed them.

﴿So give them a double punishment﴾; i.e., multiplied.

﴿of the Fire﴾ because they went astray and led others astray.

﴿He will say: "For each there is double"﴾: as for the leaders, it is because of the misguidance and leading astray mentioned; as for the followers, it is because of their disbelief and imitation.

﴿But you do not know﴾; i.e., what is for you and what is for each group of the punishment. It is also read with the letter ya' (﴿يَعْلَمُونَ﴾, "they do not know").

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 39:

﴿And the first of them said to the last of them﴾; i.e., addressing them.

﴿to the last of them﴾ when they heard God's answer to them.

﴿So you had no superiority over us﴾; i.e., it has been established that you have no superiority over us, and that we and you are equal in misguidance and in deserving the punishment.

﴿So taste the punishment﴾; i.e., the well-known punishment, the doubled one.

﴿for what you used to earn﴾ from the words of the leaders.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 40:

﴿Indeed, those who denied Our signs﴾ despite their clarity.

﴿and waxed arrogant towards them﴾; i.e., arrogant towards faith in them and acting in accordance with what they require.

﴿The gates of heaven will not be opened for them﴾; i.e., their supplications and their deeds will not be accepted, or their souls will not ascend to it, as is the case with the supplications, deeds and souls of the believers. The ta' in "tufattahu" (will be opened) is for the feminine plural "al-abwab" (the gates), and the doubling of the letter (shaddah) is for their multiplicity. It is also read with a single letter (tukhfif), and with a single letter and a ya' (yufattahu); and it is read in the active voice (building for the subject), with "al-abwab" in the accusative, the verb then referring to the signs (al-ayat); and with a ya' on the basis that it refers to God Most High.

﴿And they will not enter the Garden until the camel passes through the eye of the needle﴾; i.e., until what is a parable for great bulk enters what is known for narrowness of passage, namely the hole of a needle. In the fact that the camel is something whose nature does not include passing through the eye of a needle lies an exaggeration in expressing its improbability.

It is also read "al-jummal" (like "al-qummal"), "al-jamal" (like "al-nughar"), "al-jumal" (like "al-qufl"), "al-jumul" (like "al-nusub"), and "al-jaml" (like "al-habl"), which is a thick rope made of hemp (qunnab); and it has been said that it means the rope of a ship.

And "summ" (eye) is with a ḍammah and with a kasrah. It is also read "fi summ al-mikhyat" (in the eye of the sewing-needle), which is the sewing implement, i.e., that with which one sews, like "al-hizam" and "al-mihzam" (belt).

﴿Thus﴾; i.e., like that dreadful recompense.

﴿We recompense the criminals﴾; i.e., the class of criminals, and they are included in their company by primary inclusion.(p-228)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 41:

﴿For them there is a bed (mihad) of Hell beneath them﴾; that is, a bedding beneath them. The tanwin (nunation) in مِهادٌ is for magnification (tafkhim, emphasis), and the min in مِن جَهَنَّمَ is a min of abstraction (min tajridiyyah).

﴿And above them are coverings (ghawashin)﴾; that is, coverings. According to Sibawayh, the tanwin in غَواشٍ is a substitute (badal) for the omitted letter, due to i'lal (morphological alteration of a weak letter). According to others, it is for sarf (the full declension of the noun). It has also been read as غَواشِ, by disregarding the deleted element (ilgha' al-mahdhuf), as in the words of God, Exalted be He: ﴿And His are the ships sailing high (al-jawari al-munshaat)﴾.

﴿And thus﴾, that is, a punishment as severe as this.

﴿We recompense the wrongdoers﴾. He described them as "criminals" (al-mujrimin) at one point and as "wrongdoers" (al-zalimin) at another, to indicate that by their denial of the signs they possessed each of these two ugly attributes. The mention of crime together with being deprived of entering Paradise, and of wrongdoing together with being punished by the Fire, serves to alert the reader that this is the greatest of crimes and sins.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 42:

﴿وَالَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾: i.e., in Our signs (āyāt), or in everything that must be believed in. Thus the signs are included in it by way of primary inclusion.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحَاتِ﴾: i.e., the righteous deeds (al-a'māl al-ṣāliḥa) that were prescribed by the signs. This is in contrast to arrogance (al-istikbār) toward them.

﴿لَا نُكَلِّفُ نَفْسًا إِلَّا وُسْعَهَا﴾ is an i'tirāḍ (parenthetical interjection) placed between the mubtada' (subject), which is the al-mawṣūl (relative pronoun, الذين), and the khabar (predicate), which is the clause.

﴿أُولَئِكَ أَصْحَابُ الْجَنَّةِ﴾ is for encouragement (al-targhīb) to acquire that which leads to lasting bliss, by showing how easily it is attained and how readily it can be obtained. It was also read: (لَا تُكَلَّفُ نَفْسٌ) (no soul is burdened).

The demonstrative ism al-ishāra (أولئك, "those") is a mubtada', and aṣḥāb al-janna (أصحاب الجنة, "the companions of the Garden") is its khabar. The clause is the khabar of the first mubtada'. Alternatively, the demonstrative is a badal (apposition) to the first mubtada', which is the relative pronoun, and the khabar is aṣḥāb al-janna. What it contains of the meaning of distance (al-bu'd) signals the elevated rank of those people in excellence and nobility.

﴿هُمْ فِيهَا خَالِدُونَ﴾: a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) of aṣḥāb al-janna. It has also been permitted that it be a ḥāl of al-janna (the Garden), because it includes a pronoun referring to it. The governing element (al-'āmil) is the meaning of the idāfa (construct phrase), or the implied lām (al-lām al-muqaddara). Or it is a second khabar for ulā'ika according to the view of one who permits this. And fīhā (فيها, "in it") is related to khālidūn (خالدون, "abiding").

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 43:

﴿And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts.﴾ That is: We will extract from their hearts the causes of resentment, or We will purify their hearts of it, so that among them there will be nothing but mutual affection. The use of the past tense (ṣīghat al-māḍī) is to announce that this is certain and firmly established.

And from ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him: "Indeed, I hope that I, ʿUthmān, Ṭalḥa, and al-Zubayr will be among them."

﴿Rivers will flow beneath them.﴾ This is an addition to their pleasure and joy. The clause is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the pronoun in ṣudūrihim (their breasts), and the operating element (ʿāmil) is either the meaning of the annexation (idāfa), or the operating element within the annexed noun. Alternatively, it is a circumstantial clause of the subject of nazaʿnā (We removed), and the operating element is nazaʿnā. It has also been said that it is a resumptive (mustaʾnafa) clause, informing about the description of their states.

﴿And they will say: "Praise be to Allah, who has guided us to this.﴾ That is: to that for which this is the reward.

﴿And we would not have been guided﴾ That is: to this supreme goal, or to one of the goals of which this is part.

﴿Had Allah not guided us.﴾ That is: and granted us success in it. The lām is for emphasizing the negation. The answer to lawlā (had it not been) is omitted, relying on what precedes it to indicate it. The object of nahtadī (we would be guided) and the second object of hadānā are omitted (p-229) for the sake of clarity of meaning, or for the intention of generality as has been indicated. The clause is either resumptive or circumstantial. It has been recited as: (mā kunnā linahtadiya) etc., without the waw, in which case it is explanatory and elaborating of the first.

﴿Indeed, the messengers of our Lord came with the truth.﴾ This is the answer to an implied oath, which they uttered out of exultation and delight at what they had attained, and rejoicing at their faith, because the messengers, peace be upon them, had come to them.

The bāʾ in His statement, ﴿with the truth﴾, is either for transitivity, in which case it is connected to jāʾat (came), or for accompaniment, in which case it is connected to an implied element that serves as a circumstantial clause of the messengers; that is: "By Allah, they indeed came with the truth," or "they came accompanied by the truth."

﴿And it will be called out to them﴾; that is: the angels, peace be upon them, will call out to them.

﴿"That is the Garden"﴾ The anna is explanatory of what is in the call of the meaning of speech, or it is the light form of anna, with the pronoun of the matter omitted. The meaning of distance in the demonstrative is either because they were called out upon seeing it from a distant place, or to raise its rank and the loftiness of its status, or to indicate that it is that Garden which they were promised in the world.

﴿You have been given it as an inheritance for what you used to do﴾ in the world of righteous deeds; that is: you were given it because of your deeds, or in return for your deeds. The clause is a circumstantial clause of the Garden, and the operating element is the meaning of the demonstrative, on the basis that "that is the Garden" is a subject and predicate, or the Garden is a qualifier and the predicate is "you have been given it as an inheritance."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 44:

﴿And the companions of the Garden will call out to the companions of the Fire﴾ boasting of their own state, gloating over the companions of the Fire, and causing them grief, not merely to inform them of their state or to inquire about the state of those they addressed.

﴿That we have found what our Lord promised us to be true﴾, since we have attained this noble attainment.

﴿So have you found what your Lord promised to be true?﴾ The object of the second verb has been omitted, in order to deprive them of the rank of being addressed with honour at the time of the promise. It has been said: because what displeased them of what was promised was not, in its entirety, specifically a promise to them, such as the Resurrection, the Reckoning, and the bliss of the people of the Garden; for they had found all of that to be true, even though the promise was not specifically addressed to them.

﴿They will say: Yes﴾; that is, we found it to be true. It is also read with a kasra on the ʿayn (ʿIlm), which is a dialectal variant of this word.

﴿Then a caller will call out between them﴾. It has been said: he is the bearer of the Trumpet (ṣāḥib al-Ṣūr).

﴿between them﴾; that is, between the two groups.

﴿That the curse of God is upon the wrongdoers﴾. Here "an" is the lightened (mukhaffafa) form or the explanatory (mufassira) form. It is also read as the emphatic "anna" with "laʿnata" in the accusative, and "inna" with a kasra on the hamza, on the basis that calling out implies saying, or that "adhdhana" is treated as "qala."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 45:

﴿Those who bar from the way of Allah﴾ is a descriptive clause establishing the state of the wrongdoers (al-zalimin); or it is in the nominative case, indicating disapproval (al-dhamm); or it is in the accusative case for the same purpose.

﴿and seek to make it crooked﴾; i.e., they seek crookedness for it, by describing it as deviant and inclining away from the truth, and that is the furthest thing from both of them. The word ʿiwaj (crookedness), with a kasra on the ʿayn, is used for meanings and for physical things that are not upright, while with a fatha on the ʿayn it is used for what is upright, such as a spear or a wall.

﴿and they are, of the Hereafter, disbelievers﴾, i.e., not acknowledging it.

﴿And between them is a barrier﴾; that is, between the two groups, as in His saying: ﴿so a wall with a gate was set up between them﴾. Or it is between Paradise and Hell, so that the effect of each is prevented from reaching the other.

﴿And on the a'raf (heights)﴾; that is, on the heights and summits of the barrier, which is the wall set up between them. The word a'raf is the plural of ʿurf (عُرْف), used metaphorically from ʿurf al-faras (عُرْفُ الفَرَسِ), the mane of a horse. It is also said that ʿurf means the raised part of a thing, since by its prominence it is more recognizable than other parts.

﴿Men﴾ are a group of monotheists who fell short in their deeds. They remain between Paradise and Hell until God Most High decides regarding them what He wills. It is also said that they are a people whose ranks are elevated, such as the prophets, the martyrs, and the righteous and learned among the believers. Or they are angels who appear in the forms of men.

﴿They recognize each﴾ of the people of Paradise and the people of Hell.

﴿by their marks﴾, by the sign by which God Most High has informed them, such as the whiteness or blackness of the face. The word simā (سِيماهُمْ) has the pattern fiʿlā (فِعْلى), from sāma his camels, meaning he sent them out to pasture marked. Or it is from wasama (وَسَمَ) with the heart, as the mark on the face. They know this through inspiration, or through the teaching of the angels.

﴿And they call out﴾; that is, the men of the a'raf.

﴿to the companions of Paradise﴾ when they see them.

﴿Peace be upon you﴾, either by way of supplication and greeting, or by way of informing them of their deliverance from what is hateful.

﴿They have not entered it﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl, حال) referring to the subject of "they call out", or to its object.

And His saying, Most High: ﴿while they hope﴾ is a circumstantial clause referring to the subject of "they enter it" (yadkhulūhā). That is, they call out to them while they have not entered it, being in a state of eagerly hoping to enter it and anticipating it; that is, they have not entered it, and at the time of not entering they are hopeful.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 47:

﴿And when their sights are turned toward the companions of the Fire﴾; i.e., toward their direction. The omission of any mention of their gaze being fixed upon the companions of Paradise, and the expression of their gaze being fixed upon the companions of the Fire by "turning" (ṣarf), indicates that the first attachment is by way of desire, while the second inclination is the opposite of that.

﴿They say﴾, seeking refuge in God Most High from the evil of their state.

﴿Our Lord, do not place us with the wrongdoing people﴾; i.e., in the Fire. And in describing them with wrongdoing, without mentioning what they are in at that time of punishment and evil condition, which is what necessitates the supplication, it indicates that what they fear is not merely the negation of punishment, but also what it entails and leads to of wrongdoing.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 48:

﴿And the companions of the Heights will call out﴾ Their mention is repeated, although a pronoun would suffice, to increase the affirmation (taqrir).

﴿men﴾ from among the chiefs of the disbelievers, when they see them among the companions of the Fire.

﴿They will recognize them by their marks﴾ which indicate the evil of their condition on that Day, and their leadership in the worldly life.

﴿They will say﴾ is a substitution (badal) for "will call out."

﴿What did your gathering avail you?﴾ The "ma" here is either interrogative, for rebuke and reproach, or negative.

﴿your gathering﴾; that is, your followers and partisans, or your gathering of wealth.

﴿and what you used to be arrogant about﴾ Here "ma" is verbal-masdarial (masdariyyah), meaning: what your gathering and your persistent arrogance against accepting the truth, or against creation, availed you. The latter is more fitting with what follows it. It has also been read as "tastakthirun" (you used to pile up), from abundance (kathrah), meaning: of wealth and soldiers.

This is Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 49:

﴿Are these the ones of whom you swore that Allah would not grant them His mercy?﴾ This is part of the speech of the people of the Heights (A'raf) addressed to the men (of the Fire). The reference is to the weak among the believers, whom the disbelievers used to despise in the world, and about whom they would swear plainly that they would not enter Paradise, or would do something that indicates this, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Did you not swear before that there would be no decline for you?﴾.

﴿Enter Paradise﴾: a shift in address (talwin lil-khitab), turning the speech toward those mentioned; that is: enter Paradise in spite of (ala raghm) their noses.

﴿No fear shall be upon you﴾ after this.

﴿Nor shall you grieve﴾. Or it was said to the companions of the Heights (Ashab al-A'raf): Enter Paradise by the grace of Allah, exalted is He, after they had been held back, and had witnessed the conditions of the two groups and recognised them, and had said to them what they said.

It is more apparent that the intended meaning of the companions of the Heights is not those who fell short in deeds, because these statements and what they branch from of knowledge are not befitting to one whose state has not yet been determined.

It was also said: when they (the Heights people) rebuked the companions of the Fire, they swore that the companions of the Heights would not enter Paradise. Then Allah, exalted is He, or the angels, said in response to them: "﴿Are these...﴾" etc. It is also read: (Udkhulu, wa dakhalu) on the basis of a resumptive sentence (isti'naf), and its implied sense is: they entered Paradise, with it being said concerning them: ﴿No fear shall be upon you﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 50:

﴿And the companions of the Fire will call out to the companions of the Garden﴾, after the abode has settled for each of the two groups and the dwelling has become tranquil for them.

﴿"Pour down upon us some of the water"﴾; that is, pour it out on us. In this there is an indication that the Garden is above the Fire.

﴿"Or some of what Allah has provided you"﴾, from the rest of the drinks, so that it matches the mention of water; or from the foods, on the basis that *ifada* (pouring out) is an expression for giving abundantly.

﴿They will say﴾: this is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*) built upon a question, as if it were said: "What did they say?" So it was said: "They said."

﴿"Indeed, Allah has forbidden both of them to the disbelievers"﴾; that is, He has prevented them from them with a complete prohibition, so there is absolutely no way to that.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 51:

﴿Those who took their religion as amusement and play﴾, like the prohibition of the baheera, the sa'iba, and the like, and the whistling and clapping around the House (the Ka'ba). Lahw (diversion) is directing one's concern toward what it is not becoming to direct it toward, and la'ib (play) is seeking joy in what it is not becoming to seek.

﴿And the life of this world deceived them﴾ with its fleeting adornments.

﴿So today We will forget them﴾: We will treat them with what people do to the forgotten, by not counting them of any worth and leaving them in the Fire completely. The fa' in "fa-al-yawm" (fa-l-yawm) is fasiha (an expressive particle that signals an implied condition).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿as they forgot the meeting of this their day﴾ is in the accusative position, being an adjective (na't) of an omitted verbal noun (masdar); i.e., We will forget them with a forgetting like their forgetting the meeting of this their day, in that they did not bring it to mind and did not take it into account.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and as they used to deny Our signs﴾ is coordinated (ataf) upon "as they forgot"; i.e., and just as they were persistently denying that they were from God, Exalted is He, with a continuous denial.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 52:**

﴿And We have certainly brought them a Book which We have detailed﴾; that is, We clarified its meanings concerning the articles of faith (*al-'aqa'id*), the legal rulings (*al-ahkam*), and the admonitions (*al-mawa'iz*). The pronoun [in "brought them"] refers to the disbelievers as a whole, and the "Book" is meant generically [as a kind of scripture], or it refers to their contemporaries among them. The Book is the Qur'an.

اعلى علم (*'ala 'ilm*), "with knowledge," is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) relating to the subject of "fassalnahu" ("We have detailed it"); that is, [We detailed it] while knowing the manner of its detailing, until it came as a wise [book]. Or it relates to its object ("it"); that is, [the Book was] containing much knowledge. It has also been read as *fadalnahu* ("We have favoured it"), meaning: [We favoured it] over the rest of the books, knowing its excellence.

﴿Guidance and mercy﴾ is a circumstantial clause relating to the object ("it").

﴿For a people who do not believe﴾: because they are the ones who take advantage of its effects and draw light from its lights.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 53:

﴿Do they await anything but its ta'wil (ultimate fulfilment)?﴾ That is: what are these disbelievers waiting for, in their failure to believe in it, other than what its matter will return to, namely the manifestation of its truthfulness through the appearing of what it announced of promise and threat?

﴿On the day its ta'wil comes﴾, and that is the Day of Resurrection.

﴿Those who had forgotten it before will say﴾: that is, they had abandoned it as one abandons what is forgotten, before the coming of its ta'wil.

﴿Indeed, the messengers of our Lord came with the truth﴾: that is, it has become clear that they had indeed come with the truth.

﴿So do we have any intercessors, that they might intercede for us﴾ today, and push the punishment away from us?

﴿Or are we returned﴾: that is, are we returned to the world? It is also read in the accusative, as a conjunction with ﴿fayashfa'u﴾ (that they might intercede). Or, since "aw" (or) here means "ila an" (until), then on the first reading the thing asked for is one of two matters: either intercession to push away the punishment, or being returned to the world. On the second reading, they would have intercessors either for one of the two matters, or for a single matter, which is the return.

﴿Then we would act﴾, in the accusative, being the answer to the second interrogative; it is also read in the nominative, meaning: then we would act.

﴿Other than what we used to do﴾: that is, in the world.

﴿They have lost their souls﴾ by diverting their lives, which are their capital, toward disbelief and sins.

﴿And what they used to fabricate has gone astray from them﴾: that is, the falsehood of what they used to fabricate has become manifest, namely that the idols are partners of God Most High and their intercessors on the Day of Resurrection.

This passage begins the account of the origin of creation (*fitrah*, the original natural order) after the account of the disbelievers' return. That is: indeed your Lord and Owner is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth in six periods (﴿in six days﴾). This may mean six time-periods, as in His saying ﴿And whoever turns his back to them on such a day﴾ (8:16), or the duration of six days. What is customary is that a day is the time from the rising of the sun to its setting, but the sun did not yet exist at that time. Creating things gradually, though He had the power to originate them all at once, is evidence of choice, a lesson for observers, and an exhortation to deliberateness in affairs.

﴿Then He established Himself upon the Throne﴾: i.e., His command was established and He took dominion. Our companions (the scholars of our school) hold that *istiwa'* (establishment) upon the Throne is an attribute of Allah, without asking how. The meaning is that He, exalted is He, established Himself upon the Throne in the manner He intended, transcending settling and occupying (a place).

The *'arsh* (Throne) is the body that encompasses all other bodies. It was so named because of its loftiness, or by way of likening it to a royal throne, since affairs and plans descend from it. It is also said that it means sovereignty.

﴿He covers the night with the day﴾: i.e., He covers it with it. The reverse is not mentioned either because it is known, or because the wording admits both. For this reason it is read with *al-layla* in the accusative and *al-nahar* in the nominative. It is also read with the doubled form (*yughashshi*), to indicate repetition.

﴿Pursuing it swiftly﴾: i.e., it follows it quickly, like one who seeks it, with nothing separating the two. *Ḥathīth* is a form (*fa'īl*) from *ḥathth* (urging), and it is either an attribute of a deleted verbal noun, or a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*) of the doer or of the object, in the sense of "urging" or "being urged."

﴿And the sun, the moon, and the stars, subjected by His command﴾: i.e., He created them in a state of being subjected to His decree and direction. It is also read with *kulluhā* in the nominative, as a subject and predicate (*mubtada'* and *khabar*). (p-233)

﴿Surely His is the creation and the command﴾: for He is the originator of all, and the one who disposes of everything absolutely.

﴿Blessed is Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾: i.e., He is exalted in His oneness of divinity, and magnified in His singularity of lordship. The true sense of the noble verse – and Allah Most High knows best – is this: the disbelievers were taking lords (besides Allah), so it was made clear to them that the one worthy of lordship is one alone, Allah Most High, because He is the one to whom creation and command belong. Allah Most High created the world in an upright order and with wise governance. He originated the celestial spheres, then adorned them with the sun, the moon, and the stars, as He indicated by His saying: ﴿Then He completed them as seven heavens in two days﴾ (41:12).

He then proceeded to the lower bodies and created a body receptive to changing forms and differing configurations, then divided it into specific forms with varying effects and actions. He indicated this by His saying: ﴿He created the earth in two days﴾ (41:9); i.e., what lies in the lower direction, in two days.

Then He brought into being the three kingdoms of generated beings, first by composing their materials and then by shaping them, as He said after His saying ﴿He created the earth in two days﴾: ﴿And He placed in it firm mountains above it, and blessed it, and measured in it its sustenance, in four days﴾ (41:10); i.e., together with the first two days, as detailed in Surah al-Sajdah.

Then, when the world of dominion was complete for Him, He proceeded to govern it like a king seated upon his throne. He directed the affair from the heaven to the earth by moving the celestial spheres, guiding the stars, and alternating the nights and days.

Then He stated explicitly what is the summation and conclusion of this argument, saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Surely His is the creation and the command. Blessed is Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾.

Then He commanded that they call upon Him sincerely and humbly, and said: ﴿Call upon your Lord﴾, the One whose glorious attributes you have come to know.

﴿With humility and in secret﴾; that is, possessing humility and secrecy, for concealment is a sign of sincerity.

﴿Indeed, He does not love the transgressors﴾; that is, He does not love the supplication of those who exceed what they have been commanded in everything. Transgression in supplication is included in this in the primary sense, and by it attention is drawn to the fact that the one who supplicates must not ask for what is unbecoming to him, such as the rank of the prophets or ascending to the heavens.

It was also said: it refers to shouting in supplication and being prolix in it. And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "There will be a people who will transgress in supplication. It is sufficient for a person to say: O Allah, I ask You for Paradise and whatever brings closer to it of speech and deed, and I seek refuge in You from the Fire and whatever brings closer to it of speech and deed." Then he recited: ﴿Indeed, He does not love the transgressors﴾.

**﴿And do not cause corruption on the earth﴾** through disbelief and sins, **﴿after its reformation﴾** through the sending of the Prophets, peace be upon them, and the legislation of rulings.

**﴿And call upon Him in fear and hope﴾**. That is, be fearful, looking at the deficiency of your deeds and your not deserving (His mercy), and be hopeful, looking at the vastness of His mercy and the abundance of His grace and kindness.

**﴿Indeed, the mercy of Allah is near to the doers of good﴾** in everything. Among the forms of good conduct in supplication is that it be accompanied by fear and hope. The verb is in the masculine form, "قَرِيبٌ" (qarib, near), though the subject "رَحْمَتَ" (raḥmat, mercy) is feminine, for several reasons. Either "الرَّحْمَةَ" is taken in the sense of "الرَّحِمِ" (ar-raḥim, the womb, which is masculine in this usage), or "قَرِيبٌ" is an attribute of an omitted noun, meaning "أمْرٌ قَرِيبٌ" (a near matter). Or it is patterned on "فَعِيلٌ" (fa'il, an adjective pattern) in the sense of "مَفْعُولٌ" (maf'ul, passive participle), or it is a verbal noun like "النَّقِيضِ" (an-naqid, the cry/contradiction) and "الصَّهِيلِ" (as-sahil, the neighing), which do not take the feminine marker. Or the masculine form distinguishes "قَرِيبٌ" in the sense of a blood relative from "قَرِيبٌ" in the sense of someone else. Or it takes the masculine from the noun it is attached to, "المُضافِ إلَيْهِ" (al-mudaf ilayh, the genitive noun), just as the "مُضافٌ" (mudaf, the first term of a construct phrase) takes the feminine from the genitive noun.(p-234)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 57:

﴿And it is He who sends the winds﴾ is coordinated with the preceding sentence. It is also read as (al-rih), in the singular.

﴿as heralds of good news﴾: this is a lightened form of bushur, the plural of bashir (bearer of good news); that is, announcing (mubashshirat). It is also read with a fatha on the ba', as an infinitive of bashara-hu (he gave him good news), meaning bashirat (bringing good news), or for the sake of glad tidings (lil-bishara). It is also read as nushuran, with a damma on the nun, the plural of nashur (scattering), meaning scattering (nashirat). And nashran is read as an infinitive in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal), meaning nashirat, or as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), since sending (irsal) and scattering (nashr) are close in meaning.

﴿before His mercy﴾: He placed before His mercy, which is the rain,

for the saba (east wind) stirs up the clouds, the shamal (north wind) gathers them, the janub (south wind) pours them down, and the dabur (west wind) scatters them.

﴿until, when they have borne﴾: that is, they have carried. Its derivation is from qilla (lightness), since one who carries a thing finds it light (yastaqillu-hu).

﴿heavy clouds﴾ with water. He used the plural because it means clouds (sahà'ib).

﴿We drove it﴾: that is, the cloud. The singular pronoun is due to the singularity of the word.

﴿to a dead land﴾: that is, for its sake and its benefit, or for its revival, or for its watering. It is also read as mayt.

﴿and We sent down water with it﴾: that is, with the land, or with the cloud, or with the driving, or with the wind. The masculine form is in accordance with the interpretation of "what is mentioned."

Likewise is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿then We brought forth with it﴾. The pronoun may refer to water, which is the apparent meaning. If it refers to the land, then the ba' is for adhesion in the first case and for location in the second. If it refers to something else, then it is for causation.

﴿of all kinds of fruits﴾: that is, of all their varieties.

﴿Thus do We bring forth the dead﴾: the reference is to the bringing forth of fruits, or to the revival of the dead land; that is, just as We revive it by producing the growing power within it and renewing it with varieties of plants and fruits, We bring forth the dead from their graves, and revive them by returning souls to the material of their bodies, after gathering them and renewing them with the powers and senses.

﴿so that you may remember﴾ with one of the two taas elided; that is, that you may remember, and thus know that whoever is able to do that is able to do this without doubt.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 58:

﴿And the good land—its vegetation comes forth by the permission of its Lord﴾; i.e., the land whose soil is noble.

﴿Its vegetation comes forth by the permission of its Lord﴾ by His will and facilitation. He expressed it thus to denote the abundance of the vegetation, its goodness, and the plentifulness of its fragrance, because He placed it in contrast with His words, exalted is He: ﴿And that which is corrupt﴾ of the lands, such as the salt flats (sabakha) and the volcanic stony tracts (harra).

﴿Comes forth only scantily﴾, meagre and useless. Its being in the accusative (nakidan) is as a circumstantial qualifier (hal). The implied sense is: "And the land which is corrupt, its vegetation comes forth only scantily." The governing noun (mudaf) has been elided and the governed noun (mudaf ilayhi) put in its place, so it became nominative and concealed (mustatir).

It is also read: (لا يَخْرُجُ إلّا نَكَدًا) "comes forth only scantily" (nakadan); i.e., the land does not bring it forth except in scantiness, so that "illa nakidan" is its object. It is also read (nakadan) as a verbal noun (masdar), i.e., possessing scantiness; and (nakdan) with sukun for lightness.

﴿Thus﴾; i.e., like this wondrous variation.

﴿We vary the signs﴾; i.e., We repeat them and reiterate them.

﴿For a people who give thanks﴾ for the blessing of God, exalted is He, so that they reflect upon it and take lessons from it. This, as you see, is an example of the sending of the Messengers, peace be upon them, with the sacred laws (shara'i'), which are the water of life for hearts, to the responsible people (mukallafin), who divide into those who draw light from their illumination and those who are deprived of the spoils of its effects.(p-235)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 59:

This has been followed by what confirms and establishes it from the accounts of the earlier nations, by way of resumption (istinaf). It is said: ﴿Indeed, We sent Noah to his people﴾ is the answer to an omitted oath; that is, "By Allah, indeed We sent..." etc. The consistent use of this lam together with qad is because what follows it is liable to expectation (tawaqqu'), which is the meaning of qad, for the oath clause is only brought in to emphasize the clause sworn upon.

Noah is the son of Lamech (Lamak) son of Methuselah (Mutushalah) son of Enoch (Akhnukh), and he is Idris the Prophet, peace be upon them both. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: He (peace be upon him) was sent at the age of forty years of his life, and he remained calling his people for nine hundred and fifty years, and he lived after the Flood two hundred and fifty years, so his lifespan was one thousand two hundred and forty years.

Muqatil said: He was sent when he was a son of one hundred years. It is said: when he was a son of fifty years. It is said: when he was a son of two hundred and fifty years. He remained calling his people for nine hundred and fifty years, and he lived after the Flood two hundred and fifty years, so his lifespan was one thousand four hundred and fifty years.

﴿So he said: O my people, worship Allah﴾; that is, worship Him alone. Leaving the restriction to Him is to indicate that this is worship in its true sense, whereas worship with association is not worship at all.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿You have no god other than Him﴾; that is, no one deserving of worship, is a resumptive clause brought to give the reason for the mentioned worship, or for the command to it.

"Ghayruhu" (other than Him) with the nominative (raf') is an attribute of "ilah" (god) according to its place, which is the nominative as a subject (mubtada') or as an agent (fa'iliyyah). It has also been read with the genitive (jarr) according to its wording, and read with the accusative (nasb) as an exception (istithna'). The ruling of "ghayr" is the ruling of the noun that comes after illa (except); that is, "You have no god except Him," like your saying: "There is no one in the house except Zayd, or other than Zayd."

So "min ilah" (any god): if it is made the subject (mubtada'), then "lakum" (for you) is its predicate; or its predicate is omitted and "lakum" is for specification and clarification; that is, "For you, in existence or in the world, there is no god other than Allah."

﴿Indeed, I fear for you﴾; that is, if you do not worship Him as I have been commanded.

﴿the punishment of a tremendous day﴾ is the Day of Resurrection, or the Day of the Flood. The clause is a reason for the worship by explaining what turns one away from abandoning it, after its reason has been given by explaining what calls to it. Describing the day as tremendous is to show the greatness of what occurs in it and to complete the warning.

The chiefs (al-mala') of his people said, [as a continuation answering an implied question: what did they say to him, peace be upon him, in response to his counsel?]. The chiefs of his people, and the nobles, who fill the breasts of assemblies with their bodies, hearts with their majesty and awe, and eyes with their beauty and grandeur, said:

"Indeed we see you in error" — i.e., going astray from the path of truth and correctness. The seeing (ru'yah) here is of the heart (qalbiyyah, i.e., mental perception, not sight), and its two objects are the pronoun (the "you") and the adverbial phrase (fi dalal, "in error").

"Clear" — its being error is manifest.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 61:

﴿Qāla﴾ (He said): a resumptive sentence (isti'nāf), as explained previously.

﴿Yā qawmi﴾ (O my people): he addressed them by attributing them to himself, in order to win their hearts toward the truth.

﴿Laysa bī ḍalāla﴾ (There is no error in me): that is, there is not any sort of error. The blessings and peace of Allah be upon him intended by this the affirmation of the truth in negating error from himself, in response to the disbelievers, who had exaggerated in ascribing it to him, peremptorily describing him as being firmly established in a clear error, which they regarded as error.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Wa lākinnī rasūlun min rabbi l-‘ālamīna﴾ (But I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds) is a corrective (istidrāk) to what precedes it, in terms of what it implies: that he is at the utmost level of guidance. For the messengership of the Lord of the worlds necessarily entails this for him, as though it were said: "There is no trace of error in me, but I am at the furthest extreme of guidance."

Min (from) denotes the beginning of the limit (li-ibtidā' al-ghāya) metaphorically, and it is related to a omitted element which is an attribute of rasūlun (a messenger), emphasizing what the indefiniteness (tanwīn) conveys of intrinsic grandeur by means of relational grandeur. That is: "a messenger, and what a messenger, existing from the Lord of the worlds."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 62:

﴿I convey to you the messages of my Lord﴾ is a resumptive clause (*istinaf*, a new sentence that begins without grammatical connection to what precedes it), brought to affirm his prophethood and to detail its rulings and circumstances. It has also been said that it is another attribute of *rasul* (messenger), in the manner of the line: "I am the one whom my mother named Haydara."

It is recited as ﴿أُبْلِغُكم﴾ (*ublighukum*), from *al-iblagh* (conveying). The plural *risalat* (messages) is used either because their times differ, or because their meanings are varied, or because what is meant by them is what was revealed to him and to the prophets before him.

Specifying His lordship (*rububiyya*) to him, peace be upon him, after explaining its generality over all the worlds, serves to indicate the reason for the ruling, which is the conveying of His message to them. For his being under the lordship of God is one of the requirements of his compliance with God's command to convey His message to them.

﴿and I give you sincere counsel﴾ is coordinated with ﴿I convey﴾, explaining the manner in which the message is delivered. The addition of the letter *lam* along with the verb *nasaha* (to advise), which takes its object directly, serves to indicate the purity (*imhad*) of the counsel for them, and that it is solely for their benefit and their welfare. The use of the present tense (*al-mudari'*) indicates the renewal of his counsel to them, as His words, exalted is He, express: ﴿My Lord, I have called my people night and day﴾.

His words, exalted is He, ﴿and I know from God what you do not know﴾ are coordinated with what precedes, and are an affirmation of his prophethood, peace be upon him. That is: I know from God, through revelation, what you do not know of future matters; or I know of His affairs, mighty and majestic is He, and His overpowering might, and His severe punishment of His enemies, and that His might is not turned away from the guilty people, which you do not know.

It has been said: They had not heard of a people upon whom punishment had descended before them, so they were heedless and secure, not knowing what Noah, peace be upon him, knew by revelation.

﴿Do you wonder that a reminder from your Lord has come to you﴾ is an answer to, and a rebuttal of, what has been left unstated through their saying, "Indeed, we see you in clear error" [7:60]; from their saying, "We see you only as a human being like ourselves" [11:27]; and their saying, "Had God willed, He would have sent down angels" [41:14].

The الهَمْزَةُ (hamzah, the interrogative particle) is for denial and rebuke, and the الواوُ (waw, the conjunction) is for coordination with an implied element that the speech carries along. It is as if it were said: "Do you consider it far-fetched and wonder that there has come to you a reminder (ذِكْرٌ, dhikr); that is, a revelation (وحيٌ, wahy), or an admonition, from the Master of your affairs and your Cherisher."

﴿upon a man from among you﴾ means: through the tongue of a man of your own kind, as in His saying, "...what You promised us through Your messengers" [3:194]. You said on account of this what you said, that God, had He willed, would have sent down angels.

﴿that he may warn you﴾ is the reason (عِلَّةٌ, ʿillah) for the coming; that is, that he may caution you against the consequence of disbelief and sins.

﴿and that you may be wary of God﴾ is coordinated with the first reason, following upon it.

﴿and that perhaps you may be shown mercy﴾ is coordinated with the second reason, following upon it; that is, so that mercy may attach to you because of your piety. The purpose of the particle of hope (حَرْفُ التَّرَجِّي, harf al-tarajji, "perhaps") is to alert to the rarity of the goal, and that piety does not necessitate mercy; rather, it is bound to the bounty of God, the Exalted. The one who is pious should not rely on his piety, nor feel secure from the punishment of God, Mighty and Majestic.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 64:

﴿So they denied him﴾ — they persisted in denying him regarding his claim to prophethood, and the revelation that had been sent down to him, which he conveyed to them, and with which he warned them, its contents included (p-237). They continued in this for that lengthy period, after peace and blessings be upon him had repeated the call to them many times, and his call only increased them in flight, as expressed by the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿My Lord, I have called my people night and day﴾ and the verses that follow; for it is this (persistent rejection) that is followed by deliverance and drowning, not mere denial.

﴿So We delivered him and those with him﴾ from among the believers. It has been said they were forty men and forty women; and it has been said they were nine: his three sons and six others who believed in him.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿in the ship﴾ are connected to the settled (implied) meaning within the adverbial phrase; that is, they settled with him in the ship, or accompanied him in it, or they are connected to the verb of deliverance, meaning: We delivered them in the ark. It is also permissible that it be connected to an implied verb that occurs as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the relative pronoun, or from its pronoun within the adverbial phrase.

﴿And We drowned those who denied Our signs﴾; that is, they persisted in denying them. The intended meaning is not only the chiefs who took the lead in answering, but everyone among them and their descendants who insisted on denial. The mention of deliverance is placed before drowning to hasten the report of it and to signal the precedence of mercy, which is required by the Essence, and its precedence over wrath, whose effect appears according to their crimes.

﴿Indeed they were a blind people﴾ — blind in heart, not discerning. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: their hearts were blinded from knowing tawhid, prophethood and the Return. It is also read ﴿ʿāmīn﴾ (blinded), and the first reading is more indicative of constancy and firmness.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 65:

﴿And to ʿĀd﴾ is connected to an implied verb that is coordinated with His statement, exalted is He, "We sent" (arsalna) in the account of Noah, peace be upon him.

This implied verb is what governs His statement, exalted is He, ﴿their brother﴾; that is: "And We sent to ʿĀd their brother," meaning one of them by lineage, not by religion, as in their saying: "O brother of the Arabs."

It has been said: the governing verb for both is the verb mentioned earlier, and "their brother" is coordinated with "Noah." The first view is the preferable one. In any case, the fronting of the prepositional phrase here before the explicit object is likely to avoid a pronoun before its referent (ʾiḍmār qabl al-dhikr). What guides you to this is His statement, exalted is He, which follows: ﴿and Lot…﴾ etc. For his people were not known by a familiar name that the context would require to be mentioned as attached to them, as in the accounts of ʿĀd, Thamud, and Madyan. So in the noble arrangement, his account, peace be upon him, was differentiated from the three other accounts.

His statement, exalted is He, ﴿Hud﴾ is an ʿaṭf bayān (appositive clarification) for "their brother." He is Hud ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Rabaḥ ibn al-Khulud ibn ʿĀd ibn ʿAwṣ ibn Aram ibn Sam ibn Noah, peace be upon him. It has also been said: Hud ibn Shalikh ibn Arfakhshadh ibn Sam ibn Noah, a paternal cousin of the father of ʿĀd. He was made one of them because they would understand his speech best, would know his state best in his truthfulness and trustworthiness, and would be closest to following him.

﴿He said﴾ is an isti'naf (resumptive new clause) built upon a question arising from the narration of his being sent to them, peace be upon him. It is as if it were said: "What did he say to them?" Then it is said: "He said."

﴿He said: O my people, worship Allah﴾; that is: make Him one (waḥḥidūhu), as His statement indicates: ﴿You have no god other than Him﴾. For this is an isti'naf functioning as an explanation of the worship commanded and as a reason for it, or for the command to it. It is as if it were said: "Devote worship to Him alone, and do not associate anything with Him, for you have no god besides Him." "Ghayruhu" in the nominative is an adjective of "ilah" according to its position (i'rab maḥall), and it has been read in the genitive, taking it according to its wording.

﴿Will you not then be wary?﴾ is a rebuke and an expression of astonishment at their failure to be wary of the punishment of Allah, exalted is He, after they knew what befell the people of Noah.

The fa' here is for coordination with an implied element required by the context; that is: "Will you not reflect, or are you heedless, so that you are not wary?" Then the reproach is directed at both coordinated elements together. Or: "Do you know that, so that you are not wary?" Then the reproach is directed at the second element only.

In Surah Hud, there is ﴿Will you not then understand?﴾. Perhaps he, peace be upon him, addressed them with each of these, and the narration of each in one place has been sufficient in place of its narration in another place, just as what was mentioned there, His statement, exalted is He, ﴿You are nothing but fabricators﴾, was not mentioned here. Judge by this the state of the remaining parts of the account that were and were not mentioned, and likewise the state of their counterparts in the other accounts, especially in the dialogues that took place at multiple times. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 7, verse 66:**

﴿The chiefs of those among his people who disbelieved said﴾ is a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*, a clause that begins a new sentence without grammatical connection to what precedes it), as explained earlier. The chiefs (*al-mala'*) are described as disbelievers because not all of them were upon disbelief, as were the chiefs of the people of Noah. Rather, some of them believed in him, peace be upon him, but concealed their faith, such as Marthad ibn Sa'd. It is also said that they were described as such merely for the sake of censure.

﴿Indeed, we see you in folly﴾: that is, you are firmly established in lightness of mind, having persisted in it, in that you have abandoned the religion of your fathers. ﴿Surely they are the foolish, but they do not know﴾.

﴿And indeed, we think you are among the liars﴾: that is, in what you claim of prophethood. They said this because of their deep attachment to blind imitation (*taqlid*) and their deprivation of sound reflection.

Said [Hud], seeking to win them over and to soften their hearts, despite what he had heard from them of the vile word that called for harsh speech and insulting address.

﴿O my people, there is no foolishness in me﴾; that is, not any of it, nor any trace of its traces.

﴿But I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds﴾: this is a corrective (istidrak) to what precedes, in view of what being a messenger from the Lord of the worlds necessitates and requires of him, namely that he be in the utmost degree of rectitude and forbearance, and of truthfulness and trustworthiness. For the mission from the Lord of the worlds definitely entails this. It is as if it were said: "There is nothing in me of what you have attributed to me, but I am at the utmost degree of rectitude and truthfulness."

He did not explicitly deny lying, being content with what is implied within the scope of the corrective. The "min" (from) is for the beginning of the limit (ibtida' al-ghayah), used figuratively; it is connected to an omitted element that functions as a qualifier of "rasul" (messenger), emphasizing with an added (idafi) grandeur what the tanwin (nunation) conveyed of inherent (dhati) grandeur.

I convey to you the messages of my Lord (ﷺ)... 

Wait, I need to be careful: the instructions say to render ﷺ as (ﷺ) only where the honorific appears, and here none appears. The Arabic has no such honorific; the phrase "عَلَيْهِ السَّلامُ" is rendered as "peace be upon him" in standard English. Let me give the faithful translation.

**Translation:**

And the saying of Him, the Exalted: ﴿I convey to you the messages of my Lord﴾ is a resumptive statement (isti'naf), brought in to affirm his prophethood and to detail its circumstances. It has been said that it is another attribute of "a messenger" (rasul). The discussion concerning the attribution of "Lord" to himself, peace be upon him, after its attribution to "the worlds," and likewise concerning the plural "messages," is as has passed in the story of Noah, peace be upon him. It was also read as ﴿ublighukum﴾ (I convey to you), from al-ibla' (conveying).

﴿And I am a sincere, trustworthy counselor to you﴾. He is known for sincere counsel and trustworthiness, famous among the people for this. The nominal sentence was used to indicate permanence and continuity, and as a notification that one whose condition is this, the taint of foolishness and lying does not come near him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 69:

﴿Do you wonder that a reminder from your Lord has come to you through a man from among you﴾ The discussion here is like that which has passed in the story of Noah, peace be upon him.

﴿Through a man from among you﴾; that is, from your own kind.

﴿So that he may warn you﴾ and caution you about the consequence of what you are upon of disbelief and sins, until you attributed to me folly and lying. In the response of the Prophets, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them all, there is [a lesson for] whoever addresses them with what has no good in it, such as those falsehoods, by what is related of them of true statements expressing the utmost forbearance and dignity, and perfect compassion and tenderness, indicating their possession of the highest share of noble character, whose station is not hidden.

﴿And remember when He made you successors﴾ This begins an explanation of the arrangement of the rulings of advice (nush) and trustworthiness, and warning, and their details. The word "idh" (when) is in the accusative governed by "udhkurū" (remember) as an object, not as an adverb of time. The command to remember is directed at the time rather than at what occurred in it, although the events are the primary intended matter, for the sake of emphasizing the obligation to recall them, since commanding the remembrance of a time is a command to remember what is in it by way of demonstrative reasoning, and because the time encompasses those events, so that when it is brought to mind, they are present in it with their details, as if they were witnessed directly. Perhaps it is conjoined to an implied element, as if it were said: Do not wonder at that, or reflect upon your affair, and remember the time when He, exalted is He, made you successors.

﴿After the people of Noah﴾; that is, in their dwellings, or in the earth by His making you kings, for Shaddad ibn 'Ad was among those who ruled the inhabited part of the earth, from the sands of 'Alij to the coast of 'Oman.

﴿And increased you in stature﴾; that is, in creation and formation, or among the people.

﴿Broadly⦆ [i.e., in height and strength], for there was none in their time like them in the magnitude of their bodies. Al-Kalbi and al-Suddi said: the height of the tallest among them was one hundred cubits, and the height of the shortest was sixty cubits.

﴿So remember the bounties of Allah﴾ which He has bestowed upon you of the various kinds of blessings, of which this is one part, and this is a repetition of the reminder for the sake of greater affirmation, and a generalization after a specification.

﴿That you may prosper﴾ so that this may lead you to gratitude, which leads to deliverance from distresses and attainment of what is sought.

﴿They said﴾, responding to those great admonitions.

﴿Have you come to us so that we worship Allah alone﴾; that is, so that we devote worship exclusively to Him.

﴿and abandon what our fathers used to worship﴾. They objected to his peace be upon him coming to devote worship exclusively to Allah the Exalted and turning away from worshipping idols, out of absorption in imitation (taqlid) and love for what they and their forefathers had been accustomed to.

As for the meaning of "coming" (al-maji'): it may be his peace be upon him coming from his place of worship and dwelling; or it may be coming from the heavens, in mockery; or it may be intending and undertaking something, metaphorically, as is said in its opposite: "he went to revile me," without intending the literal sense of going.

﴿So bring us what you threaten us with﴾ of punishment, and what is indicated by His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿Will you not then fear Allah?﴾

﴿if you are among the truthful﴾; that is, in reporting the descent of punishment. The answer to "if" (in) is omitted, as what has been mentioned indicates it; that is, "then bring it."

(p-240)

﴿He said: "Indeed there has befallen you"﴾; i.e., it has become due and necessary, or it has descended upon you because of this your obstinacy. This is based on treating what is expected as if it had already occurred, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿The command of God has come﴾.

﴿from your Lord﴾; i.e., from His direction, exalted is He. The placing of the first adverbial complement (ẓarf) before the second, even though the starting point of a thing precedes its end, is for the sake of hastening to make clear that the disliked matter has struck them.

Likewise is their placement before the subject, which is His words, exalted is He: ﴿abomination﴾, together with what this carries of arousing eagerness for the postponed element. And because the subject has a certain length due to what is conjoined to it, His words, exalted is He: ﴿and wrath﴾, placing them before it might disrupt the harmony of the noble composition.

And ﴿rijs﴾ (abomination) means punishment, from irtijās, which is agitation, and wrath with the intent of vengeance. Their tanwin (indefiniteness) is for magnification and awe-inspiring intensity.

﴿Do you dispute with me over names﴾ that are bare of what they name.

﴿which you have named﴾; i.e., you have named by them.

﴿you and your fathers﴾: this is a denunciation and condemnation of their denial of his coming, peace be upon him, calling them to worship God alone and to abandon the worship of idols. That is: Do you dispute with me over things you have named as gods, which are nothing but mere names, with no portion of divinity in them at all? For the one who truly deserves worship in essence is none other than the One who brought all things into being. And if they deserved it, that would be by God's appointment, exalted is He, either through sending down a sign or establishing a proof, and both are impossible.

This is His words, exalted is He: ﴿God has sent down no authority for them﴾. And since that is not within the realm of possibility, the falsity of what they hold has been established.

﴿So wait﴾ is consequent upon His words, exalted is He: "﴿there has befallen you﴾"; i.e., so wait for what you seek by your saying: "﴿bring us what you promise us﴾" and so on.

﴿Indeed I am with you among those who wait﴾ for what will befall you.

The fa' in His words ﴿So We delivered him﴾ is a fasiha (a fa' that signals an unstated clause), as in His words ﴿and it burst forth﴾. The meaning is: what happened happened, and so We delivered him.

﴿And those who were with him﴾: that is, in the religion.

﴿By a mercy﴾: that is, a great mercy whose extent cannot be measured.

His words ﴿from Us﴾: that is, from Our side. It is connected to an omitted element that serves as a qualifier of "mercy," emphasizing its inherent greatness, which is understood from its being indefinite and given further grandeur by the genitive construction.

﴿And We cut off the root of those who denied Our signs﴾: that is, We completely uprooted them and destroyed them to the last one.

﴿And they were not believers﴾ is conjoined to "denied" and falls under the same grammatical role as the relative clause: that is, they persisted in disbelief and denial and never refrained from it.

The mention of the deliverance before the destruction has already had its secret explained, and it contains an indication that the basis of salvation is faith in God Most High and belief in His signs, just as the cause of ruin is disbelief and denial.

Their story is that ʿAd were a people in Yemen, in al-Ahqaf, who had spread out through the lands between ʿUman and Hadramawt. They had idols they worshipped: Sada, Sumud, and Ilhaba. God Most High sent to them Hud as a prophet. He was among the best of them in lineage and excellence. They denied him and increased in arrogance and tyranny. So God withheld rain from them for three years until they were afflicted with hardship. When calamity befell people, they would seek relief from God at His Sacred House, both Muslim and polytheist. At that time the people of Mecca were the Amaliq, the sons of ʿImliq ibn Lawadh ibn Sam ibn Nuh, and their chief was Muʿawiya ibn Bakr. So ʿAd sent seventy men from their notables to Mecca. It was said they included Ibn ʿAnz and Martad ibn Saʿd, who was concealing his Islam. When they arrived, they stayed with Muʿawiya ibn Bakr, who was outside the Sacred Precinct on the outskirts of Mecca. He housed and honored them, for they were his maternal relatives and in-laws. They stayed with him for a month, drinking wine while his two singing-girls sang to them. When he saw how long they stayed and how absorbed they were in amusement, forgetting the purpose for which they had come, it troubled him. He said: "My maternal relatives and in-laws are being destroyed, and these men are as they are." He was too shy to speak to them, fearing they would think he found their stay burdensome. So he mentioned this to the two singing-girls, and they said: "Say a poem and we will sing it to them, so they do not know who said it." Muʿawiya then said:

Ala ya Qil, woe to you, rise and make a sound, perhaps God will give us to drink a cloud.

So that He waters the land of ʿAd, for ʿAd have come to the point that they cannot express speech.

When the two girls sang it, they said: "Your people are calling for help against the calamity that has befallen them, and you have been slow to help them. Enter the Sacred Precinct and pray for rain for your people." Martad ibn Saʿd said to them: "By God, you will not be given rain by your supplication. But if you obey your prophet and repent to God Most High, you will be given rain." He then openly declared his Islam. They said to Muʿawiya: "Keep Martad from us, so that he does not come with us, for he has followed Hud and abandoned our religion." Then they entered Mecca, and he said: "O God, give ʿAd rain as You used to give them." So God Most High produced three clouds: white, red, and black. Then a caller called out to him from the sky: "O Qil, choose for yourself and for your people." He said: "I choose the black one, for it has the most water." So it came out over ʿAd from a valley called al-Mughith. They rejoiced at it and said: ﴿This is a cloud bringing us rain﴾. But a violent wind came to them from Us and destroyed them. Hud and the believers with him were saved, and they came to Mecca and worshipped God Most High there until they died. (p-241)

﴿And to Thamud, their brother Salih﴾ is coordinated with what came before in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And to 'Ad, their brother Hud﴾, and agrees with it in placing the prepositional phrase before the object. Thamud is a tribe of the Arabs. They were named after their great forefather Thamud ibn 'Abir ibn Iram ibn Sam ibn Nuh, peace be upon him.

It was said: they were named thus for the scarcity of their water, from the thamad (a small quantity of water), and it was read with tanwin (ṣarf), interpreting it as the tribe. Their dwellings were al-Hijr, between the Hijaz and al-Sham, extending to Wadi al-Qura.

Salih's brotherhood to them, peace be upon him, is by lineage, like Hud's, for he is Salih ibn 'Ubayd ibn Asif ibn Masih ibn 'Ubayd ibn Hadhir ibn Thamud. Since the report of his being sent to them is a likely occasion for the question, "What did he say to them?", an answer was given to it by way of resumption (istinaf, a resumptive clause): ﴿He said: O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him﴾. The discussion of its like has already passed.

﴿There has certainly come to you a clear proof (bayyinah)﴾, that is, a sign and a manifest miracle testifying to my prophethood. It is among the words that function like al-Abtah and al-Abraq in being used without mention of the things they describe, in singular and plural, like ṣāliḥ in singular and plural. Likewise ḥasanah and sayyi'ah, whether they are attributes of deeds, of recompense, or of a state of ease or hardship; for this reason they were made to govern the operators.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿from your Lord﴾, is connected to "has come to you", or to an omitted element that is an attribute of bayyinah, as has been mentioned many times. What is meant by it is the she-camel. This speech from him, peace be upon him, was not the first thing he addressed them with after calling them to monotheism; rather he said it after advising them and reminding them of Allah's blessings, and they did not accept his speech and denied him. Do you not see what is in Surah Hud of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He brought you into being from the earth and made you its inhabitants...﴾, to the end of the verses?

It is related that when 'Ad was destroyed, Thamud settled their lands and succeeded them on the earth. They multiplied and lived long lives, so much so that a man would build a sturdy dwelling which would collapse during his lifetime. So they carved houses out of the mountains. They were in abundance and ease of living, so they transgressed against Allah, exalted is He, corrupted the earth, and worshipped idols. Allah, exalted is He, sent to them Salih, and they were an Arab people, and Salih was of the middle of their lineage. He called them to Allah, mighty and majestic, and none followed him except a few weak people. He warned them and admonished them, so they asked him for a sign. He said: "What sign do you want?" They said: "Come out with us to our festival on a day known to them of the year, and you call upon your god and we call upon our gods. If your god is answered for you, we will follow you, and if ours is answered for us, you will follow us." Salih, peace be upon him, said: "Yes." So he went out with them. They called upon their idols and asked for a response, but they did not answer them. Then their chief Jundu' ibn 'Amr said, pointing to a solitary rock at the side of the mountain, which is called al-Kathibah: "Bring forth for us from this rock a she-camel, pregnant (mukhtarijah), hollow-sided and hairy-humped (wabra'), and if you do, we will believe you and respond to you." (Al-mukhtarijah is the one that resembles the Bactrian camel.) So Salih, peace be upon him, took their covenants that if he did this they would surely believe and affirm. They said: "Yes." So he prayed and called upon his Lord, and the rock labored like a woman in labor with her child, and it split open, and out came a she-camel, ten months pregnant, hollow-sided and hairy-humped as they had described, whose inner contents none knows but Allah, exalted is He, while their nobles watched. Then she gave birth to a young one like her in size. Jundu' and a group of his people believed, but some of their leaders prevented their descendants from believing. The she-camel remained with her young one, grazing the trees and drinking water, and she used to come to water on alternate days. On her day she would lower her head into the well and not raise it until she drank all that was in it, then she would spread her legs, and they would milk as much as they wished until their vessels were full, so they drank and stored. When the heat came she would summer on the back of the valley, and their livestock would flee from her, and she would descend to its bottom. When the cold came she would winter in the bottom of the valley, and their herds would flee to its back. This was difficult for them. Two women, 'Unayzah, mother of Ghanam, and Sadaqah, daughter of al-Mukhtar, adorned to them the slaughter of her, because she harmed their livestock, and they were both owners of many herds. So they slaughtered her, divided her meat, and cooked it. Her young one ran off until he climbed a mountain called Qarah and cried out three times. Salih, peace be upon him, had said to them: "Catch the young camel, perhaps the punishment will be lifted from you," but they could not overtake it. After its cry the rock split and it entered it. Salih said to them: "Tomorrow your faces will be yellow, and the day after your faces will be red, and on the third day your faces will be black, then the punishment will overtake you in the morning." When they saw the signs they sought to kill him, but Allah, exalted is He, delivered him to the land of Palestine. When the fourth day came and the forenoon rose, they embalmed themselves with aloe and shrouded themselves in leather, then a cry came to them from the sky and a quake from the earth, so their hearts were cut to pieces and they perished.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿This is the she-camel of Allah, a sign for you﴾, is a resumptive clause (istinaf) brought to explain the bayyinah. The addition of the she-camel to the Majestic Name is for glorifying her, and because she came from Him, exalted is He, without known causes or customary intermediaries; for this reason she was a sign, and what a sign. ﴿For you﴾ is an explanation of for whom she is a sign.

The accusative of āyah (ﷻ, sign) is in the circumstantial (ḥāl) position, and the operator in it is the meaning of the demonstrative (ishārah).
