It is permissible that ﴿the she-camel of Allah﴾ be a substitute (badal) for ﴿this﴾, or an explicative apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) for it, or a second subject (mubtada'), with ﴿for you﴾ as the predicate (khabar), the operator in it being āyah.

﴿So leave her﴾ is a consequence (tafrī') of her being one of the signs of Allah, exalted is He, for that necessitates not interfering with her.

﴿She will eat upon the earth of Allah﴾ is the answer to the imperative; that is: the she-camel is the she-camel of Allah and the earth is the earth of Allah, exalted is He, so leave her to eat what she eats on the earth of her Lord; you have no right to come between her and it. It was also read ﹛taʾkulu﹜ (she eats) with the nominative, on the basis that it is in the position of a circumstantial (ḥāl): i.e., eating upon it.

The absence of mention of drinking is either because it is sufficed by mention of eating, or because it is generalized to include it as well, as in the poet's saying:

I fed her straw and cold water.

This was mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For her is a drink, and for you is a drink on a known day﴾.

﴿And do not touch her with harm﴾: he forbade the touching which is the preliminary to striking with evil, which includes all kinds of harm. The word harm (sū') is indefinite for the sake of emphasis in the prohibition; that is: do not in any way harm her with anything that would injure her at all, do not drive her away, and do not disturb her, in honor of the sign of Allah, exalted is He.

﴿Lest there seize you a painful punishment﴾ is the answer to the prohibition. It is related that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when he passed by al-Hijr during the expedition of Tabuk, said to his companions: "None of you should enter the town, nor drink from its water, nor enter upon these punished people unless you are weeping, lest there befall you what befell them."

The Prophet (ﷺ) also said to 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him: "O 'Ali, do you know who is the most wretched of the first generations?" He said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "The slayer of the she-camel of Salih. Do you know who is the most wretched of the last generations?" He said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "Your slayer."

ـ Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 74:

﴿And remember when He made you successors after ʿĀd﴾; i.e., successors in the land, or successors to them, as has passed.

﴿and settled you in the land﴾; i.e., He made for you a dwelling and a place to live in the land of al-Ḥijr, between the Ḥijāz and Syria.

﴿You take from its plains palaces﴾: this is a resumptive clause (istiʾnāf) explaining the manner of the settlement; i.e., you build lofty palaces in its plains, or you build from the softness of the earth, using what you know of it of gypsum (al-raṣh), mud brick (al-labin), and fired brick (al-ājurr).

﴿and you hew the mountains﴾ (p-243); i.e., the rocks. It was also read as (taṇḥatūna) with a fatḥah on the ḥāʾ, and (tanāḥatūna) with the fatḥah lengthened, as in the verse of the poet:

*yunbāʿu min dhifrā ʾasīlin ḥurratin*

Al-naḥt (hewing) is the planing of a hard thing, so the accusative of "the mountains" is as a direct object (mafʿūl bihi).

As for the accusative of His words, exalted is He, ﹛houses﹜ (buyūtan), it is as a circumstantial qualifier that is anticipated (ḥāl muqaddarah) from them, as you say: "I sewed this garment as a shirt." It has also been said: the accusative of "the mountains" is by dropping the preposition, i.e., "from the mountains," and the accusative of "houses" is as a direct object. It has also been permitted that hewing (al-naḥt) be taken to include the meaning of taking (al-ittikhādh), so both are in the accusative as direct objects. It has been said: they used to dwell in the plains in summer and in the mountains in winter.

﴿So remember the bounties of God﴾, which He has bestowed upon you of what has been mentioned, or all of His bounties of which these are part.

﴿and do not commit corruption in the land, causing mischief﴾; for the due of His bounties, exalted is He, is that they be given thanks, not neglected or forgotten. How then with disbelief and wickedness in the land through corruption?

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 75:

﴿The chiefs of those of his people who were arrogant said﴾; that is, they transgressed and became proud. It is a resumption (isti'naf), as has passed, and it has been read with a waw as a conjunction (atf) upon what precedes it, namely the Almighty's words: "﴿O my people﴾ ..." and so on.

The lam in the Almighty's words ﴿to those who were deemed weak﴾ is for communication (li'l-tabligh).

The Almighty's words ﴿to those of them who believed﴾ are a substitute (badal) for the relative pronoun (al-mawsul), by repeating the governing element, as a substitute of the whole (badal al-kull) if the pronoun in ﴿of them﴾ refers to ﴿his people﴾, and as a substitute of part (badal al-ba'd) if it refers to ﴿those who were deemed weak﴾, on the basis that among those deemed weak there were some who did not believe. The first is the preferred reading, since there is no reason to direct the address first to all the weak, especially since the answer is given to the believers among them, on the basis that the deeming weak was specific to the believers; that is, they said to the believers whom they had deemed weak and considered lowly.

﴿Do you know that Salih is one sent from his Lord?﴾ They said this by way of mockery of them.

﴿They said: Indeed we are believers in that with which he has been sent.﴾ They turned away from the answer that corresponds to their question, which would have been to say "Yes," or "We know that he is sent from Him, exalted is He," hastening to affirm the truth and to display the firm, continuous faith they possessed, which the nominal sentence (al-jumlah al-ismiyyah) indicates, and as an alert that the matter of his being sent is so manifest that it should not be asked about; rather, what is worthy of being asked about is faith in it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 76:

﴿Those of them who were arrogant said﴾ The relative pronoun (al-mawsul, "those who") is repeated along with its relative clause (silah), although a pronoun would have sufficed; this is to signal that they said what they said in a manner of insolence (utuww) and arrogance (istikbar).

﴿Indeed, we are disbelievers in that which you have believed in﴾ And the reason they did not say "Indeed, we are disbelievers in that with which he was sent" is to display their opposition to them and to reject their statement.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 77:

﴿So they hamstrung the she-camel﴾; i.e., they slaughtered her. The hamstringing is attributed to all of them, although the actual doing was by some of them, either because of their association with it, or because it was done with their approval, so it is as if all of them did it. And in this there is an exaggeration of the gravity of the matter and its horror, to the extent that its calamity reached all of them, which is not hidden.

﴿And they transgressed against the command of their Lord﴾; i.e., they were arrogant in refusing to comply with it, namely the commands and prohibitions that Salih, peace be upon him, had conveyed to them.

﴿And they said﴾, addressing him, peace be upon him, in a manner of challenge and confounding, according to their claim:

﴿O Salih, bring us what you threaten us with﴾; i.e., of the punishment. The unrestricted phrasing is because it was known to him with certainty.

﴿If you are among the messengers﴾, for your being one of them requires the truthfulness of what you say of the promise and the threat. (p-244)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 78:

﴿So the earthquake seized them﴾; that is, the quaking (al-zalzalah), but not immediately after they said what they said, rather after there had befallen them what befell them of the first stages of the punishment during the three days, as its detail has passed.

﴿So they became in their abode﴾; that is, they became in their land and their country, or in their dwellings.

﴿Prostrate (jathimin)﴾: lifeless, dead, with no movement in them. The root of al-jutum (jathm) is al-buruk (kneeling down), as it is said: "The people are juthum," that is, seated, without movement in them, and they do not utter a sound (nabsah).

Abu 'Ubaydah said: al-jutum is used for people and birds, and al-buruk for camels. The meaning is that they were in that state at the onset of the descent of the punishment upon them, without agitation or movement, as occurs at a customary death. What is contained in this of severity of seizure and swiftness of assault is not hidden. O Allah, we seek refuge in You from the descent of Your wrath and the alighting of Your anger.

"Jathimin" is a predicate (khabar) of "asbahu," and the adverbial phrase (zarf) is connected to it; there is no room for it to be the predicate. Or "jathimin" is a circumstantial clause (hal), since otherwise the information about their being in their abode would become the primary intended matter, while their being prostrate would be a subordinate qualifier not intended in itself. It has been said: wherever the earthquake (al-rajfah) is mentioned, the abode is singular, and wherever the cry (al-sayhah) is mentioned, it is plural, because the cry came from the sky, so its reach is greater and more forceful than the earthquake; thus each of them is paired with what is most fitting to it.

﴿So he turned away from them﴾, upon witnessing what had befallen them. He turned away distressed, grieving over the faith they had missed, sorrowful on their account.

﴿And he said: "O my people, I had certainly conveyed to you the message of my Lord and given you sincere counsel"﴾ through encouragement and warning, and I expended my utmost effort on your behalf, but you did not accept that from me.

The form of the present tense in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿But you do not love those who give sincere counsel﴾, is a narration of a past state; that is, your established condition is to continue in hatred of those who give sincere counsel and enmity toward them. He (ﷺ) addressed them with this, in the manner of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) addressing the people of the well of Badr, when he said: "Indeed we have found what our Lord promised us to be true; have you found what your Lord promised you to be true?"

It was also said: he turned away from them before the punishment descended upon them, at the moment he (ﷺ) observed its signs; he turned away departing from them, disavowing their persistence in what they were upon.

It is narrated that their slaughter of the she-camel took place on Wednesday, and the punishment descended upon them on Saturday. It is also narrated that he went out with one hundred and ten of the Muslims while weeping, then he turned and saw the smoke rising, and he knew that they had perished. They were a thousand and five hundred households. It is also narrated that he returned with those who were with him, and they settled in their dwellings.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 80:

﴿And Lot﴾ is in the accusative, governed by a suppressed verb, and coordinated with what preceded. The non-mention of those to whom he was sent, placed before the accusative (as occurred in what came before and after), has already been explained in the story of Hud, peace be upon him. He was Lot son of Haran son of Terah, the nephew of Abraham. He was from the land of Babylon in Iraq together with his uncle Abraham. Then (Abraham) emigrated to al-Sham and settled in Palestine, and he settled Lot in al-Urdunn, which is a district in al-Sham. Then God Most High sent him to the people of Sodom (Sadum), which is a town in Homs.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿when he said to his people﴾ is an adverbial clause (zarf) for the suppressed verb mentioned; that is: We sent Lot to his people at the time he said to them ... etc.

Perhaps the restriction of his sending, peace be upon him, by this is because his being sent to them was not at the first moment of his arrival among them.

It has also been said: it is a substitute (badal) for "Lot," a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal), on the basis that its accusative status is governed by "remember" (udhkur); that is: remember the time when he, peace be upon him, said to his people: ﴿Do you commit the abomination﴾ by way of reproachful, rebuking denunciation; that is: Do you do that deed which is extremely ugly, persisting in (p-245) wickedness and evil?

﴿that no one in the worlds has committed before you﴾: "what has preceded you with it" means: no one has done it before you, with the "ba'" being for transitivity (ta'diyah), as in his, peace be upon him, saying: "Ukkasha has preceded you with it," from your saying: "I preceded him with the ball," that is: I struck it before him.

The "min" in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿from anyone﴾ is superfluous (zaidah), for emphasizing the negation and conveying the meaning of comprehensiveness.

In His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿from among the worlds﴾, the "min" is partitive (tab'id), and the sentence is a new independent clause (mustanafah) brought for emphasizing the disapproval and intensifying the rebuke and reproach, for directly committing the ugly act and inventing it is uglier. God Most High first denounced them for committing the abomination, then rebuked them for being the first to do it. Although the composition of the noble arrangement is on the negation of their being preceded, without addressing their being precursors, the intended meaning is that they are precursors to everyone else among the worlds, as its verification has been explained many times over, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against God﴾.

Or it is brought as an answer to an assumed question, as if it had been said on their behalf: "Why should we not do it?" So it was said, as an explanation of the cause and a manifestation of the deterrent: ﴿No one has preceded you with it﴾, due to its extreme ugliness and the evil of its path, so how can you do it?

'Amr ibn Dinar said: No male mounted a male until the people of Lot. Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: They had fruits and villages the like of which did not exist in the world, so people targeted them and harmed them. Then Iblis appeared to them in the form of an old man, saying: If you do such-and-such to them, you will be rid of them. They refused. When people pressed them, they targeted them, and they encountered young boys in the morning and they were corrupted, and this became entrenched among them.

Al-Hasan said: They did not do that except with strangers. Al-Kalbi said: The first one upon whom that act was done was the wicked Iblis, when he appeared to them in the form of a handsome young man, invited them to himself, and then they played with that deed.

"You indeed approach men" is a new (independent) statement, explaining that abomination. It is also read with two clear hamzas, and with the second hamza softened without elongation, and also with elongation (madd). This is an emphasis on the earlier denunciation and an intensification of the rebuke. The addition of "إنّ" and the "لام" adds further rebuke and reproach, as if that act were something that could not be imagined as coming from anyone, so it is stressed with strong emphasis. The use of the word "الرِّجال" (men) rather than "الغِلمان" (boys), "المِردان" (beardless youths), or similar terms is an intensification of the rebuke.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿شَهْوَةً﴾ (desire) is either an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu) or a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (hal). In restricting the act to desire, there is a description of them as mere beasts, and an admonition that a rational person should have as his motive for intimacy the seeking of offspring and the continuation of the species, not the fulfilment of appetite. It is also possible that the intended meaning is denunciation of them and reproach for their desiring that vile and detestable deed, as his saying, Exalted is He, indicates: ﴿مِن دُونِ النِّساءِ﴾ (apart from women), that is, going beyond the women who are the object of desire, as his saying, Exalted is He, indicates: ﴿هُنَّ أطْهَرُ لَكُمْ﴾ (they are purer for you).

﴿بَلْ أنْتُمْ قَوْمٌ مُسْرِفُونَ﴾ (Rather, you are a people who exceed the limits). This is a turning away from the preceding denunciation to a report of their state, which led them to commit the like of such acts, namely the habit of excess in everything. Or it is a turning away from denunciation of this act to blame for all their faults. Or it is a turning away from an implied omission, meaning: there is no excuse for you in it; rather, you are a people whose habit is excess.

(p-246) is a page marker in the source; I'll keep it as is in the text.

**Verse 82:** ﴿And the answer of his people was not but that they said﴾; that is, the arrogant among them, those who took charge of commanding and forbidding, and who presumed to bind and loose.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿except that they said﴾ is an exceptive (istithna' mufarragh, "emptied exception," i.e., an exception from a general category with no stated subject) from the most general of things; that is, nothing whatsoever was the answer from the side of his people except their saying, that is, to some of them, to the others who were directly handling the affairs, turning away from addressing him, peace be upon him.

﴿Expel them﴾; that is, Lot and those with him of his family who believed.

﴿from your town﴾; that is, except this statement, which it is impossible to be an answer to the speech of (p-246) Lot, peace be upon him. It is also read with the nominative *jawab* on the basis that it is the subject of *kana*, and *illa an qalu... ilakh* is its predicate, and this is the more evident reading.

Although the first (reading) is stronger in grammatical construction (sina'ah), because the more definite deserves to be the noun (of kana). In any case, the intent is not that nothing proceeded from them in the way of an answer to Lot's discourses and admonitions except this false statement, as is what comes quickly to understanding; rather, in the last instance of the exchanges that took place between them and him, peace be upon him, nothing proceeded from them except this shameful word; otherwise many trivialities had proceeded from them before that, as is related of them in the other noble surahs. This is the way (to understand) its counterparts that come in the form of restriction (qasr).

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed they are people who purify themselves﴾ is a justification for the command to expel them. Describing them as purifying themselves is for mockery and derision of them, and (for) their purifying themselves from indecencies and filth, and boasting of the uncleanness in which they are, as is the religion of the rogues and the miscreants.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 83:

﴿So We saved him and his family﴾; i.e., the believers among them.

﴿Except his wife﴾: an exception from "his family," for she was concealing her disbelief (kufr).

﴿She was among those who remained behind﴾; i.e., those who stayed behind in their dwellings and perished therein. The masculine form (al-taghlib, "predominance of the masculine") is used for the sake of predominance, and to clarify that she deserves what those who committed the foul deed (al-fahisha) deserve.

The sentence is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), coming as an answer to a question arising from her being excepted from the rule of salvation, as if it were said: "What was her state?" So it was said: "She was among those who remained behind."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 84:

﴿And We rained upon them a rain﴾; that is, a kind of rain that was strange. Its nature is explained by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We rained upon them stones of baked clay﴾.

Abu 'Ubayda said: "matara" is used for mercy, and "umtira" is used for punishment. And al-Raghib said: "matara" is used for good, and "umtira" is used for punishment. The correct view is that "amtarna" means: We sent upon them the sending of rain (irsal al-matar).

It has been said: the Mu'tafikah (the overturned cities) were five cities. It has been said: they were four thousand, between Syria and Medina, and God rained upon them sulphur and fire. It has been said: those who remained among them were swallowed up by the earth, and stones rained upon their travellers and stragglers. It has been said: they were first rained upon, and then swallowed up by the earth.

It is narrated that a merchant among them was in the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram), and the stone stood over him for forty days until he finished his trade and left the Sacred Precinct, whereupon it fell upon him. It is also narrated that his wife turned toward her dwellings, and a stone struck her, and she died.

﴿So look how was the end of the criminals﴾: an address to everyone capable of reflection and contemplation, expressing wonder at their condition and a warning against their deeds.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 85:

﴿And to Madyan [We sent] their brother Shu'ayb.﴾ This is a conjunction (ʿatf) with his statement, ﴿And to ʿAd [We sent] their brother Hud﴾, and what is conjoined to it. Here the fronting of the prepositional phrase over the object has been observed, as in the conjoined clause; that is: "And We sent to them," and they were the descendants of Madyan ibn Ibrahim, peace be upon him, Shu'ayb ibn Mika'il ibn Yashjar ibn Madyan.

It is also said: Shu'ayb ibn Thuwayb ibn Madyan. It is also said: Shu'ayb ibn Yathrun ibn Madyan. He was called "the orator of the prophets" (khatib al-anbiya', the best of the prophets in argument) because of the excellence of his address to his people. They were people who cheated in measures and weights, along with their disbelief.

﴿He said﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) built upon a question arising from the narration of his being sent to them, as if it were said: "What did he say to them?" And so it was said: "He said."

﴿O my people, worship God; you have no god other than Him﴾: its explanation has passed many times.

﴿Indeed, a clear proof has come to you﴾; that is, a miracle.

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿from your Lord﴾ is connected to "has come to you," or to an omitted element that serves as a relative clause describing its subject, confirming its intrinsic grandeur derived from its indefiniteness, with its added grandeur; that is: a great, manifest proof coming from your Lord and the Master of your affairs.

His miracle, peace be upon him, is not mentioned in the Noble Qur'an, just as most of the miracles of the Prophet ﷺ are not mentioned. Among them is what is narrated of the staff of Musa, peace be upon him, fighting the dragon when he handed over his sheep to him; and among them is the birth of sheep that were striped exclusively when he promised that the striped ones would be his from among their offspring; and among them is the staff of Adam, peace be upon him, falling into his hand in the seven times; because all of that was before Musa, peace be upon him, was made a prophet.

It is also said: the proof (bayyinah) is his coming, peace be upon him, as in His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿O my people, tell me, if I am upon a clear proof from my Lord﴾; that is, an evident argument and a luminous demonstration, and both are used to express what God gave him of prophethood and wisdom.

﴿So give full measure﴾; that is, the measuring vessel (al-mikyal), as occurred in Surah Hud.

This is supported by His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿and the balance﴾, for what comes first to mind from it is the instrument, although it is permissible for it to be a verbal noun, like al-mi'ad. It is also said: the instrument of measuring, and the weighing is on the basis of an implied element. The fa' (then) indicates the sequence of the command upon the arrival of the proof. It is permissible that it be coordinating (ʿatif) with "worship," for worship of God, may He be exalted, necessitates abstaining from the prohibited acts, the greatest of which after disbelief is cheating, which they used to practice.

﴿And do not diminish people's goods﴾ which you buy with these two, relying on their completeness, whatever the thing and whatever the quantity, for they used to cheat in the great and the small, and in the little and the much.

It is also said: they were tax-collectors who would not leave anything without levying a tax on it. Zuhayr said:

"Is there in every market of Iraq a levy, and on every dirham that a man sells, a tithe?"

﴿And do not cause corruption on the earth﴾; that is, through disbelief and injustice.

﴿after its reformation﴾: after the prophets and their followers had set its affairs and its people aright by implementing the laws, or they had made reform therein; and its attribution to it is like the attribution of "the plotting of the night and the day."

﴿That is better for you﴾: a reference to acting upon what he commanded them and forbade them from. The meaning of being better is either increase in general, or in humanity and good repute, and what they seek of profit and gain; for when people know them for trustworthiness, they are eager to deal and trade with them.

﴿If you are believers﴾; that is, if you believe me in this statement of mine.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 86:

﴿And do not sit on every path, threatening [people] and turning away from the way of Allah﴾; i.e., on every route of the religion, such as the Shaytan (devil). And the path of truth, although it is one, branches out into knowledge, limits and rulings; and whenever they saw anyone beginning on any of these, they would prevent him.

It is said: they would sit at the lookout posts, and say to whoever wanted to go to Shu'ayb: "He is a liar; let him not tempt you away from your religion," and they would threaten whoever believed in him. It is also said: they would cut off the road.

﴿and turning away from the way of Allah﴾; i.e., the way on which they sat, so the apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun, to clarify "every path," to indicate the greatness of what they were turning people away from, and to denounce what they were upon. Or [the referent is] belief in Allah, or every path, on the basis that it is an expression for the routes of the religion.

The words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿whoever believes in him﴾, are the object of "turning away" by the principle of giving precedence to the nearer [verb], for had it been the object of "threatening," it would have been said: "and turning them away," and "threatening" would be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "do not sit."

﴿and seeking to make it crooked﴾; i.e., and seeking for the way of Allah to be crooked, by casting doubts, or by describing it to the people as crooked, while it is farthest of all things from any trace of crookedness. (p-248)

﴿And remember when you were few, and He multiplied you﴾ through blessing in offspring and wealth.

﴿And observe how was the end of the corrupters﴾ among the past nations, such as the people of Noah, and those after them: 'Ad, Thamud and their likes; so take warning from them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 87:

﴿And if there is a group among you who have believed in that with which I have been sent﴾ — of the laws and rulings (al-shara'i').

﴿And a group who have not believed﴾; that is, in it (i.e., in what I was sent with), or they did not perform (the act of) belief.

﴿So be patient until Allah judges between us﴾; that is, between the two groups, by giving victory to the righteous (al-muhiqqun) over the falsifiers (al-mubtilun). So this is a promise to the believers and a warning to the disbelievers.

﴿And He is the best of judges﴾, since there is no one who can reverse His judgment and no injustice (haif) in it.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 88:**

﴿The chiefs of those of his people who were arrogant said﴾ is a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*) answering an implied question that the discourse itself suggests, as if it were said: "What did they say after they heard these admonitions from Shu'ayb, peace be upon him?" It was said: The eminent ones of his people who were arrogant, presuming over him, peace be upon him, did not content themselves with merely disobeying him and refusing obedience to him, but went to such lengths of insolence and arrogance that they intended to subjugate him, peace be upon him, together with those who followed him among the believers, and they dared to compel them with the threat of expulsion, and they addressed him with this by way of emphatic oath.

﴿"We will surely expel you, O Shu'ayb, and those who believe with you"﴾: the expulsion is attributed to him, peace be upon him, first, and to the believers second, by conjoining them to him, to draw attention to his being the original agent of the expulsion and their following him in it, as indicated by the words of Allah, Exalted: ﴿with you﴾, for it is connected with the expulsion, not with the belief. The placement of the vocative with his proper name between the two conjoined nouns serves to add emphasis and a threat, arising from the extreme of impudence and tyranny; that is: "By Allah, we will surely expel you and your followers."

﴿"from our town"﴾: out of hatred for you and to repel your temptation (*fitnah*), which results from cohabitation and proximity.

As for the words of Allah, Exalted: ﴿"or you will certainly return to our religion"﴾, it is conjoined to the answer of the oath; that is: "By Allah, one of the two matters will definitely occur," while the primary intent is the return, and the mention of the negation and the expulsion was only for the sake of mere compulsion and constraint, as is made clear by his, peace be upon him, not addressing the answer concerning the expulsion. It is as if they said: "We will not leave you among us until you enter our religion." Their including him, peace be upon him, in the address of return, although it is impossible that he was in their religion before that, is only by way of the group being given precedence over the single individual. They did not say "or we will restore you" in the manner of what preceded, because their intention was that they should return to it by way of compliance, out of fear of expulsion, by choosing the lesser of two evils, not their being returned by all forms of coercion and torment.

﴿He said﴾ is a resumptive clause as before; that is: He, peace be upon him, said in rejection of their false statement and in denial of their wicked oaths.

﴿"Even though we were averse?"﴾ The hamzah here is for denying the occurrence and negating it, not for denying what occurs and finding it reprehensible, like the one in His words, Exalted: ﴿"Even if I brought you clear evidence?"﴾. It is permissible that the interrogation in it remains in its own state. It has been mentioned repeatedly that the word *law* (لَوْ, "even if/even though") in such a context is not for clarifying the non-existence of a thing in the past because of the non-existence of something else in it, so no answer is considered for it, which has been omitted, relying on what precedes it indicating it by an intentional consideration, except when intending to explain the grammatical analysis according to the technical rules of grammar. Rather, it is for clarifying the realization of what the preceding speech conveys (p-249), either directly or indirectly, of the affirmed or negated ruling, in every assumed state among the states accompanying it in general terms, by placing it before the state most distant from it and most contrary to it, so that by its establishment or its negation together with it, its establishment becomes manifest, or its negation together with all other states becomes manifest by way of priority, since whenever a thing is realized together with a strong contrary, it is all the more fitting that it is realized together with something else.

For this reason, no other states are mentioned along with it, and it suffices with mentioning the conjunction *wa* (and), which conjoins the sentence to its counterpart opposite it, which encompasses all the different states when they are multiple. This is the meaning of their saying that it is for surveying the states in a general manner. This meaning is evident in the affirmative and negative declarative, and in the command and prohibition, as in your saying: "So-and-so is generous, he gives even if he is poor," or "miserly, he does not give even if he is rich," and as in your saying: "Be good to him even if he mistreats you," and "Do not humiliate him even if he humiliates you," because it remains in its state, sound from anything that would change it.

As for what we are concerned with here, there is in it a kind of obscurity due to its being altered by the introduction of the denial upon it. Nevertheless, the basis in all of them is one, except that the word *law* in the cited forms is attached to the very verb mentioned before it, and that what is intended to clarify its realization in every state is its own signified meaning, and that the sentence is a state (*hal*) of its pronoun, or of what is connected to it, and that what falls within the scope of *law* is established as it is in its being improbable. This differs from what we are concerned with, because the word *law* in it is attached to a verb suppressed (*muqaddar*) which the mentioned one requires, and that what is intended to clarify its realization in every state is its signified meaning and not the signified meaning of the mentioned one, and that the sentence is a state of its pronoun and not of the pronoun of the mentioned one, as will come.

And the primary intent is the denial of its signified meaning from the standpoint of its being accompanied by the mentioned state; as for assuming its accompaniment with other states, it is for broadening the scope. And what falls within the scope of *law* is not intended to be deemed improbable in itself, but it is intended to convey that it is an established matter, though it has been presented in the form of improbability for the sake of exaggeration in denial, from the perspective that returning is something that is denied when aversion is a matter that is considered improbable; so how much more so when aversion is an established matter, and the addressees are dealt with according to their own belief, in order to bring them down from the rank of obstinacy. The meaning of aversion here is not merely the aversion of the believers to returning to the religion of disbelief initially, such that it might be said that it is known to them, so how could it be improbable in their view? Rather, it is only their aversion to him after the threat of expulsion, which was made equal to killing in His words, Exalted: ﴿And if We had prescribed for them...﴾ the verse, for they used to deem it improbable and hoped that at that point they would choose to return out of fear of expulsion, since many a disliked thing is chosen when there comes what is more severe and more dreadful than it.

The estimated sense is: "Would we return to it if we were not averse, and even if we were averse, being indifferent to compulsion?" So the sentence is in the accusative position as a state of the suppressed verb's pronoun, as indicated, since its outcome is: "Would we return to it in a state of non-aversion, and in a state of aversion," as a denial of what their abominable word conveys by its generality, that of returning in whatever state it may be. However, it suffices with mentioning the second state, which is the most severe of the states, the most contrary to returning and the furthest from it, as an alert that it is the one that actually occurs, and with confidence that it sufficiently replaces the first, because the return which the denial relates to, when it is realized together with aversion according to what their speech requires, then it is all the more fitting that it is realized together with its absence. If you say: the negation derived from the denial interrogative here is in the position of explicit negation.

There is no doubt that the priority there is considered with respect to the negation. Do you not see that the more appropriate for realization in the example of negation, in the unmentioned state, namely the absence of wealth, is the non-giving and not the negation itself? So it should have been that the more appropriate for realization here, in the state of non-aversion, is the non-return and not the return itself, since it is what our saying "would we return" indicates, because it has the meaning of "we would not return." So why did the situation differ between them?

I say: because the basis of priority is the ruling (p-250) whose realization in every state is intended to be clarified. In the example of negation, that is the non-giving derived from the mentioned negated verb. As for what we are concerned with, it is the return itself derived from the suppressed verb, since it is what the preceding speech requires, namely their saying: "you will surely return."

As for the interrogation, it is outside of this and comes upon it in order to nullify what it conveys and to negate what it requires, not that it is part of its completion as in the form of negation. To clarify: between the two negations there is a semantic difference by which their rulings differ, one of which is the consideration of priority in one of them with respect to itself, and in the other with respect to its complement. For this reason, it is not valid to substitute one for the other in an absolute sense. Do you not see that if you said in place of "would we return to it..." etc.: "We will not return to it even if we were averse," the meaning would be gravely corrupted? Because the signified meaning of the first is the negation of return restricted to the state of aversion, and the signified meaning of the second is the restriction of the negated return by it. That is because the particle of negation directly attaches to the verb itself and negates it, and what is mentioned after it returns to it in terms of it being negated. As for the interrogative hamzah, it directly attaches to the verb after its restriction by what follows it, because its signifying denial and negation is not a signification by fixed convention like the signification of the particle of negation, such that its meaning is connected to the very verb that follows it, and what follows it returns to it in terms of it being negated. Rather, it is an intellectual signification derived from the context of the speech. Therefore, what is mentioned after the verb must necessarily be among its impediments and motives for denying and negating it, so as to serve as a clear indicator diverting the hamzah from its literal meaning to the meaning of denial and negation. Then, since the intention is to negate the ruling in every state while confining oneself to mentioning some of them, which suffices without mentioning the rest, because its realization together with it entails its realization together with others by way of priority, and since the state of aversion when it is a restriction of the return itself is like that (i.e., sufficient without mentioning the other states), since the realization of return in a state of aversion necessarily entails its realization in a state of non-aversion, and when it is a restriction of its negation it is otherwise (i.e., not sufficient without mentioning the others), since the negation of return in a state of aversion does not entail its negation in other states; rather the matter is reversed, for its negation in a state of will necessarily entails its negation in a state of aversion, definitively. The first was correct because it conveys the negation of return in both states while confining itself to what mentions the one that suffices without mentioning the other.

The second was not correct, because it does not convey that in the aforementioned manner. If it is said: what is the reason for both being correct when the two conjuncts are mentioned together, such that it is valid to say: "We will not return to it if we were not averse," just as it is valid to say: "Would we return to it if we were not averse, and even if we were averse," although the estimated is in the status of the pronounced? We say: its reason is that each of them conveys a meaning that is correct in itself, not that the meaning of one of them is identical to the meaning of the other, nor that they are mutually implicative and agreeing in all rulings. How could that be, when the signified meaning of the first is that return is negated in both states, and the signified meaning of the second is that the negation of return in both states is established, and it is an invalidator of the negation of return in both states, which is negated? Both meanings are correct in themselves, validating the negation of return in both states when both are mentioned together. However, the second validates the negation of return in both states while confining itself to mentioning the state of aversion, contrary to the first meaning, for it validates its negation in both states while confining itself to mentioning the state of will.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 89:

﴿We have indeed fabricated a lie against Allah, if we return to your religion﴾ (p-251) That is: a tremendous lie, whose magnitude cannot be estimated.

﴿If we return to your religion (millah)﴾ which is shirk (associating partners with Allah), and the answer to the conditional is omitted, because what precedes it indicates it; that is: if we return to your religion.

﴿After Allah has delivered us from it﴾ then we have indeed fabricated a tremendous lie against Allah, since we would then be claiming that Almighty Allah has a rival, while "there is nothing like unto Him," and that it has become clear to us that what we were upon of Islam is false, and that what you were upon of disbelief is true. And what fabrication could be greater than that? It has also been said that it is the answer to an omitted oath, from which the lam has been dropped; its estimated form being: "By Allah, we have indeed fabricated ..." and so on.

﴿And it is not for us﴾; that is: it is not right for us and it is not proper for us.

﴿To return to it﴾ in any state whatsoever, or at any time whatsoever.

﴿Unless Allah should will it﴾; that is: except in the state of the will of Almighty Allah, or at the time of His will for our returning to it.

This is among the things that scarcely could occur, as indicated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord﴾, for mention of the title of His lordship over them is among the things that indicate the impossibility of His will for their apostasy, definitively. Likewise His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿After Allah has delivered us from it﴾, for His delivering them from it is among the proofs of His not willing their return to it.

It has been said: its meaning is: "unless Allah should will our abandonment (khidhlan)." It has also been said: in it is evidence that disbelief is by the will of Almighty Allah. In any case, the intent of this is not to explain that returning to it is within the realm of possibility and a matter of likely occurrence, based on the premise that His will is of that sort; rather, it is to explain the impossibility of its occurrence, as if it were said: "It was not for us to return to it, unless Allah our Lord should will it, and far-fetched is that," by the evidence of what has been mentioned of the factors necessitating His not willing it for them.

﴿Our Lord has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾ So He is encompassing of all that has been and all that will be of things, among which are the states of His servants, their resolutions and intentions, and what is fitting for each one of them. So it is impossible, from His kindness, that He would will our return to it after He has delivered us from it, given that we hold fast to Him alone, as His saying, Exalted is He, expresses: ﴿In Allah we have put our trust﴾; that is: regarding that He should make us firm upon what we are upon of faith, and complete His favor upon us by delivering us from polytheism entirely. The use of the glorious Name in the place of the pronoun is for the sake of intensifying supplication and entreaty.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, decide between us and our people in truth﴾ is a turning away from debating with them, following what became apparent to him, upon him be prayer and peace, that they are of such obstinacy and stubbornness that faith from them cannot be conceived at all; and it is a turning to Allah, Exalted is He, in supplication for the separating of what is between him and them in a manner befitting the condition of each of the two parties; that is: judge between us in truth. The "fataha" means judgment; or: make our matter manifest so that what is between us and them is made clear, and the one who is right is distinguished from the one who is wrong, from "fataha al-mushkil" when he explained it.

﴿And You are the best of judges﴾ is a concluding phrase confirming the content of what precedes it under both meanings.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 90:

﴿And the chiefs of those among his people who disbelieved said﴾ is coordinated with "﴿The chiefs of those who were arrogant said﴾..." etc. Perhaps these are other than those arrogant ones, and lower in rank than them; their role is to act as intermediaries between them and the common people, and to take care of their affairs as the arrogant see fit.

It is also permissible that they are the very same as the first group, and the change of the relative clause is because the basis of this their saying is disbelief, just as the basis of their previous saying was arrogance. That is: their nobles who persisted in disbelief, for their own followers, after they witnessed the steadfastness of Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) and those believers who were with him in faith, and feared that they would win over their people, deterring them from faith in him and turning them away from it, by way of emphatic oath, "By Allah, ﴿if you follow Shu'ayb﴾ and enter into his religion and abandon the religion of your fathers,

﴿then you will indeed be losers﴾"; that is: in religion, for exchanging guidance for misguidance, or in the worldly life, for the loss of what you would gain through fraud and cheating in measure.

"Idhan" is a particle of response and consequence, placed parenthetically between the subject of "inna" and its predicate, and the clause takes the place of the two answers: the condition and the oath which the lam preceded (p-252).

﴿So the earthquake seized them﴾; that is, the quake (al-zalzalah). Likewise in Surah al-'Ankabut. And in Surah Hud: ﴿And the cry seized those who did wrong﴾; that is, the cry of Jibril, upon him be peace. It may have been one of the beginnings of the earthquake. Thus their destruction was attributed at times to the immediate cause and at other times to the remote cause.

﴿So they became in their abode﴾; that is, in their city. In Surah Hud: ﴿in their homes﴾.

﴿Prostrate﴾; that is, dead, remaining in their places, with no escape from them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 92:

﴿Those who denied Shu'ayb—﴾ this is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining their ruin on account of the evil of their statement earlier: ﴿We will surely expel you, O Shu'ayb, and those who believe with you from our town﴾, and their punishment in return for his opposition to them.

The relative pronoun (al-mawsul) is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is the saying of the Most High: ﴿as if they had never prospered therein﴾; that is, they were utterly uprooted and became as though they had never dwelt in their town at all. That is, they were punished for their saying that, and they became those who were expelled from the town, an expulsion after which there would never be any return.

And the saying of the Most High: ﴿Those who denied Shu'ayb—they were the losers﴾ is another resumptive clause explaining their ruin on account of their final statement. The relative pronoun is repeated, with the relative clause unchanged, for the sake of emphasis and to signal that what was mentioned in the relative clause is what necessitated the two punishments. That is: those who denied him, peace be upon him, were punished for their final statement, and so they became the losers in this world and the next, not those who followed him, peace and blessings be upon him. By this restriction (qasr) the explicit mention of his deliverance, peace be upon him, is dispensed with, as occurs in Surah Hud in the saying of the Most High: ﴿And when Our command came, We delivered Shu'ayb and those who believed with him...﴾ etc.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 93:

﴿So he turned away from them and said: "O my people, I had certainly conveyed to you the messages of my Lord and advised you sincerely."﴾ He (ﷺ) said this after they had perished, out of grief over them, because of the intensity of his sorrow for them.

Then he disapproved of this in himself, saying: ﴿So how should I grieve﴾, I grieve with an intense grief,

﴿over a disbelieving people?﴾; that is, persisting in disbelief, who are not deserving of grief, because of their deserving what descended upon them due to their disbelief. Or he said it as an excuse for not having grieved intensely over them. The meaning: I had certainly exerted myself in conveying and warning, and expended my utmost effort in advising and showing compassion, but you did not believe my words, so how should I grieve over you? It was also read: (ʾĪsā) with two imālas.

﴿Never did We send a prophet to any town﴾: This is a general statement covering the conditions of all the nations, following the detailed account of the nations already mentioned. The particle "min" (مِن) is extra (zā'idah), used to emphasize the negation, and the descriptive qualifier is omitted; that is, "a prophet who was denied, or whom its people denied."

﴿except that We seized its people﴾: This is an exceptive construction of the type called istithnā' mufarragh (an exception in which the element excluded has no stated antecedent, so it is governed by the most general sense of the context) and is in the most general sense of conditions. The verb "akhadhnā" (أخذنا) is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause of the subject of "arsalnā." A past-tense verb does not follow "illā" except under one of two conditions: either the implied "qad" (قد) is understood, as in this verse, or "qad" accompanies the verb, as in your saying: "Zayd is only one who has indeed stood" (مَا زَيْدٌ إِلَّا قَدْ قَامَ). The sense is: "Never did We send a prophet among the nations of the destroyed towns, among the prophets, in any condition, except in the condition of Our seizing its people."

﴿with misery﴾: with poverty and destitution.

﴿and adversity﴾: with harm and sickness. However, this does not mean that the beginning of the sending coincides with the aforementioned seizing; rather, the seizing follows from it and is never separated from it in the end, because of their arrogance toward following their prophet and their haughtiness against him, as the nations mentioned did.

﴿so that they might humble themselves﴾: That they might submit and abase themselves, and lay down the cloaks of pride and might from their shoulders, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We indeed sent to nations before you, and We seized them with misery and adversity, that they might humble themselves﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 95:

﴿Then We replaced﴾ is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon "We seized" (akhadhna) and falls within its ruling.

﴿in place of the evil﴾ that afflicted them, for the aforementioned term.

﴿the good﴾; that is: We gave them, in place of what they had been in of hardship and trial, ease and abundance, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We tested them with good things and bad things﴾.

﴿until they multiplied﴾; that is: they increased in number and in equipment, from "afa al-nabat" (the plant grew), when it increased and became dense, and blessing made them insolent.

"They said" without pausing to consider that what had befallen them of the two conditions was a trial from God, glorified is He.

﴿Indeed, our fathers were touched by adversity and prosperity﴾, just as it touched us, and this is nothing but the custom of time (ʿadat al-dahr), which alternates among people between adversity and prosperity, without there being any cause that leads to either of them or any consequence that follows from them. Perhaps the mention of prosperity after adversity is meant to indicate that it follows adversity, so there is no harm in it.

﴿Then We seized them﴾ immediately after that.

﴿suddenly﴾, a sudden seizing of the most severe and dreadful kind.

﴿while they did not perceive﴾ it, and did not entertain in their minds any thought of calamities, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given...﴾, the verse. The meaning of "seizing suddenly" is not their destruction in the blink of an eye, as with the destruction of 'Ad and the people of Lot; rather it encompasses that, and between the seizing and the completion of the destruction there pass days, as in the case of Thamud.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 96:

﴿And if the people of the towns⦈; that is, the towns that were destroyed, indicated by His saying, ﴿in a town﴾. It has been said: it is Mecca and the towns around it. It has also been said: it is the category of towns encompassed by what has been mentioned here, in an initial sense of inclusion.

﴿had believed﴾ in what was revealed to their prophets, taking heed from what befell them of affliction through adversity and ease.

﴿and had been mindful of God﴾; that is, of disbelief and sins. Or: they were mindful of what they had been warned of through the tongues of the prophets, and did not persist in the vile deeds they had committed, and did not attribute God Most High's trial to the customary course of time. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, said: they affirmed the Oneness of God and guarded against shirk.

﴿We would have opened for them blessings from the heaven and the earth﴾: We would have widened good things for them and made them easy for them from every side, in place of the various kinds of punishment that had befallen them, some of which came from the heaven and some from the earth. It has been said: what is meant is rain and vegetation. It has also been read as (la-fattahna) with the doubled letter, for intensification.

﴿But they denied﴾; that is: but they did not believe and did not guard against evil. The first has been mentioned alone, as it entails the second.

﴿So We seized them for what they had been earning﴾ of the various kinds of disbelief and sins, of which among their number was their saying: ﴿Our fathers were touched﴾... and so on. This seizing is an expression for what is in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So We seized them suddenly﴾, not for barrenness and drought as has been said; for those two had already been removed by the replacement of the good for the bad.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 97:

﴿Do the people of the towns feel secure﴾; that is, the people of the towns mentioned, (p-254) by placing the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun. This is to signal that the basis of the rebuke is the security of each group from the punishment that came upon them, not the security of all the nations together, for each group among them was struck by a particular punishment that did not extend beyond them to others, as will come later.

The hamza (al-hamza, the interrogative particle) is for denying the actual occurrence and finding it abhorrent, not for denying and negating its occurrence, as Abu Shama and others have said. The evidence is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿None feels secure from the plot of Allah except the people who are losers﴾.

The fa' (fa', the conjunction) is for coordination with "We seized them" (akhadhnahum), and what lies between them is a parenthetical clause (i'tiradh, interjected phrase) placed between them, to hasten to explain that the seizing mentioned is from what their hands had earned. The meaning is: After that seizing, do the people of the towns feel secure?

﴿That His punishment comes upon them by night (bayatan)﴾; that is, as a verb of tabyit (spending the night / attacking by night), or at a time of bayat, that is, while they are spending the night, or while they are being attacked by night. It is originally a verbal noun meaning al-baytutah (passing the night), and it comes with the meaning of tabyit, just as salam means taslim.

﴿while they are asleep﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the pronoun hum (them) that is apparent, or to the concealed pronoun in bayatan.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 98:

﴿Do the people of the towns feel secure﴾ is a denial following a denial, for the sake of intensifying the severe rebuke. For this reason it does not say: "Then do the people of the towns feel secure that Our punishment will come upon them by night while they are sleeping, or in the forenoon while they are playing?" And it has been recited as "aw" (أوْ) with the "waw" vowelless (sukun), for the sense of alternation (tardid).

﴿That Our punishment comes upon them in the forenoon﴾; that is, at the time of the forenoon (ḍaḥwah al-nahar), which is originally the light of the sun when it has risen.

﴿While they are playing﴾; that is, they are amusing themselves out of extreme heedlessness, or they are occupied with what does not benefit them, as though they were playing.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah al-A'raf (7), verse 99:**

﴿Do they then feel secure from the plan of Allah?﴾ This is a repetition of the rebuke (al-nakir) to increase its affirmation (al-taqrir). "The plan of Allah" (makr Allah) is a metaphor (isti'arah) for His gradual leading of the servant on (istidraj, the gradual drawing of a person toward punishment while he is unaware) and His seizing him from where he does not expect. What is meant by it is the coming of His punishment (ba's) at the two times mentioned. For this reason the first and the third are joined by the letter fa' in the rebuke, and both point to the security being the result of the aforementioned seizing. As for the second, it is a completion of the first.

﴿None feels secure from the plan of Allah except the losing people.﴾ That is, those who have lost their own souls and have neglected the natural disposition (fitrah) of Allah upon which He created people, and the near readiness (isti'dad) that is derived from reflecting on the signs.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 100:

﴿Is it not clear to those who inherit the earth after its former inhabitants?﴾; that is: they succeed those nations of the past who were destroyed before them and inherit their dwellings. The intended people are the people of Makkah and those around it. The verb of guidance (yahdi) is followed by the preposition "li-" (to) either because it is treated as if it were the verb "lam" (to make clear), as if it were said: "Were they heedless, and was guidance not made for them ..." etc.; or because it carries the sense of "clarifying" (tabyin), with the object omitted, and the subject under both interpretations is the conditional clause; that is: has it not been made clear to them what the outcome of their affair will be?

﴿That if We willed, We would smite them for their sins﴾; that is: the matter is that if We willed, We would smite them for the recompense of their sins, or because of their sins, just as We smote those before them. It is also read as "nahdi" with the first-person plural of majesty (We guide), in which case the clause is its object.

﴿And We seal upon their hearts﴾ is coordinated with what is understood from His words, exalted is He, "Has it not been made clear?", as if it were said: "They do not take guidance," or "they are heedless of guidance," or "of reflection and contemplation." Or it is a new sentence separate from it, meaning: "And We seal." It is not permissible to coordinate it with "We would smite them" in the sense of "We sealed," because that would lead to negating the sealing from them, since it falls within the context of the answer to "law" (if).

﴿So they do not hear﴾; that is: the reports of the destroyed nations, let alone pondering and considering them, and benefiting from the guidance contained within them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 101:

﴿Those cities﴾ is a resumptive sentence (jumla musta'nafa) functioning as a summary (fadhlaka) of the stories that precede it, indicating the extent of the misguidance (ghawaya) of the nations mentioned and their persistence in it after the Messengers came to them with clear miracles. "Those" (tilka) is a demonstrative referring to the cities of the destroyed nations, the lam in al-qura being for specification (lil-'ahd), and it is the subject (mubtada').

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We relate to you some of their news﴾ is its predicate (khabar). The use of the present tense (sighat al-mudari') signals that the story has not yet ended. The "min" (min) is partitive (lil-tab'id), meaning: some of their accounts that contain admonition and reminder. It has also been said: "tilka" is the subject, "al-qura" is its predicate, and what follows is a circumstantial clause (hal), or a second predicate according to those who permit the second predicate to be a sentence, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then behold, it was a serpent moving swiftly﴾.

The opening of the speech with mention of "the cities" and the attribution of "the news" to them, although what is related is the news of their people and the intent is to explain their conditions, is as indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And certainly their Messengers came to them with clear proofs﴾. This is because recounting their complete destruction in the manner of total annihilation, such that it includes their dwellings too through their being swallowed by the earth and the quake, and their remaining desolate and abandoned, is more awesome and more dreadful.

The "ba'" in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿with clear proofs﴾ is connected either to the verb mentioned, in which case it is for transitivity (lil-ta'diya), or to an omitted element that stands as a circumstantial clause (hal) from its subject, meaning: "accompanied by clear proofs." However, this does not mean that each Messenger came with a single proof, but with many clear proofs specific to him, determined for him according to what wisdom requires, for the consideration of the division of individuals among individuals applies only among the Messengers and the collective of nations.

The sentence is a resumptive sentence explaining the completeness of their obstinacy and stubbornness; that is: by God, there came to every nation of those destroyed nations their Messenger specific to them, with manifest miracles, abundant and successive upon them, clearly majestic as proof of the truth of his mission, which necessarily requires faith.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So they were not to believe﴾ is an explanation of the continuation of their non-belief in the past time, not of the non-continuation of their belief. The arrangement of their state upon the coming of the Messengers with clear proofs is by the particle fa', because persistence in an act after the arrival of what requires abandoning it, though it is in reality persistence in it, is in terms of its description a new act and a fresh deed, as in the saying: "I admonished him, but he did not desist; I called him, but he did not answer." The lam is for emphasizing the negation; that is: it was not valid nor fitting for a people from those nations at any time that they should believe in everything; that was impossible for them until they met what they met, owing to the extreme of their obstinacy and the severity of their stubbornness in disbelief and transgression.

Then, if what is related of them is the last state of each people among them, the intended meaning of their non-belief mentioned here is their insistence upon that after the repeated admonitions; and by what is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿because of what they had denied before﴾ is their denial from the time of the coming of the Messengers until the time of insistence and obstinacy. That was not made the primary intended meaning as the first was, but was made a relative clause (silat al-mawsul), as an indication that it is evident in itself, while what needs clarification is their non-belief after the clear signs had been repeatedly presented and the manifest miracles had concurred, which would have compelled them to accept if they had been people of intellect.

The relative pronoun (al-mawsul) to which belief and denial are attached, affirmatively and negatively, is an expression for all the laws brought by each Messenger, both their roots and their branches. And if what is related is all the conditions of each people among them, then what was mentioned first is their continuous disbelief from the time of the coming of the Messengers, etc.; and what was indicated last is their denial before their coming. Thus the relative pronoun mentioned must be taken as an expression for the roots of the laws upon which all the Messengers unanimously agreed and to which they called their nations most emphatically, being impossible to alter or change, such as the creed of monotheism (millat al-tawhid) and its necessary consequences.

The meaning of their denial of them before the coming of their Messengers: (p-256) is that they were not in an era of ignorance in which they never heard the word of monotheism at all; rather, each of those nations would hear of it from the remnants of those before them and deny it. Then their state after the coming of their Messengers was like their state before that, as if no one had been sent to them.

The restriction of denial and non-belief to what was mentioned of the roots is because the status of the remainder is evident by the indication of the text, for when they did not believe in what all the Messengers unanimously agreed upon, it is more fitting that they would not believe in what only some of them uniquely brought. The fact that this denial was not made the primary intended meaning is because what the orbit of punishment and retribution revolves around is the denial occurring after the call, as indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We would never punish until We have sent a Messenger﴾.

What occurred before it was mentioned only to explain their deep-rootedness in disbelief and denial, and under either interpretation the three pronouns agree in their reference. It has been said: the pronoun in "kadhdhabu" refers to their forefathers, and the meaning is: the sons would not believe in what the fathers denied; and the difficulty in this is not hidden. It has also been said: the meaning is that they would not have believed even if We had revived them after their destruction and returned them to the abode of obligation, with what they had denied before, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if they were returned, they would revert to what they were forbidden﴾.

It has also been said: the "ba'" is causal and "ma" is verbal (masdariyya), meaning: because of their habituation to denying the truth and their training in it before the sending of the Messengers. What appeared in Surat Yunus of the disagreement of the majority in taking the verbal "ma" as among the nouns, as is the opinion of al-Akhfash and Ibn al-Sarraj, so that the pronoun in "bihi" may refer back to it, does not apply here.

﴿Thus﴾; that is: like that strong and firm sealing.

﴿God seals upon the hearts of the disbelievers﴾; that is: of those mentioned and others, so that the signs and warnings scarcely affect them. In it is a warning to the listeners. The mention of the noble Name directly, by way of iltifat (shift in speech), is to instill awe and to bring in dread.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 102:

﴿And We did not find for most of them﴾; that is, most of the nations mentioned. The lam is connected to the verb "wajada" (to find), as in your saying: "ma wajadtu lahu malan" (I did not find wealth for him); that is, "ma sadaftu lahu malan wa la laqitu-hu" (I did not come upon wealth for him, nor meet him).

Or it is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the phrase ﴿of covenant﴾ in His words, Exalted is He, because it is originally a qualifier of the indefinite noun; when it was placed before it, it took the accusative as a hal. The original sense is: "We did not find a covenant belonging to most of them."

And "min" (from) is extra (mazida), for the sense of comprehensiveness; that is, "We did not find for most of them any fulfilment of covenant," for they broke what they had covenanted with God regarding, when adversity and hardship touched them, saying: ﴿If You deliver us from this, we will surely be among the thankful﴾. So the restriction of this matter to most of them is not because some of them used to fulfil their covenants, but because some of them neither made covenants nor fulfilled them.

It has been said: the intended "covenant" is what God, Exalted is He, enjoined upon them of faith and piety, through the setting up of signs and the sending down of proofs. And it has been said: "ma 'ahadu" (what they covenanted) refers to the time of the address ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾; so the intended "most of them" is all of them. And it has been said: the pronoun refers to the calamity, and the clause is parenthetical, since most of them do not fulfil covenants in any sense.

﴿And indeed We found most of them﴾; that is, most of the nations; that is, We knew them, as in your saying: "wajadtu Zaydan dha hifaz" (I found Zayd to be one of retentive memory). It has been said: the first also is like this, and "in" is the light form of "inna," with an omitted pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n); that is, "inna al-sha'na wajadnahum" (indeed the matter is that We found them).

﴿Corrupt﴾ (fasiqin): going out of obedience, breaking covenants. According to the Kufans, "in" is a negation particle and the lam means "illa" (except); that is, "ma wajadnahum illa fasiqin" (We found them none but corrupt).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 103:

﴿Then We sent after them Moses﴾; that is, We sent him after the passing of the events of the messengers mentioned, or after the destruction of the nations related (in the narrative). The explicit statement of this, together with the indication of ﴿thumma﴾ (then, "then") for delay (tarakhi), serves to announce that his sending, upon him be peace, followed the course of the divine custom (sunnah) of sending messengers one after another (tatra). The fronting of the prepositional phrase before the direct object (al-maf'ul al-sarih) is, as has passed many times, for the sake of giving attention to the fronted element and building suspense toward the delayed one.

﴿with Our signs﴾: this is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial state (hal) from the object of ﴿ba'athna﴾ (We sent), or as a qualifier (sifah) of its verbal noun (masdar). That is: We sent him, upon him be peace, accompanied by Our signs, or We sent him in a sending accompanied by them. These are the nine detailed signs: the staff, the white hand, the years (of drought), the diminishing of fruits, the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, and the blood, as will come in detail.

﴿to Pharaoh﴾: it is a title for every ruler of Egypt from the Amalekites, just as Khosrow is a title for every ruler of Persia, and Caesar a title for every ruler of the Romans. His name was Qabus, and it is said: al-Walid ibn Mus'ab ibn Rayyan.

﴿and his chiefs﴾: that is, the nobles of his people. Their specific mention, despite the generality of his mission (upon him be peace) to all his people, is because they were all commanded to worship the Lord of the worlds, exalted is His authority, and to abandon the great, hideous (idea) which the tyrant claimed and which his rebellious faction accepted from him, owing to their originality (asalah) in managing affairs and the following of others by them in coming forth and in holding back (in matters).

﴿but they wronged themselves through them﴾: that is, they disbelieved in them. The term ﴿zulm﴾ (wrongdoing) is treated as ﴿kufr﴾ (disbelief), because they belong to one category, or it is included within the meaning of disbelief or denial; that is, they wronged by being disbelievers in them, or by being deniers of them, or they disbelieved in them in place of the faith that is their due because of their clarity. For this meaning, ﴿zalamu﴾ was placed in the position of ﴿kafaru﴾.

It is also said: they wronged themselves through them, by exposing themselves to the everlasting punishment, or they wronged people by hindering them from faith in them. What is intended by it is the continuance in disbelief in them until they met the punishment they met. Do you not see His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So look how was the end of the corrupters﴾? Just as their wronging through them entails that dreadful end, so the relating of their wronging through them entails the command to look upon it.

﴿How﴾ is the predicate (khabar) of ﴿kana﴾ (was), fronted before its subject because it requires initial position (al-sadarah). The clause is in the place of accusative after the removal of the preposition; that is: look with the eye of your intellect at the manner of what We did to them. The placing of ﴿the corrupters﴾ in the position of the pronoun ﴿them﴾ serves to announce that wrongdoing necessarily entails corruption.

"And Moses said" — this is a new independent statement, introduced to explain in detail what was stated in summary in what precedes it, namely the manner in which the signs were made manifest and the outcome for the corrupters.

"O Pharaoh, indeed I am a messenger" — i.e., to you.

"from the Lord of the worlds" — in the manner whose explanation has already passed.

﴿حَقِيقٌ عَلى أنْ لا أقُولَ عَلى اللَّهِ إلا الحَقَّ﴾ (It is fitting for me that I should not say about God except the truth.) This is an answer to what the mind is led to by the account of their wrongdoing toward the signs, namely their denial of him, peace and blessings be upon him, in his claim to prophethood. Its original form was ﴿حَقِيقٌ عَلَيَّ أنْ لا أقُولَ﴾ ("It is fitting upon me that I should not say..."), as in the reading of Nafi', and the preposition was changed to ﴿عَلى﴾ to avoid confusion (al-ilbas), as in the words of the poet:

*"And the spears are made to suffer by the stout red-maned ones."*

Or because "what is incumbent on you is incumbent on him" (ma lazimaka faqad lazimtahu). Or for the sake of emphasizing the description of truthfulness. The meaning is: "It is incumbent upon me to say the truth, that I be the one who says it; he is not pleased except with one like me speaking it." Or ﴿حَقِيقٌ﴾ is taken to include the sense of ﴿حَرِيصٌ﴾ (eager), or ﴿عَلى﴾ is placed in the position of ﴿الباء﴾ (bi, "with") to indicate firm attachment, as in their saying: "I was shot on the bow (rumitu 'ala al-qaws)," and "I came in a good state (ji'tu 'ala hal hasanah)." This is supported by the reading of Ubayy (ibn Ka'b) with ﴿الباء﴾ (bi haqiqun an la aqula, "with the attachment..."). It was also read: ﴿حَقِيقٌ أنْ لا أقُولَ﴾.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿قَدْ جِئْتُكم بِبَيِّنَةٍ مِن رَبِّكُمْ﴾ (I have certainly come to you with a clear proof from your Lord.) This is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf, a new clause that begins anew) which affirms what came before it: that he is a messenger from the Lord of the worlds, and that he is worthy to speak the truth. This statement was not made by him, peace be upon him, as the reply of Pharaoh that follows it here; rather it came after the dialogue related by His saying: ﴿قالَ فَمَن رَبُّكُما...﴾ (He said, "Who then is your Lord, O Moses?") and His saying: ﴿وَما رَبُّ العالَمِينَ...﴾ (He said, "And what is the Lord of the worlds?"), and its mention has been omitted here for the sake of brevity.

The ﴿مِن﴾ (min, "from") is connected either to ﴿جِئْتُكم﴾ (I have come to you), in which case it denotes the inception of the end-point (ibtida' al-ghaya) in a metaphorical sense, or to an omitted word that stands as an attribute of ﴿بَيِّنَةٍ﴾ (a clear proof), conveying its magnitude by the genitive construction (idafa), which reinforces its inherent magnitude derived from the glorifying tanwin (tanwin al-tafkhim). The attribution of the name of the Lord to the addressees, after its attribution to the worlds earlier, is to emphasize the obligation of believing in it.

﴿فَأرْسِلْ مَعِيَ بَنِي إسْرائِيلَ﴾ (So send with me the Children of Israel.) That is: let them go, so that they may go with me to the Holy Land, which was the homeland of their forefathers. Pharaoh had enslaved them after the extinction of the tribes (al-asbat), using them and imposing on them grueling labors. God, exalted is He, rescued them through Moses, peace be upon him. Between the day Joseph entered Egypt and the day Moses entered it, peace be upon them both, there were four hundred years.

The fa' (so) indicates the sequence of sending, or the command to it as a consequence of what preceded it: his mission, peace be upon him, and his coming with the clear proof.

﴿He said﴾: this is a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*) that answers a question the discourse naturally leads to, as if it were said: "What did Pharaoh say to him, peace be upon him, when he said to him what he said?" So it is said: "He said."

﴿If you have come with a sign﴾; that is, from the One who sent you, as you claim.

﴿then produce it﴾; that is, bring it forth, so that you may establish your messengership through it.

﴿if you are among the truthful﴾ in your claim. For your being among those known for truthfulness necessarily requires that you show the sign.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 107:

﴿So he threw his staff, and behold, it was a manifest serpent (thu'ban mubin)﴾; that is: its matter was clear, with no doubt about its being a serpent (thu'ban), which is a great snake (al-hayyah al-'azimah). The choice of the nominal sentence (al-jumlah al-ismiyyah) indicates the complete speed of the transformation and the permanence of the attribute of serpent-hood in it, as if it were originally so.

It is narrated that when he threw it, it became a serpent (thu'ban) that was ash'ar (hairy/with thick hair), gaping its mouth between its jaws, eighty cubits wide. It placed its lower jaw on the ground and its upper jaw on the wall of the palace. Then it turned toward Pharaoh, and he fled from it and defecated.
