The people fled, pushing against one another, and twenty-five thousand of them died. Pharaoh cried out: "O Musa, I implore you by the One who sent you, seize it! I will believe in you and send the Children of Israel with you." So he took it, and it returned to being a staff.

Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 7, verse 108:

﴿And he drew out his hand﴾; that is, from his collar (jayb), or from beneath his armpit.

﴿and behold, it was white to the onlookers﴾; that is, white with a luminous whiteness, outside the normal course, such that the spectators gathered around it in wonder at its state. It is related that he showed Pharaoh his hand, and Pharaoh said: "What is this?" He said: "Your hand." Then he put it into his collar, while he was wearing a woolen garment (midra'at suf), and drew it out, and behold, it was white with a luminous whiteness whose ray overpowered the ray of the sun. Moses, peace be upon him, was very dark-complexioned (adam shadid al-udmah). It has also been said: "white to the onlookers" means that it was not white by its natural constitution (fi jiblliha).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 109:

﴿Said the chiefs (al-mala') of the people of Pharaoh﴾ (p-259); that is, the nobles among them, who were the people of his counsel (mashura).

﴿Indeed, this is a knowing sorcerer﴾; that is, one who excels in the knowledge of magic (sihr) and is skilled in it. They said this in confirmation of Pharaoh and in endorsement of his words, for this very statement is attributed to them in Surat al-Shu'ara'.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 110:

﴿He wants to drive you out of your land﴾; that is, out of the land of Egypt.

﴿So what do you command?﴾ With the nun pronounced with a fatha (fa-mādhā ta'murūna, with the nun vocalized with a fatha, i.e. ta'murūna, with the first person suffix omitted). The "mā" in "mādhā" is in the accusative position, as it is the second object (maf'ūl thānī) of "ta'murūna", with the preposition elided. The first object is omitted, and the implied meaning is: "By what matter do you command me?" This is part of the speech of Pharaoh, as in His Exalted saying: ﴿That is so that he may know that I did not betray him in secret﴾; that is, "If this is the case, then what do you advise me regarding his matter?"

This was said by the chiefs before him, by way of conveying it to the common people. So His saying, exalted is He, ﴿They said: Delay him and his brother﴾ is, according to the first view, which is the more apparent, a report of the words of the chiefs whom Pharaoh consulted. According to the second view, it is a report of the words of the common people, which the chiefs addressed. What weakens the second view is that the address is to Pharaoh, and consultation is not among the duties of the common people. The meaning is: postpone his affair and his brother's, and send them away from you until you see your opinion about them and arrange their matter. It is also read as ﴿أرجئه﴾ (arji'hu) and ﴿أرجه﴾ (arjihi), from the verbs ارجأه (arja'ahu) and ارجاه (arjahu), both meaning "to delay."

﴿And send into the cities gatherers﴾. It is said that the cities are the cities of Upper Egypt (Sa'id Misr), and that the chief sorcerers and their most skilled practitioners were in the farthest cities of Upper Egypt. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that they were seventy sorcerers who had learned sorcery from two Magian men from the people of Nineveh, the city of Yunus (peace be upon him) at Mosul. This is refuted by the fact that Magianism appeared through Zoroaster, and he came after Musa (peace and blessings be upon him).
﴿They will bring you every skilled sorcerer﴾; i.e., one who is adept at sorcery. It is also read as (bi-kulli sahhārin ʿalīm), and the clause is the response to the imperative.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 113:

﴿And the sorcerers came to Pharaoh﴾ after Pharaoh had sent to them the summoners (al-hashirin). That he did not explicitly name them, as in his saying, ﴿Then Pharaoh sent summoners to the cities﴾, is to indicate the haste of Pharaoh in sending, and the eagerness of the summoners and the sorcerers in complying.

﴿They said﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) linked to a question arising from the narration of the sorcerers' coming, as if it were said: "What did they say to him when they came to him?" So it is answered: they said, relying on what they possessed and confident in their victory: ﴿Indeed, for us there will surely be a reward, if we are the victorious﴾, by way of informing of the certainty and obligation of the reward, as if they said: "There must be for us a great reward then." Or by way of a confirmatory interrogative (istifham taqriri) with the interrogative hamzah deleted; it has also been read with the hamzah affirmed.

Their saying "﴿if we are﴾" is merely to specify the condition upon which the reward is established, not because of any doubt on their part regarding victory. The placement of the pronoun (nahnu) and the adornment of the predicate with the definite article (al-) are for restriction (qasr); that is: "if we are the victorious, not Moses."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 114:

﴿He said, "Yes."﴾ And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed, you will be among those brought near.﴾ is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon an omitted element, which the affirmative particle has taken the place of (sadda maddahu ḥarf al-ījāb), as if he had said: "Indeed, for you there is a reward, and indeed, along with that, you will be among those brought near," for the sake of emphasis in encouragement. It is narrated that he said to them: "You will be the first to enter my assembly and the last to leave it."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 115:

﴿They said﴾ is a resumptive statement (isti'naf), as already mentioned. It is as if it were asked: "What did they do after that?" So it was said: "They said, attending to their matter, addressing Musa, peace be upon him."

﴿O Musa, either you throw﴾: either you throw first.

﴿Or we will be the throwers﴾; that is: what we throw first, or those who perform the throwing first. They gave him, peace be upon him, the choice of beginning with the throwing, out of regard for courtesy (adab), and to show firmness (jaladah), and that their condition would not differ by going first or last. But their desire was to go first, as is indicated by their altering the structure of the utterance by making the predicate definite, by inserting the separating pronoun (damir al-fasl), and by emphasizing the attached pronoun.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 116:

﴿Said: "Throw."﴾ Heedless of their command; that is, throw what you are going to throw.

﴿So when they threw﴾ what they threw.

﴿They bewitched the eyes of the people﴾ by making them imagine what has no reality.

﴿And they struck them with terror﴾; that is, they went to great lengths to frighten them.

﴿And they produced a great magic﴾ within its category. It is related that they threw thick ropes and long staves, which looked like serpents filling the valley, with some of them coiling over others.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 117:

﴿And We revealed to Musa: "Throw your staff," and behold, it swallowed up what they were fabricating.﴾ The fa' here is fasihah (an elliptical fa', indicating an omitted clause); that is: so he threw it, and it became a serpent, and behold, it was the sign. It was omitted to convey Musa's peace be upon him haste in throwing, and the extreme speed of the transformation, as if its swallowing of what they were fabricating had occurred immediately upon the command to throw. The present-tense form (talqafu) is used to evoke the vivid image of the awesome swallowing.

Al-ifk (ifk): turning something away and reversing it from its customary aspect. The "ma" (ma) is either a relative pronoun or a descriptive particle, with the returning pronoun omitted; that is: what they fabricate and falsify. Or it is a verbal-noun (masdariyyah) particle, in which case it, together with the verb, carries the sense of a passive noun: what is fabricated.

It is related that when it swallowed up a valley's worth of wood and ropes, Musa lifted it and it returned to being a staff as it was. Allah Most High, by His overwhelming power, either annihilated those enormous bodies, or broke them into fine particles. The sorcerers said: "Had this been sorcery, our ropes and staffs would have remained."

﴿So the truth was established﴾; i.e., it was confirmed, because its matter became manifest.

﴿and what they had been doing was nullified﴾; i.e., the falsity of what they had been persisting in doing became evident.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 119:

﴿So they were overcome﴾; i.e., Pharaoh and his people.

﴿There﴾; i.e., in their assembly.

﴿And they turned back humiliated﴾; i.e., they became abased and stunned, or they returned to the city abased and subdued.

The first interpretation is the apparent one, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the sorcerers were thrown down prostrating﴾. For that took place in the presence of Pharaoh, certainly; that is, they fell prostrate, as though someone had cast them down, owing to the intensity of their falling. How could it be otherwise, when the truth had overwhelmed them and compelled them to that?

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verses 121–122:

﴿They said: "We have believed in the Lord of the worlds,"﴾ ﴿the Lord of Musa and Harun.﴾ He substituted the second for the first (badal), lest it be imagined that their intended meaning was Pharaoh. On the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, he said: When the sorcerers believed, six hundred thousand of the Children of Israel followed Musa.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verses 121–122:

﴿They said: "We have believed in the Lord of the worlds,"﴾ ﴿the Lord of Musa and Harun.﴾ He substituted the second for the first (badal), lest it be imagined that their intended meaning was Pharaoh. On the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, he said: When the sorcerers believed, six hundred thousand of the Children of Israel followed Musa.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 123:

﴿Pharaoh said﴾, rebuking the sorcerers and reproaching them for what they had done.

﴿Did you believe in Him﴾ with a single hamza. This may be a plain statement that carries the sense of reproach, or it may be a reproachful interrogative with the hamza of interrogation omitted, as was explained in ﴿Surely for us there will be a reward﴾. It has also been read with both hamzas pronounced in full, and with the first pronounced in full while the second is eased and pronounced between-between (bayna bayn, a vowel sound intermediate between the hamza and the letter it softens); that is, "Did you believe in God, the Exalted?"

﴿Before I gave you permission﴾; that is, without my giving you permission, as in His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Were the sea ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord were exhausted﴾. It does not mean that permission from him was possible in this matter.

﴿Surely this is a stratagem you have plotted﴾; meaning: what you have done is not something the circumstances required from you, given the might of the Majestic One and the manifestation of the miracle; rather it is a trick you have devised in collusion with Moses.

﴿In the city﴾; meaning Egypt, before you went out to the appointed meeting. It is related that Moses, peace be upon him, and the chief of the sorcerers met, and Moses said to him: "Tell me, if I defeat you, will you believe in me and bear witness that what I have brought is the truth?" The sorcerer said: "By God, if you defeat me, I will certainly believe in you," while Pharaoh was listening to them both, and it was this that gave rise to this statement.

﴿So that you may drive its people out of it﴾; that is, the Copts, and that it may be purely yours and the Children of Israel's. These are two insinuations that he cast into the ears of the common Copts when they witnessed the raising of the banners of the miracle and saw the sorcerers bowing their necks before it and being unable to restrain themselves from believing in it. By these two he sought to prevent them from believing in the prophethood of Moses, peace be upon him, by showing that the sorcerers' faith was founded on an agreement between them and Moses, and that their purpose in this was to drive the people out of the city and to end their rule. It is well known that leaving familiar homelands and well-known blessings is something that cannot be borne. So the accursed one combined the two insinuations, to keep the Copts firm in what they were upon and to stir up their enmity towards him, peace be upon him.

Then he followed the two with a threat, so as to show them that he had strength and power to resist, and he said ﴿Soon you will know﴾; that is, the consequence of what you have done. This is a threat that he delivered in a general manner, for the sake of intimidation.

Then he followed it with the detail, saying: ﴿Surely I will cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides﴾; that is, a limb from every side.

﴿Then I will crucify you all﴾, to disgrace you and to make an example of your kind. It is said: he was the first to institute this, so God Most High legislated it for highway robbers, to magnify their crime; and for this reason God Most High named it "waging war against God and His Messenger."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 125:

﴿They said﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) that comes as an answer to a question which naturally suggests itself to the mind, as if it were said: "What did the sorcerers say when they heard Pharaoh's threat? Were they affected by it, or did they remain steadfast in the religion they were in?" So it is said: "They said, steadfast in what they had adopted of faith."

﴿Indeed, to our Lord we are returning﴾; that is, by death without doubt. So whether that (threat) comes from you or not, we do not care about your threat. Or: indeed, to the mercy and reward of our Lord we are returning, if you do that to us. It is as if they found it pleasant, out of their longing for the meeting with Allah the Exalted. Or: indeed, we all are returning to our Lord, so He will judge between us and you.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 126:

﴿And you do not resent us﴾; that is, you do not disapprove of or find fault with us.

﴿except that we believed in the signs of our Lord when they came to us﴾. This is the best of deeds and the root of virtues. It is not something from which we could turn away in seeking your approval. Then they turned away from addressing him, to show the resolve in their hearts regarding what they had said, and to affirm it.

So they sought refuge with Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and said: ﴿Our Lord, pour upon us patience﴾. That is, pour upon us of patience what overwhelms us as water overwhelms, or pour upon us what purifies us from the filth of burdens and the defilement of sins, namely patience in the face of Pharaoh's threat.

﴿And cause us to die as Muslims﴾, steadfast in the Islam You have granted us, not swayed from the threat. It was said: he did to them what he had threatened. It was also said: he was not able to do it, due to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿You two and whoever follows you will be the victors﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 127:

﴿And the chiefs of the people of Pharaoh said﴾, addressing him after they had witnessed the matter of Musa, peace be upon him.

﴿"Will you leave Musa and his people to cause corruption in the land?"﴾; that is, in the land of Egypt, by turning the people against you and diverting them from following you.

﴿"And leave you"﴾ is a conjunction with "to cause corruption" (yufsidu), or it is the answer to the interrogative with the waw, as in the verse of al-Hutay'a:

"Did I not be your neighbour, and between me and you there would be love and brotherhood?"

That is: Will it be from you that you leave Musa, and that he leaves you? It has also been read with the nominative (wa-yadharuka), as a conjunction with "Will you leave" (atadharu), or as a resumptive clause (isti'naf), or as a circumstantial clause (hal). It has also been read with the jussive (sukun), as if it were said: "they cause corruption and he leaves you," like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"So that I may give charity and be among the righteous"﴾ (fa-asaddaqa wa-akun).

﴿"And your gods"﴾ and your objects of worship. It was said that he used to worship the stars. It was also said that he made idols for his people and commanded them to worship them as a means of drawing near to him, and for this reason he said: ﴿"I am your Lord, the Most High"﴾. It has also been read as (wa-ilahataka), that is, your worship.

﴿He said﴾, responding to them.

﴿"We will kill their sons and keep their women alive"﴾, just as we used to do to them before. This is so that it may be known that we remain in the same state of domination and supremacy, and it should not be imagined that he is the boy about whom the astrologers and soothsayers ruled that our kingdom would perish at his hands. It has also been read as (sa-naqtulu) with the lightened form.

﴿"And we are above them, dominant"﴾, just as we were; our condition has not changed at all, and they remain subdued under our hands as before.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 128:

﴿Musa said to his people﴾, as consolation for them and a promise of a good outcome, when they heard the words of Pharaoh and were distressed by them.

﴿Seek help in Allah and be patient﴾ over what you have heard of his false statements.

﴿Indeed, the earth belongs to Allah﴾; that is, the land of Egypt, or the genus of land, and it [Egypt] is included in it by primary inclusion. (p-263)

﴿He gives it as inheritance to whomever He wills of His servants, and the final outcome is for the God-fearing﴾, those among whom you are. In this is an announcement that seeking help in Allah the Exalted and patience are among the gates of taqwa (God-consciousness, piety). It has also been read as ﴿wal-'aqibata﴾ with the accusative, in coordination with the noun of ﴿inna﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 129:

﴿They said﴾; that is, the Children of Israel.

﴿"We were harmed"﴾; that is, at the hands of Pharaoh.

﴿"before you came to us"﴾; that is, with the Message. By this they mean the slaying of their sons before the birth of Musa, peace be upon him, and after it.

﴿"and after you came to us"﴾; that is, as a Messenger. They mean: his threat to them of repeating the slaying of the sons, and all the other forms of tyranny, injustice and torment that he inflicted upon them out of enmity toward Musa, peace be upon him. As for the servitude and humiliation in which they were made to work, with various kinds of labor and menial tasks, as has been said, these are not among the things that befell them through him, peace be upon him; therefore, mention of it has little connection to the context.

﴿He said﴾; that is, Musa, peace be upon him, when he saw the intensity of their distress at what they had witnessed, consoling them by stating explicitly what he had hinted at in his words: ﴿Indeed, the earth belongs to Allah﴾ ... and so on.

﴿"Perhaps your Lord will destroy your enemy"﴾ who did to you what he did and threatened to repeat it.

﴿"and make you successors in the land"﴾; that is, make you successors in the land of Egypt.

﴿"and then see how you will act"﴾: whether well or badly, so that He will recompense you according to the deeds that appear from you. In this there is emphasis for consolation and confirmation of the matter.

It has been said: perhaps the use of the verb of hoping (ʿasā, "perhaps") is because he, peace be upon him, was not certain that they themselves, or their children, would be the ones made successors. It is related that Egypt was only conquered in the time of Dawud, peace be upon him. And this is not supported by His words, exalted is He: ﴿And We caused the people who had been oppressed to inherit the eastern and western parts of the land﴾; for what is immediately understood is the succession of the oppressed themselves, not the succession of their children. Rather, the coming of the verb of hope is in keeping with the manner of majesty.

And indeed We seized the people of Pharaoh with years (of drought)...

This begins the detailed account of the initial stages of the promised destruction, and gives notice that He, exalted is He, did not grant them respite after that; they were not in ease and comfort. Rather, the causes of their destruction were arranged, and they passed from one state to another until the punishment of uprooting (ʿadhāb al-istiʾṣāl) descended upon them.

The sentence is introduced with an oath (qasam) to show concern for its content. The word al-sunīn (the years) is the plural of sanah (year), and what is meant is the year of drought. There are two dialects (lughatān) concerning it. The more well-known is to treat it as a sound masculine plural, so it takes the waw in the nominative, the yāʾ in the accusative and genitive, and its nūn is dropped when it is in a construct state (iḍāfah).

The second dialect is to apply the case endings to the nūn, but only with the yāʾ (i.e., in the oblique), either with its tanwīn retained or with it dropped. Al-Farrāʾ said: "In this dialect it is diptote (maṣrūfah) according to the Banū ʿĀmir, and non-diptote (ghayr maṣrūfah) according to the Banū Tamīm. The reason for dropping the tanwīn is lightening (takhfīf), and in that case the nūn is not dropped for the iḍāfah." On this usage came the verse of the poet:

"He called me from Najd, for its years
Have played with us, making us grey while making us beardless (young)."

And a ḥadīth has come: "O Allah, make them (the years) upon them like the years of Yūsuf," and "sinīn kasinīn Yūsuf" is attested in both dialects.

And a decrease in the fruits (wa-naqṣin mina al-thamarāt): by the striking of blights (ʿāhāt). On the authority of Kaʿb: "There will come upon the people a time when the palm tree will bear only a single date." Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "As for the years, they were for their desert dwellers and the people of their livestock, and as for the decrease in fruits, it was in their cities."

So that they may take heed (laʿallahum yadhdhakkarūn): that they may remember, be admonished by that, and realize that it was on account of their sins, and desist from what they are upon of arrogance (ʿutuww) and obstinacy (ʿinād). Al-Zajjāj said: "Conditions of hardship soften hearts and make them desirous of what is with Allah, mighty and majestic, and of returning to Him, exalted is He. Do you not see His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when harm touches man, he calls upon Us, lying on his side, or sitting or standing﴾?"

The discussion of the meaning of "la'alla" and its position (maḥall) has already passed, in the explanation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So that you may be righteous﴾ at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 131:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But when good came to them﴾ etc., is an explanation of their lack of reflection and their persistence in error; that is: when abundance, fertility and other good things came to them.

﴿They said, "This is ours"﴾; that is, it is due to us and we deserve it.

﴿But if an evil befell them﴾; that is, drought and calamity.

﴿They ascribed it as an omen to Moses and those with him﴾; that is, they considered them a bad omen (tashaʾum) and said: "We were struck only because of their ill omen." This, as you see, is evidence of the utter hardness of their hearts and the extremity of their ignorance and dullness, for hardships soften hearts and make dispositions gentle, especially after witnessing the signs. Yet they were such that nothing of them had any effect on them; rather they increased in insolence and obstinacy.

The definite form of "good" (al-hasanah) and its mention with the particle of certainty (idha, "when") signifies that it occurs frequently and that the will is attached to it in its essence. Likewise, the indefinite form of "evil" (sayyi'ah) and its introduction with the particle of doubt (in, "if") indicates that it occurs rarely and that the will is attached to it only incidentally.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, their omen is with Allah﴾ is a resumptive statement sent down from Him, exalted is He, to refute their false saying and to establish the truth in this matter. It is introduced with the attention-drawing word (alā, "indeed/beware") to highlight the great concern with its content. That is: the cause of their good is nothing but with Him, exalted is He, namely His decree and His will, which includes wisdom and benefits; or the cause of their misfortune, which is their evil deeds, is nothing but with Him, exalted is He; that is, it is recorded in His presence, for it is what brought upon them that which displeases them, and not anything other than it. It has also been read as "innama tayruhum" (their omen), which is a collective noun of ṭā'ir (bird/omen), and it has been said that it is its plural.

﴿But most of them do not know﴾ this, so they say what they say, as is related of them. The attribution of lack of knowledge to most of them signifies that some of them do know that what befalls them of good and evil is from Allah, exalted is He, or that they know that what befalls them of calamities and trials is nothing but what their hands have earned; but they do not act in accordance with that out of obstinacy and arrogance.

﴿وَقالُوا﴾ [And they said.] This begins an explanation of another part of the punishments with which the people of Pharaoh were afflicted, which are themselves clear signs, and of their refusal, despite these, to turn back from their disbelief and obstinacy. That is: they said after they had seen what they saw of the matter of the staff, the years (of drought), and the loss of fruits.

﴿مَهْما تَأْتِنا بِهِ﴾ [Whatever you bring us.] The word "مَهْما" (mahma, meaning "whatever") is used for both condition and consequence. Its origin is "ما" (ma), the conditional particle, to which the additional "ما" was joined for emphasis, as it was joined to "أَيْنَ" (ayna, "where") and "إنَّ" (inna) in "أَيْنَما تَكُونُوا" (wherever you are) and "إمّا نَذْهَبَنَّ بِكَ" (whether We take you away). Except that the alif of the first "ما" was changed into a "هاء" (ha), to avoid repeating two similar sounds. This is the sound opinion.

It was also said: "مَهْ" (mah) is a word used by a person forbidding something, joined to the conditional "ما", and its position is nominative as a subject, or accusative by a verb whose meaning is explained by what follows; that is, "whatever sign you show us."

﴿مِن آيَةٍ﴾ [with any sign.] This explains "مَهْما" and their naming of it.

﴿لِتَسْحَرَنا بِها﴾ [to bewitch us with it.] This shows the full extent of their insolence and extremism, and their calling guidance to the truth "sorcery" and "the blinding of the eyes." The two pronouns in the genitive refer to "مَهْما". The first is masculine out of regard for the wording, since it is ambiguous, and the second is feminine out of regard for the meaning, since it is specified by "آيَةٍ" (sign), as in His saying: ﴿Whatever mercy Allah grants to people, none can withhold it; and whatever He withholds, none can release after Him﴾.

﴿فَما نَحْنُ لَكَ بِمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ [so we will not believe you.] That is: we will not confirm you as truthful, nor believe in your prophethood.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 133:

﴿So We sent upon them﴾ as punishment for their crimes, especially for their saying this.

﴿The flood﴾; that is, the water that overflowed them, covered their dwellings and their tilled fields, whether from rain or a torrent. It has also been said that it is smallpox; it has been said that it is sudden death; and it has been said that it is plague.

﴿And the locusts and the lice﴾. It has been said that the lice are large ticks; and it has been said that they are young locusts before their wings have grown.

﴿And the frogs and the blood﴾. It is narrated that they were rained upon for eight days in intense darkness, so that no one could leave his house. The water entered their houses until they stood in it up to their collarbones, while not a single drop of it entered the houses of the Children of Israel, even though those houses were among theirs. The water overflowed onto their land and stagnated, preventing them from tilling and from carrying out their affairs, and this lasted seven days. They said to him, upon him be peace: "Pray to your Lord for us to remove this from us, and we will believe in you." He prayed, and it was lifted from them, and there grew of the grass and herbage what had never been known before. Yet they did not believe. So Allah sent the locusts upon them, and they ate their crops, their fruits, their doors, their roofs, and their garments. They turned in fear to him, upon him be peace, for what has been mentioned, so he went out into the desert and pointed his staff toward the east and the west, and the locusts returned to the regions from which they had come. Yet they did not believe. So Allah, exalted is He, let loose the lice upon them, and it consumed what the locusts had left. It would fall into their food and enter between their garments and their skins, sucking at them. They turned to him a third time, and it was lifted from them. They said: "We are now certain that you are a sorcerer." Then Allah sent the frogs upon them, such that no cloth or food was uncovered without frogs being found in it. Their beds would be full of them, and they would leap into their cooking pots while they were boiling, and into their mouths when they spoke. They turned to him a fourth time, humbled themselves, and covenants were taken from them. He prayed, and Allah removed it from them, but they broke the covenant. So Allah sent the blood upon them, and their water turned to blood, so that when a Copt and an Israelite gathered around a single vessel, what was on the Copt's side would become blood, while what was on the Israelite's side remained water as it was. And if he sucked from the mouth of an Israelite, it would become blood in his mouth. It has also been said: Allah sent nosebleeds upon them.

﴿Signs﴾: a state (ḥāl) of the accusatives mentioned.

﴿Distinct﴾: clearly explained; no intelligent person would be confused that they are the signs of Allah, exalted is He, and His retribution. It has also been said: they were separated from one another in order to test their states, and there was a month between every two of them, and the duration of each one was a week. It has also been said that he, upon him be peace, remained among them for twenty years after he overcame the sorcerers, showing them these signs at leisure.

﴿But they were arrogant﴾; that is, they were arrogant toward belief in them.

﴿And they were a people of criminals﴾: a parenthetical clause affirming the content of what precedes it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 134:

﴿And when the punishment (rijz) fell upon them﴾; that is, the punishment mentioned in detail. The alif-lam here is for the genus (li-l-jins), encompassing each of the detailed signs; that is, whenever one of those punishments befell them, they would say each time: ﴿O Musa, call upon your Lord for us by what He has covenanted with you﴾; that is, by His covenant with you, which is prophethood, or by what was entrusted to you, that you should call upon Him and He would answer you as He answered you in your signs. This is a complement (silah) of "call upon" (ud'u), or a circumstantial phrase (hal) from the pronoun in it, meaning "call upon God, seeking nearness to Him through what He has covenanted with you," or it is related to an omitted element indicated by their request, like: "Grant us aid in what we seek by the right of what You have with You."

Or it is an oath, answered by the statement of the Exalted: ﴿If you remove from us the punishment (rijz)﴾ that has fallen upon us.

﴿We will indeed believe in you and we will indeed send with you the Children of Israel﴾; that is, we swear by the covenant of God with you that if you remove... etc.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 135:

﴿So when We removed from them the plague (rijz) until a term which they were to reach, behold, they broke their word.﴾ That is: until a limit of time which they were to reach; so after it they would be punished or destroyed.

﴿Behold, they broke their word﴾ is the answer of "lamma" (when). That is: when We removed it from them, they immediately fell into breaking the covenant without reflection or pause.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 136:

﴿So We took vengeance upon them﴾; that is: We intended to take vengeance upon them for the sins and crimes they had committed beforehand. For His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿so We drowned them﴾ is the very same as the vengeance upon them, so it is not correct to insert the particle fa (fa, "so") between the two. It is permissible that what is meant is the absolute sense of vengeance upon them, with the fa being explanatory (tafsiriyyah), as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Noah called out to his Lord and said, "My Lord..."﴾ and so on.

﴿In the sea﴾: in the sea whose bottom cannot be reached. It was said: in its deepest part (lujjah).

﴿Because they denied Our signs and were heedless of them﴾: this is a causal explanation for the drowning; that is, their drowning was due to their denial of the signs of God, Exalted is He, their turning away from them, and their failure to reflect upon them, to the extent that they became as those completely heedless of them.

Although the fa indicates that the drowning follows from what preceded it, namely the breaking of covenant (naks), he nonetheless stated the cause explicitly, as a notice (iwdan) that the basis of all of that is the denial of the signs of God, Exalted is He, and turning away from them, so that this would be a deterrent for the listeners from denying the manifest signs upon the hand of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and turning away from them.

And We caused the people who had been deemed weak to inherit the eastern and western parts of the land which We had blessed. [Note: translating faithfully below.]

Let me correct that: I should translate the passage as instructed, without notes.

**Translation:**

﴿And We caused to inherit the people who were deemed weak﴾; that is, through enslavement and the slaughter of sons. The combining of the past and future forms (of the verb) indicates the continuation and renewal of the weakening. They are the Children of Israel. They were mentioned with this description to show the completeness of God's kindness toward them and the magnitude of His favour to them in raising them from the depths of humiliation to the height of honour.

﴿the eastern and western parts of the land﴾; that is, its eastern and western sides, where the Children of Israel took possession after the Pharaohs and the Amalekites, and they disposed of its eastern and western regions as they wished.

God's words ﴿which We had blessed﴾; that is, with fertility and abundance of provision, is a qualifier of "the eastern and western parts." It was also said that it qualifies "the land," but this has weakness because of the separation between the qualifier and the qualified by the conjoined noun, as in your saying: "qāma Umm Hind wa-Abūhā al-ʿāqilah" (the wise one).

﴿And the good word of your Lord was fulfilled﴾, which is His promise to them of victory and establishment, as indicated by His words: ﴿And We wished to bestow favour upon those who were deemed weak in the land, and to make them leaders and to make them the inheritors﴾. It is also read as "kalimāt" (words), due to the multiplicity of promises. The meaning of "tammat" is: it passed and continued.

﴿upon the Children of Israel, because of their patience﴾; that is, because of their patience in the hardships which they endured from Pharaoh and his people.

﴿And We destroyed﴾; that is, We ruined and annihilated.

﴿what Pharaoh and his people used to make﴾, of buildings and palaces; that is, and We destroyed what Pharaoh was making, with "Pharaoh" being the subject of "kāna" and "yaṣnaʿu" being the predicate placed first, and the nominal clause being the relative clause of "mā," with the returning pronoun omitted. It was also said: the subject of "kāna" is a pronoun referring back to the relative "mā," "yaṣnaʿu" is predicated of Pharaoh, and the clause is the predicate of "kāna," with the returning pronoun also omitted, the sense being: "and We destroyed that which Pharaoh himself was making..."

It was also said: "kāna" is redundant, "mā" is a verbal-noun (maṣdariyyah), and the sense is: "what Pharaoh made..." It was also said: "kāna" is redundant as mentioned, and "mā" is a relative noun, with the returning pronoun omitted, its sense being: "and We destroyed what Pharaoh made" (i.e., its making). The shift to the present form under these two opinions serves to bring the scene vividly before the mind.

﴿and what they used to erect﴾ of gardens, or what they used to raise of building, like the tower of Haman. It is also read as "yaʿrushūn" with a damma on the "r," though the kasra is more eloquent. This is the end of the story of Pharaoh and his people.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 138:

And His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And We brought the Children of Israel across the sea﴾ marks the beginning of the account of the Children of Israel and an explanation of the abominable matters they introduced after Allah, Mighty and Majestic, had rescued them from the dominion of Pharaoh, bestowed upon them great blessings that call for gratitude, and showed them great signs before which towering mountains would crumble. This serves as consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and as an awakening for the believers, so that they do not neglect taking account of their own souls and watching over their own conditions.

Jawaza (جاوَزَ) here has the meaning of jaza (جازَ), and it is also read as jawwaznā (جَوَّزْنا) with the doubled letter, which likewise means jaza; it takes the particle bi (بِ) after it, so the meaning is: We caused them to cross the sea. It is related that Musa (peace be upon him) led them across on the day of ʿĀshūrāʾ, after Allah, Exalted is He, had destroyed Pharaoh, and so they fasted it in gratitude to Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

﴿Then they came﴾; that is, they passed by.

﴿upon a people﴾. It was said: they were from Lakhm. And it was said: they were from the Amalekites, the Canaanites, whom Musa (peace be upon him) had been commanded to fight.

﴿who were devoted to some idols of theirs﴾; that is, they persisted in worshipping them and kept to them constantly. It is also read with a kasra on the kaf (يَعْكِفُونَ). Ibn Juraij said: their idols were images of cows, and this was the beginning of the affair of the calf.

﴿They said﴾ when they witnessed their state.

﴿O Musa, make for us a god﴾, an image that we may worship.

﴿just as they have gods﴾. The kaf (الكافُ) is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a description of ilahan (إلَهًا). Ma (ما) is a relative pronoun, and lahum (لَهم) is its complement, and ālihatun (آلِهَةٌ) is a substitute for ma. The sense is: make for us a god existing in the manner of that which they have established for themselves.

﴿He said, "Indeed you are a people who act in ignorance."﴾ He (peace be upon him) marvelled at this statement of theirs immediately after they had witnessed the greatest sign and the mightiest miracle, so he described them with absolute ignorance, since there is no ignorance greater than what had become manifest from them.

He reinforced it with His saying: ﴿Indeed, these﴾, meaning the people who worship those images.

﴿are doomed﴾; that is, destroyed and broken to pieces.

﴿in what they are engaged in﴾; that is, in the false religion. God Most High will ruin and demolish the religion they follow, soon, and will smash their idols and leave them crushed to fragments. The nominal sentence (al-jumla al-ismiyya) was used only to indicate certainty.

﴿and vain﴾; that is, utterly perished.

﴿is what they have been doing﴾ in worshipping them. Although their purpose in that was drawing near to God Most High, it is pure disbelief. This is not like His saying: ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust﴾, as some have supposed. What is meant there is the acts of righteousness they performed in the Jahiliyya (the pre-Islamic period). In themselves these are good deeds, and had they been accompanied by faith they would have entailed their rewards. They were nullified only because they were accompanied by disbelief. (p-268)

The placement of "these" as the subject of inna, and the fronting of the predicate within the sentence that serves as its predicate, marks idol-worshippers as those exposed to destruction, shows that it does not go beyond them at all, and establishes it as a binding decree upon them. This is to warn them of the consequence of what they sought and to make hateful to them what they loved.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 140:

﴿He said: "Shall I seek for you a god other than Allah"﴾ This begins the explanation of the affairs of Allah, the Exalted, which necessitate restricting worship to Him alone, after the explanation that what they asked to be worshipped is something whose worship cannot be sought at all, being destroyed and false. For this reason, "he said" was placed between the two, even though each of them is the speech of Musa, upon him be peace.

The interrogative is for denial, astonishment and rebuke. The insertion of the hamzah (interrogative particle) before "ghayra" (other than) indicates that what is being denied is that the one sought be other than Him, the Exalted, because the denial is directed at the "otherness" itself and not at the restriction of worship to something other than Him, the Exalted. The accusative of "ghayra" is as the object of "abghi" (I seek), with the lam elided; that is: "abghi lakum" (I seek for you), meaning: I seek for you other than Allah, the Exalted.

As for "ilahan" (a god), it is either a specification (tamyiz), or a circumstantial qualifier (hal), or it is in the circumstantial position from "ilahan", which is the object of "abghi", on the basis that the original is: "abghi lakum ilahan ghayra Allah", so "ghayra Allah" is an adjective of "ilahan", and when the adjective of an indefinite noun was fronted, it became accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal).

﴿And He has preferred you over the worlds﴾; that is: and the state is that He, the Exalted, has singled you out with blessings that He did not give to others. In this there is an alert to what they did of bad conduct, in that they repaid Allah's singling them out from among their peers with what they did not deserve, by graciously resorting to the basest of His creatures and making it a partner to Him, the Exalted. Woe to them and to what they worship.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 141:

﴿And [remember] when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh﴾: This is a reminder to them, from Him (glory be to Him), of the blessing of deliverance from the dominion (malakah) of Pharaoh. It is also read as "najjaynakum" (from al-tanjiyah), and it is read as "anjakum," in which case it is addressed from the side of Musa (upon him be peace); that is: remember the time of Our delivering you.

﴿from the people of Pharaoh﴾: from their dominion, not merely by rescuing you from their hands while they remained in their power and capability, but by destroying them completely.

As for His (exalted) saying, ﴿they were afflicting you with a dreadful torment﴾: from sama (to impose), as in sama-hu khasfan, meaning he assigned it to him or imposed it upon him. It is either a resumed statement explaining what He delivered them from, or a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the addressees, or to the people of Pharaoh, or to both together, since it includes the pronouns of both.

As for His (exalted) saying, ﴿they slew your sons and spared your women﴾: it is a substitute (badal) for "yasumunakum," clarifying or explaining it.

﴿And in that﴾: in that deliverance or in the dreadful torment.

﴿was a trial﴾: that is, a blessing or a tribulation.

﴿from your Lord﴾: from the Master of your affair, for both blessing and affliction come from Him (glory be to Him and exalted).

﴿a great [trial]﴾: whose magnitude cannot be measured.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 142:

﴿And We appointed for Moses thirty nights﴾ It is related that Moses, peace be upon him, promised the Children of Israel, while they were in Egypt, that if Allah destroyed their enemy, he would bring them a Book containing an explanation of what they should do and what they should abstain from. When Pharaoh was destroyed, Moses, peace be upon him, asked his Lord for the Book, and He commanded him to fast thirty days, which was the month of Dhu al-Qa'dah. When he completed the thirty days, he noticed a change in the smell of his mouth, so he used the siwak (tooth-stick). (p-269) The angels said: "We used to smell the fragrance of musk from your mouth, and you have spoiled it with the siwak."

It is also said: Allah, exalted is He, revealed to him: "Do you not know that the odour of the mouth of one who fasts is more pleasing to Me than the scent of musk?" So Allah, exalted is He, commanded him to add ten days to it from Dhu al-Hijjah for this reason.

This is the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We completed it with ten﴾. The expression "nights" is used for them because they are the best parts of the months. It is also said: Allah, exalted is He, commanded him to fast thirty days and to do in them what would bring him closer to Allah, exalted is He; then the Torah was sent down to him during the ten, and he spoke with Him therein. The mention of the forty has been stated briefly in Surat al-Baqarah and is detailed here.

"Wa'adna" means "waʿadna" (We promised), and it has been read thus. It is also said: the form (wāʿadnā) is on its original pattern, based on treating Moses' acceptance as equivalent to a promise. "Thirty" is the second object of wā'adnā, with an elided genitive: i.e., the completion of thirty nights.

﴿So the appointed time of his Lord was completed as forty nights﴾; i.e., reaching forty nights.

﴿And Moses said to his brother Aaron﴾ when he set out for the private conversation, as he had been commanded.

﴿Take my place﴾; i.e., be my successor.

﴿among my people﴾ and watch over them in what they do and abstain from.

﴿And act righteously﴾ concerning whatever of their affairs needs setting right, or be a reformer.

﴿And do not follow the way of the corrupters﴾; i.e., do not follow those who pursue corruption, and do not obey those who call you to it.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 7, verse 143:**

﴿When Musa came at Our appointed time⦆ at Our time which We had appointed for him. The lam here indicates exclusivity (ikhtisas), meaning: his coming was specifically for Our appointed time.

﴿and his Lord spoke to him⦆ without an intermediary (wasita), as He speaks to the angels, peace be upon them. It is related that he (peace be upon him) heard that speech from every direction. This is a reminder that hearing the speech of the Mighty and Majestic is not of the same kind as hearing the speech of human interlocutors.

﴿He said: My Lord, show me Yourself, that I may look upon You⦆ That is: show me Your essence, by enabling me to see You, or manifest Yourself to me so that I may look at You and see You. This is evidence that seeing Him, exalted is He, is permissible in general, since requesting the impossible is impossible for the prophets, especially a request that implies ignorance of the affairs of God, exalted is He. For this reason He answered him with His words, exalted is He: "You will not see Me" (lan tarani), rather than "I will not see" (lan ara), "I will not show You" (lan urika), or "you will not look at Me" (lan tanzura ilayya). This is a reminder that he was incapable of seeing Him, because seeing depends on an enabling condition (mu'idd) in the one who sees, and that condition had not yet been realized in him. Making the question a means of rebuking his people, who said: ﴿Show us God openly⦆, is an error. For if seeing were impossible, it would have been obligatory for him to declare them ignorant and remove their doubt, as he did when they said: ﴿Make for us a god⦆, and for him not to follow their path, as he said to his brother: ﴿and do not follow the way of the corrupters⦆.

Using the answer as proof of its impossibility is even greater error, since the report that he has not seen Him does not indicate that He will never be seen, or that no one else will ever see Him, let alone that it indicates impossibility. Claiming that it is a matter of necessity (darura) is either arrogance or ignorance of the reality of seeing.

﴿He said⦆ is a resumptive statement (isti'naf), built upon a question arising from the discourse, as if it were said: "What did the Lord of Might say when Musa said what he said?" So it was answered: "He said."

﴿You will not see Me, but look at the mountain. If it remains in its place, then you will see Me⦆ This is a corrective statement (istidrak) to explain that he could not bear it. The conditioning of seeing upon the mountain's remaining in place also indicates permissibility, since what is conditional upon something possible is itself possible. As for the mountain, it is said to be the mountain of Urdunn (Jordan).

﴿Then when his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain⦆ That is: His greatness became apparent to it, and His power and command confronted it. It was also said: the mountain was given life and sight until it saw Him.

﴿He made it crumble to dust⦆ reduced to pieces and crushed. The words daka and daqq are brothers, like shakk and shaqq. It was also read as (dakka'), meaning level ground. From the same root is the she-camel (naqa dakka'), which has no hump. It was also read as (dukkan), the plural of dakka', meaning pieces.

﴿Musa fell down senseless⦆ unconscious from the terror of what he saw.

﴿When he recovered⦆ Recovery (ifaqa) is the return of reason and understanding to a person after they have departed through some cause.

﴿He said⦆ in glorification of what he had witnessed.

﴿Glory be to You⦆ That is: exalting You above my asking You anything without Your permission.

﴿I repent to You⦆ That is: from the boldness and presumption of asking without Your permission.

﴿And I am the first of the believers⦆ That is: in Your greatness and majesty. It was also said: the first to believe that You cannot be seen in this world. It was also said: that it is not permissible to ask without Your permission.

﴿He said, "O Musa..."﴾ This is a resumptive clause (istinaf), brought to console him, peace be upon him, for not being granted his request to see (Allah). It is as if it were said: "If I have denied you the sight, I have given you great blessings that I have given to no one else among the worlds. So seize them and persevere in giving thanks for them."

﴿Indeed I have chosen you﴾; that is, I have selected you, taken you as a chosen one (safwah), and preferred you.

﴿above the people﴾; that is, above your contemporaries. Harun, although he was a prophet, was commanded to follow him, and he was not a Kalim (one spoken to directly by Allah) nor a bearer of a law (sahib shar'.

﴿with My messages﴾; that is, with the leaves (asfar) of the Tawrah (Torah). It is also read as: "bi-risalati" (in the singular).

﴿and with My speech﴾, and with My speaking to you without an intermediary.

﴿So take what I have given you﴾; that is, what I have bestowed upon you of the nobility of prophethood and wisdom.

﴿and be among the grateful﴾ for what you have been given of great blessings. It is said: the request to see (Allah) was on the Day of 'Arafah, and the giving of the Torah was on the Day of al-Nahr (the Day of Sacrifice).

And We wrote for him on the tablets of everything (㉄) — that is, of what they need in matters of their religion.

﴿a admonition and detailed explanation of everything﴾ is a substitute for the prepositional phrase "for him"; that is, We wrote for him everything of admonitions and the detailed explanation of the rulings. There is disagreement about the number of the tablets, their substance, and their size. It is said they were ten tablets; it is said seven; it is said two. It is said they were of emerald, brought by Jibril (peace be upon him); it is said of green chrysolite, or of red ruby.

It is also said that God Most High commanded Musa to cut them from a hard rock, which He softened for him, so he cut them with his hand and split them with his fingers. From al-Hasan (may Allah be pleased with him): they were of wood that descended from the heaven, in which was the Torah, and their length was ten cubits.

It is also said that the Torah was sent down, and it was seventy camel-loads, of which a portion was read in a year; only four persons read it: Musa, Yusha', 'Uzayr, and 'Isa (peace be upon them). From Muqatil (may Allah be pleased with him): it was written on the tablets: "Indeed I am Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Do not associate anything with Me, do not cut off the road, do not commit adultery, and do not disobey your parents."

﴿So take it﴾ is by implying a verb of speech coordinated with "We wrote"; that is, We said: take it.

﴿with strength﴾ means with earnestness and resolve. It is also said it is a substitute for the Most High's words: "﴿Take what I have given you﴾", and the pronoun refers to the tablets, or to "everything," since it carries the meaning of "things," or to the message, or to the Torah.

﴿And command your people to take the best of it﴾; that is, the best of what is in it, such as pardon and patience, in preference to retaliation and vindication, by way of recommendation and urging the choice of the more excellent. As in the Most High's words: ﴿And follow the best of what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾. Or it refers to its obligatory matters, for they are better than the permissible.

It is also said the meaning is: they should take it and the best of its connections. Qutrub said: that is, by its goodness, and all of it is good, as in the Most High's words: ﴿And the remembrance of Allah is greater﴾. It is also said that it means to interpret a word that admits two meanings, or many meanings, according to the most fitting of its possibilities with truth, and the closest of them to correctness.

﴿I will show you the abode of the defiantly disobedient﴾ is a shift of address and a turning of the speech toward his people (peace be upon him) by way of iltifat, urging them to earnestness in carrying out what they were commanded. Either in the manner of warning and intimidation, where the meaning of "the abode of the defiantly disobedient" is the land of Egypt and the dwellings of 'Ad and Thamud and their like; for seeing them, when they are empty of their people and in ruins upon their foundations, requires reflection and restraint from deeds like those of their people, lest what befell those befall them.

Or in the manner of promise and encouragement, where the meaning of "the abode of the defiantly disobedient" is either the land of Egypt alone, or together with the land of the tyrants and the Amalekites in al-Sham, for it too was granted to the Children of Israel and written for them, as His words, Mighty and Majestic, indicate: ﴿O my people, enter the holy land which Allah has prescribed for you﴾.

The meaning of "showing" is causing to enter by way of inheritance, and this is supported by the reading of one who recited ( سَأُورِثُكم ) with the letter thāʾ, as in the Most High's words: ﴿And We caused the people who had been oppressed to inherit the eastern and western parts of the earth﴾. It was also read ( سَأُورِيكم ), and perhaps it is from awray tu al-zand, that is: I will make it clear to you.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 146:

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿I will turn away from My signs those who are arrogant on the earth﴾ is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) brought to warn them against arrogance, which necessitates not reflecting upon the signs, which are what was written on the tablets of the Torah of admonitions and rulings, or what includes them and other than them of the created signs (al-ayat al-takwiniyyah), among which is what was promised to be shown of the abode of the wicked. The meaning of turning them away from them is sealing upon their hearts such that they can hardly reflect upon them or take lessons from them, due to their persistence in what they are upon of arrogance and haughtiness, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when they swerved, Allah caused their hearts to swerve﴾.

And the fronting of the prepositional phrase before the direct object is to show concern for what is fronted and to create suspense for what is delayed, although in the delayed element there is a kind of length which its fronting would disturb the harmonious correspondence of the parts of the sublime composition. That is: I will seal upon the hearts of those who consider themselves great and see for themselves superiority and merit over creation, so they do not benefit from My revealed and created signs, nor seize the spoils of their effects. So do not follow their path, lest you become like them.

It has also been said: the meaning is: I will turn them away from nullifying them, even if they strive as Pharaoh strove to nullify the signs he saw, but Allah, exalted is He, refuses except to establish the truth and eliminate falsehood. On this view, the more fitting interpretation of "the abode of the wicked" is the land of the tyrants and giants who were renowned for wickedness and arrogance on the earth, and showing it to the addressees means their entry into Syria and their settling in its dwellings and homes, as indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O my people, enter the holy land which Allah has prescribed for you﴾.

His saying, exalted is He: "﴿I will turn away from My signs﴾ ..." etc. is a response to an implied question arising from the promise of entering Syria, on the basis that the signs refer to what was recited just before and its like, and turning them away from them means removing them from the position of opposing and resisting them, because their reports occurred and the rulings and effects of them became manifest through their destruction at the hand of Musa, peace be upon him, when he traveled after the wandering (al-tih) with those of the Children of Israel who remained, or with their descendants, according to the differing narrations, to Jericho, with Yusha' ibn Nun at its vanguard, and he conquered it, and the Children of Israel settled in Syria and possessed its eastern and western regions. It is as if it were said: how will they see their abode while they are in it? So it was said: I will destroy them. He turned to the word "turning away" only so that they might increase in confidence in the signs and tranquility through them.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿without right﴾ is either attached to "arrogance," meaning: they are arrogant with what is not right, which is their false religion and their excessive injustice; or it is connected to an omitted element which is a circumstantial clause (hal) of its agent, meaning: they are arrogant while being involved in what is not right.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if they see every sign, they will not believe in it﴾ is conjoined to "they are arrogant," included with it under the ruling of the relative clause. By "sign" is meant either the revealed one, so its seeing means witnessing it by hearing it; or what includes it and other miracles, so its seeing means witnessing in general, encompassing both hearing and sight. That is: if they witness every one of the signs, they will not believe in it, according to the generality of the negation and not the negation of generality; that is, they disbelieve in each one of them, because they do not perceive them as they are. This, as you see, supports the reading of "turning away" as sealing.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if they see the way of right guidance, they will not take it as a way﴾ is conjoined to what precedes it and is included in its ruling; that is, they do not turn toward the truth nor follow its path at all, because Satanic qualities have overtaken them and they are disposed toward deviation and swerving. It was read with two fathas, and it was read: "al-rashad," and all three are dialectal forms, like "al-suqm," "al-saqam," and "al-saqam."

﴿And if they see the way of error, they will take it as a way﴾; that is: they choose it for themselves as a continuous course from which they hardly turn aside, because it accords with their false desires and leads them to their appetites.

﴿That﴾ is a reference to what was mentioned of their arrogance, their not believing in any of the signs, their turning away from the way of right guidance, and their complete turning toward the way of error. It is the subject (mubtada') whose predicate is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿because﴾; that is: it occurs because of the fact that

﴿they denied Our signs﴾ which indicate the falsehood of the vices they are characterized by, and the truth of their opposites.

﴿and they were heedless of them﴾, not reflecting upon them; otherwise they would not have done what they did of falsehoods. It is permissible that it refers to what was mentioned of the turning away, and the indication of the causality of what is in the relative clause does not prevent this; how not, when it has passed that this, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is because they disobeyed...﴾ the verse, may refer to the infliction of humiliation and wretchedness, and the incurring of great wrath, while that is explicitly causally attributed to disbelief in the signs of Allah.

It has also been said: the position of the demonstrative is accusative as an infinitive (masdar); that is: I will turn them away with that turning because of their denial of Our signs and their heedlessness of them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 147:

﴿And those who denied Our signs and the meeting of the Hereafter﴾; that is, and [those who denied] their meeting the Abode of the Hereafter, or their meeting what Allah the Exalted promised in the Hereafter of recompense. The place of the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) is in the nominative case, as the subject of a nominal sentence (mubtada').

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿their deeds have become void﴾ is its predicate (khabar); that is, the falsity of their deeds has become manifest, those deeds which they had performed, such as maintaining the ties of kinship, relieving the distressed, and the like. Or, their deeds have become void after they had been hoped to benefit them, on the assumption of their belief in them.

﴿Are they recompensed?﴾; that is, they are not recompensed.

﴿except for what they used to do﴾; that is, except the recompense for what they used to do of disbelief and sins.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 148:

﴿And the people of Musa took, after him,﴾; i.e., after his departure to the Mount (al-Tur).

﴿from their ornaments﴾: this is connected to "took" (ittakhadha), like the first preposition (min) in the sense that the two prepositions differ in meaning: the first (min) is for origin (ibtida'), while the second is for partitive (tab'id) or explanatory (bayan). Alternatively, the second is connected to an omitted element that occurred as a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to what follows it; for if it were delayed, it would have been a qualifier (sifa) of it.

The attribution of the ornaments to them, although they belonged to the Copts, is due to the slightest association, since they had borrowed them from their owners shortly before the drowning, so they remained in their hands. As for their possessing them after the drowning, that depends on the Children of Israel's acquisition of the spoils of the Copts, and they were under mutual protection among themselves, so the saying of theirs does not support it: ﴿We were burdened with loads of the people's adornments﴾.

Al-huliyy, with a damma on the ha' and a kasra on the lam, is the plural of hal'y, like thady and thudiyy; it was also read with a kasra on the ha' by assimilation, like dili (dilyy), and it was read: ( hilyihim ) in the singular.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿a calf﴾ is the object of "took", placed after the prepositional phrase for the reason already mentioned of giving attention to what is fronted and creating suspense toward what is delayed, together with the fact that it involves some length which fronting would disrupt the harmony of the parts of the noble composition. It was said that it is transitive to two objects in the sense of "making", and the second object is omitted; i.e., a god.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿a body﴾ is an apposition to "a calf", or a lifeless form possessing blood and flesh, or a body of gold without a spirit in it.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿that had a lowing﴾; i.e., the sound of a cow. It was read with a jim and a hamza (ju'a') and it is the crying out; it is a qualifier of "a calf".

It is narrated that when the Samiri had fashioned the calf, he put into its mouth dust from the hoofprint of Jibril, peace be upon him, which he had taken at the splitting of the sea, or at his turning toward the Mount, and so it became alive. It was also said that he fashioned it by some kind of trick, whereby wind would enter its inside and it would make a sound. The first view is more suitable in light of what is in Surat Ta-Ha. The attribution of the taking to them, though it was his act, is either because he was one of them, or because they approved of it so that they are as if they did it, or because the intended meaning of "taking" is their taking it as a god, not its making and fashioning.

﴿Did they not see that it does not speak to them﴾: this is a resumptive statement brought to rebuke and denounce them, to weaken their minds and to call them foolish for what they undertook of the reprehensible act, which is taking it as a god; i.e., did they not see that there is nothing in it of the attributes of divinity, since it does not speak to them?

﴿and does not guide them to a path﴾ in any way at all, so how could they take it as a god?

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then they took it﴾; i.e., they did that.

﴿and they were wrongdoers﴾; i.e., placing things in other than their proper places. So this was not the first reprehensible act they committed. The clause is a parenthetical concluding statement, and the repetition of "they took it" serves to double the denunciation and to set the objection upon it.

The commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 149:

﴿And when they were struck with remorse﴾; that is, they regretted what they had done with the utmost regret. This is a metonymy (kinaya) for that, since the regretful, grieved person bites his hand in distress, so his hand becomes "fallen into" (maskutan fiha). It is also read as "saqata" (in the active form), meaning the biting fell upon it (fiha), so "the hand" is literal. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is that remorse fell into their souls, either by way of metaphor combined with metonymy (isti'ara bi'l-kinaya) or by way of figurative representation (tamthil).

﴿and they saw that they had gone astray﴾ by taking the calf; that is, it became clear to them to the point that they were certain of it, as though they saw it with their own eyes. The mention of their remorse is placed before this seeing, although it comes after it, in order to hasten to explain it and to indicate the extreme speed of its occurrence, as though it preceded the seeing.

﴿They said﴾, by Allah,

﴿"If our Lord does not have mercy on us"﴾ by sending down a repentance that expiates,

﴿"and forgive us"﴾ our sins by overlooking our wrongdoing. Mercy is placed before forgiveness, even though clearing away (takhliya) ought to precede adorning (tahliya), either to hasten to what is the primary aim, or because mercy here means the general intention of good for them, which is the origin of sending down the expiating repentance for their sins.

The lam in "la'in" (in "in lam") is a preparatory lam for the oath, as has been indicated. The lam in His words, Exalted is He, ﴿"we will surely be among the losers"﴾ is the answer to the oath. What is related of them concerning the remorse, the seeing and the saying, although it occurred after Musa (peace be upon him) returned to them, as the verses in surah Ta-Ha indicate, is placed here so that what came from them of speech and action is related in one place (p-274).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 150:

﴿And when Musa returned to his people﴾ This begins an account of what Musa, peace be upon him, did after his return from the appointed meeting (mithaq), following the account of what his people had done after him.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿angry and grieved﴾ are two states of Musa, peace be upon him, or the second is a state of the pronoun within "angry" (ghadban). Asif means one who is extremely angry; it is said it means one who is sorrowful.

﴿He said: "Evil is what you have done in my stead after me"﴾; that is: evil is what you did after my absence, in that you worshipped the calf after you had seen my action of affirming the oneness of God Most High, negating partners from Him, and making worship sincerely for Him; or after my commanding you to that, and your restraining from what your eyes had longed for, when you said: ﴿Make for us a god just as they have gods﴾.

It is the right of successors to conduct themselves in the manner of the one who appointed them. So the address is to the worshippers, namely al-Samiri and his followers. Or it means: evil is what you did in standing in my place without observing my covenant, in that you did not restrain the worshippers from what they did. In this case the address is to Harun and those believers with him, as indicated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He said: "O Harun, what prevented you, when you saw them going astray, ﴾ ﴿from following me? Did you then disobey my command?"﴾.

It is also permissible that the address is to all of them, on the basis that the meaning of "successor" encompasses both of the matters mentioned. And "ma" is an indefinite descriptive noun explaining the implied subject of "bi'sa" (evil), and the object of the dispraise is omitted; its estimation: "Evil is the succession that you succeeded me in after me, your succession."

﴿Did you hasten the command of your Lord?﴾; that is: you left it incomplete, by way of including in 'ajila the meaning of 'sabaqa' (to precede). It is said: 'ajila 'an al-amr, when one leaves the matter incomplete. Or: did you hasten the promise of your Lord that He made to me of the forty (nights), and did you estimate my death, and did you change after me just as nations changed after their prophets.

﴿And he threw down the tablets﴾, casting them out of intense anger and extreme vexation, out of zeal for the religion. It is related that the Torah was seven sevenths in seven tablets; when he threw them, they broke, and six sevenths of them, which contained the detailed explanation of everything, were lifted up, and there remained one seventh, which contained the admonitions and the rulings.

﴿And he seized his brother by the head﴾, by the hair of his head, peace be upon them both.

﴿dragging him towards himself﴾ is a state of the pronoun in "seized". He, peace be upon him, did this supposing that he had fallen short in restraining them. Harun was three years older than him, peace be upon them both, and he was gentle-natured, and for this reason he was more beloved to the Children of Israel.

﴿He said﴾; that is: Harun, addressing Musa, peace be upon them both.

﴿"O son of my mother"﴾, with the omission of the particle of address, and the singling out of the mother in mention, although they were full brothers, because the mother's right is greater and more deserving of consideration, especially as she was a believing woman who had endured fears and hardships on his account. It was read with a kasra on the mim with the ya' dropped for lightness, like a vocative noun attached to the ya'; the reading with a fatha is for further lightness, or by analogy with "khamsata 'ashar" (fifteen).

﴿"Indeed the people deemed me weak and nearly killed me"﴾, to remove the suspicion of shortcoming in his regard; the meaning: I exerted my effort in restraining them until they overpowered me, deemed me weak, and came close to killing me.

﴿"So do not let the enemies rejoice over me"﴾; that is: do not do to me what would be a cause for their gloating over me.

﴿"And do not place me among the wrongdoing people"﴾; that is: do not count me among their number in censure, or in attributing to me shortcoming. This supports the view that the address is to all of them. Or: do not believe that I am one of the wrongdoers, while I am innocent of them and of their wrongdoing. (p-275)

﴿Qala﴾ (He said) is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), answering a question that arises from the narration of Harun's (peace be upon him) apology. It is as if it were said: "What did Musa say at that point?" And it was said: "He said."

﴿My Lord, forgive me﴾; that is: for what I did to my brother, without a sin established on his part.

﴿And my brother﴾, in case some shortcoming occurred from him in restraining those people from the great evil they committed. He (peace be upon him) asked forgiveness for him in order to satisfy his brother and to show the gloaters his approval, so that their gloating over him and his brother would not be complete, and to indicate that he himself was in need of seeking forgiveness, since it was incumbent upon him to fight them.

﴿And admit us into Your mercy﴾, by increasing the favor after forgiving what has passed from us.

﴿And You are the Most Merciful of the merciful﴾. So there is no wonder in our being included in the thread of Your vast mercy in this world and the Hereafter. The sentence is an interjected concluding clause (i'tiraDh tadhyili), confirming what precedes it.

Indeed, those who took the calf (i.e., persisted in taking it and continued to worship it), like the Samiri and his followers among those whose hearts had been saturated with it. This is made clear by the fact that the second relative clause refers to those who repented, for that is explicit evidence that the first relative clause refers to the persistent.

﴿Will befall them﴾: i.e., in the Hereafter.

﴿Wrath﴾: i.e., great, whose magnitude cannot be measured, entailing all kinds of punishments, because their crime is among the greatest of crimes and the most abominable of sins.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿from their Lord﴾: i.e., their Master. It is connected to ﴿will befall them﴾, or to something omitted that is an adjective of ﴿wrath﴾, emphasizing what the indefiniteness (tanwin) conveys of intrinsic magnificence with the magnificence of attribution. I.e., it is existing from their Lord.

﴿And humiliation in the life of this world﴾ is the humiliation of estrangement, by which proverbs are coined, and the wretchedness that encompasses them and their descendants all together, and the humiliation specific to the Samiri, of isolation from people and of being afflicted with "no touching" (la misas).

It is narrated that their remnants today say this, and if anyone else touches one of them, they all become feverish at that moment. The placing of what befell them within the scope of the sin (the future particle) despite its having passed is by way of giving precedence to the condition of the later generations over that of the earlier ones.

It has been said: the intended ones are those who repented, and by the wrath is meant what they were commanded to do of killing themselves. The sin has been excused on the grounds that this is a report of what God, exalted is He, informed Musa, peace be upon him, when He informed him of the trial of his people and their taking of the calf, that wrath from their Lord and humiliation would befall them, so it would be prior to the wrath. But you know that the coherence and the context of the noble text clearly reject this.

How could it not, when His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Thus do We recompense the fabricators﴾ calls out against it, for they are martyrs who repented, so how is it possible to describe them afterward with fabrication? Also, God, exalted is He, does not recompense all fabricators with this recompense, whose outward aspect is subjugation and whose inner aspect is gentleness and mercy.

It has been said: the intended ones are their descendants who were contemporaries of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), for reproaching children for the deeds of their fathers is well known and familiar. From it is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And when you killed a soul...﴾ to the end of the verse, and His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And when you said, "O Musa..."﴾ to the end of the verse.

The intended wrath is the wrath of the Hereafter, and the humiliation is what befell them of killing, expulsion, and imposition of the jizyah (poll tax) upon them. It has been said: the intended by the relative clause are those who actually took the calf, and by the pronoun in ﴿will befall them﴾ are their descendants. There is no doubt that inserting the condition of these in the midst of describing the condition of those who took it is like separating the wood from its bark.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 153:

﴿And those who committed evil deeds﴾, whatever evil it was. (p-276)

﴿Then repented﴾ of those evil deeds.

﴿After them﴾; that is, after committing them.

﴿And believed﴾, with sound, sincere faith, and occupied themselves with establishing what is required by it of righteous deeds, and did not persist in what they had done, unlike the first group.

﴿Indeed your Lord, after them﴾; that is, after that repentance accompanied by faith.

﴿is Forgiving﴾ of sins, however great and however many they are.

﴿Merciful﴾, exceedingly bountiful in bestowing the various forms of mercy in this world and the Hereafter. The mention of the title "Lord" together with the attribution to his pronoun, upon him be peace, is for honour.

﴿And when the anger subsided from Moses﴾ This begins the account of the rest of the story, after the people's division into those who persisted (in sin) and those who repented was explained, and after an indication, in summary, of the outcome of each group.
