That is, when his anger calmed down because of his brother's apology and the people's repentance. This clearly shows that what is related of their regret and its consequences took place after Moses, peace be upon him, had returned.

In this noble composition there is eloquence and emphasis, as the anger that moved him to what he did, both in action and in speech, is treated as if it were the one giving the command, urging him to act with domineering severity. The expression of its calming by "silence" (al-sukut) is clear. It is also read as sakana, sakata, and askata, with the agent being God Most High, or his brother, or the repentant people.

﴿he took up the Tablets﴾ that he had thrown down.

﴿and in their inscription﴾: that is, in what was copied onto them. The word nuskhah is written on the pattern fu'lah in the sense of maf'ul (object), like khutbah (sermon). It is also said: "in what was copied from them," that is, from the broken Tablets.

﴿was guidance﴾: that is, a clarification of the truth.

﴿and mercy﴾ to creation, by guiding them to what contains good and righteousness.

﴿for those who fear their Lord﴾: The first lam is connected to an omitted element which is a description of mercy, that is, existing for them. Or it is the lam of purpose (lam al-ajal), that is, guidance and mercy for their sake. The second lam is for strengthening the action of the verb placed later, as in God's words: ﴿If you are skilled at interpreting dreams﴾. Or it is also the lam of cause (lam al-'illah), with the object omitted; that is, they fear sins for the sake of their Lord, not for show and reputation (al-riya' wa al-sum'ah).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 155:

﴿And Musa chose from his people seventy men﴾ This begins the explanation of how repentance was sought and how it came about. "Ikhtara" (chose) is transitive to two objects, the second of which is preceded by "min" (from); that is, he chose from among his people, with the preposition omitted and the verb made to reach the object directly, as in his saying:

"He chose you from among the people when their characters decayed, and he who was hoped for was afflicted with ill, and the cup of favour..."

That is: he chose you from among the people.

﴿seventy men﴾ is the object of "ikhtara," placed after the second object for the reason mentioned many times before, namely the concern with what is foremost and the arousing of anticipation for what is delayed.

﴿for Our appointed time﴾ the one We appointed after what happened from his people had happened, not the appointed time of the speech mentioned before that, as has been said.

Al-Suddi said: God the Exalted commanded him to come to Him with men from the Children of Israel who would apologise to Him, the Exalted, for the worship of the calf, and He made them an appointment. So peace be upon him chose from his people seventy men.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: he chose them so that they might repent to Him, the Exalted, for what they had done, and ask Him for repentance on behalf of those they had left behind among their people. They said: peace and blessings be upon him chose six from every tribe, and then two were added, so he said: "Let two of you remain behind," and they disputed over it. So peace and blessings be upon him said: "Indeed, for him who stays behind is like the reward of him who goes forth." So Caleb and Joshua remained, and the rest went with him. He commanded them to fast, to purify themselves, and to purify their garments. He went out with them to Mount Sinai, and when they drew near the mountain, a cloud covered it, and Musa entered the cloud with them, and they fell down prostrate. They heard Him, the Exalted, speaking to Musa, commanding him and forbidding him as He willed, and that was the command to slay themselves in repentance.

﴿So when the quaking seized them﴾ for what they had presumed to ask of him, namely the seeing (of God). It is reported that when the cloud cleared, they came to Musa, peace be upon him, and said: ﴿We will not believe you until we see God openly﴾, whereupon the quaking seized them, that is, the thunderbolt, or the quaking of the mountain, and they swooned from it, that is, died.

Perhaps by their saying "We will not believe you" they meant: "We will not accept that the one who commanded what we heard, the command to slay ourselves, is God the Exalted, until we see Him," since they analogised the seeing of Him to the hearing of His speech by a corrupt analogy. Then, when Musa witnessed that terrible state...

﴿He said: My Lord, if You had willed, You would have destroyed them before, and me also﴾; that is, when they were negligent in forbidding the worship of the calf, and did not separate from its worshippers when they saw their persistence in it.

﴿and me also﴾ too, when I asked You for the seeing; that is, if You had willed to destroy us for our sins, You would have destroyed us then. By this, peace be upon him, intended to remind of the earlier pardon in order to draw down the subsequent pardon, for acknowledging sin and giving thanks for blessing, which binds what is present and draws what is more, means: we were deserving of destruction, and there was no barrier to it except the absence of Your will for it; since You showed kindness to us and pardoned us those offences, it is no wonder that You should also pardon us this offence.

To take the statement as a wish is ruled out by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us did?﴾; that is, those who do not know the details of Your affairs and do not verify the slippery matters. The interrogative particle is either for denying that destruction has occurred, in trust in God's kindness, as Ibn al-Anbari said, or for entreaty, as al-Mubarrad said; that is, do not destroy us.

﴿It is only Your trial﴾ is a resumptive sentence confirming what precedes it, and an apology for what they did by stating the source of their error; that is: the trial into which the foolish fell, and because of which they said the great things they said, is nothing but Your trial, that is, Your affliction and testing, in that You made them hear Your speech, so they were tempted by it and did not verify, and so they coveted what was beyond it, following the corrupt analogy.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿You lead astray by it whom You will, and guide whom You will﴾ is either a resumptive sentence explaining the ruling of the trial, or a circumstantial clause from "Your trial"; that is, being a trial by which [some] are led astray... etc.; that is, You lead astray by means of it whom You will to be led astray, so he does not come to verify, and You guide whom You will to guidance to the truth, so he does not waver in such matters, and his faith is strengthened by them.

﴿You are our Protector﴾; that is, the one who manages our affairs in this world and the next, and our Helper and Guardian, and none other than You.

﴿So forgive us﴾ the sins we have committed. The "fa" is for ordering the supplication upon what precedes it of protection, as if it were said: whoever the Protector wills, grant forgiveness and mercy. It has been said that his peace and blessings, in venturing to say "It is only Your trial..." etc., was a great presumption, so he asked God the Exalted for its forgiveness and pardon.

﴿and have mercy upon us﴾ by pouring upon us the effects of mercy in this world and the next.

﴿And You are the best of the forgivers﴾ is a concluding parenthetical clause confirming the supplication that precedes it, and the singling out of forgiveness for mention is because it is the most important in this context.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 156:

﴿And ordain for us﴾; that is, appoint for us. It was also said: make obligatory, establish, and confirm.

﴿in this world a good [thing]﴾; that is, blessing and well-being, or a good quality. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "Accept our embassy and return us with forgiveness and mercy."

﴿and in the Hereafter﴾; that is, and ordain for us in it also a good [thing], which is the excellent reward and Paradise.

﴿Indeed, we have turned back to You﴾; that is, we have repented and returned to You. It derives from hada, yahudu (to return), and it was read with a kasra on the ha', from hadahu, yahiduhu (to move and incline it). It may be in the active voice, or in the passive voice with the meaning "we inclined ourselves," or "we were inclined to You."

As for the possibility that the well-known reading is in the passive voice according to the dialect of those who say "'udi al-mariḍ" (the sick person was visited), although this is a weak dialect, it is unbecoming of the sublime revelation. The clause is a resumptive sentence (istinaf) brought to give the reason for the supplication, for repentance is something that is made obligatory before it by the binding of the inevitable promise. Opening it with the particle of confirmation serves to show full eagerness and desire for repentance.

The meaning is: we have repented and returned from the great disobedience that we committed, for which we came to you to apologize, and from what occurred here of asking to see [You]. It is far from Your kindness and bounty that You would not accept the repentance of those who repent.

It was said: when the quake seized them, they all died, and Moses, peace be upon him, began to supplicate Allah the Exalted until He revived them. It was also said: they trembled, their joints were nearly separated, and they came close to destruction, so Moses, peace be upon him, feared and wept, and Allah the Exalted removed it from them.

﴿He said﴾: a resumptive sentence that came as an answer to a question the discourse leads to, as if it were said: "What did Allah the Exalted say when Moses, peace be upon him, supplicated?" So it was said: "He said."

﴿My punishment — I afflict with it whom I will﴾. Perhaps when He, mighty and majestic, made the repentance of those who worshipped the calf to be by their killing themselves, Moses, peace be upon him, included in his supplication a request for lightening and facilitation, when he said: "And ordain for us in this world a good [thing]," that is, a good quality free from hardship and severity, for in the killing of themselves there is an evident punishment and severity. So He, the Exalted, answered that My punishment is such that I afflict with it whom I will punish, without any interference from anyone else in it, and they are among those whom My will has encompassed. For this reason their repentance was mixed with worldly punishment.

﴿And My mercy encompasses all things﴾; that is, its nature is to encompass in this world the believer and the disbeliever, indeed everything that falls under the description of "thing," from among the accountable and others. Your people have received a share of it within the worldly punishment. The attribution of affliction to punishment is in the present tense, and the attribution of encompassing to mercy is in the past tense, as an indication that mercy is required by the Essence, whereas punishment is required by the disobedience of the servants, and the will is considered also in the matter of mercy.

The absence of explicit mention of it [the will with mercy] serves to indicate its utmost clarity. Do you not see His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So I will ordain it﴾; that is, I will establish it and appoint it. For it is branched off from the consideration of the will, as if it were said: "So when the matter is as such," that is, as mentioned, the affliction of My punishment and the vastness of My mercy for everyone whom I will, "I will ordain it" as an ordainment in the manner you supplicated by your saying: "And ordain for us in this [world]..." etc.; that is, I will ordain it pure, not mixed with worldly punishment.

﴿for those who are mindful﴾; that is, of disbelief and of disobedience, either from the beginning or after having become involved in them. In this there is an allusion to his people, as if it were said: "Not for your people, because they are not mindful, so what has been decreed for them of mercy suffices them, even if it is accompanied by worldly punishment."

﴿and who give zakat﴾ (p-279). In this too there is an allusion to them, since zakat was burdensome for them. Perhaps prayer was not mentioned, despite its excellence over other acts of worship, because it is sufficed by mindfulness, which is an expression for performing all the obligations and abstaining from all the forbidden acts. The mention of giving zakat is for the allusion that has passed.

﴿and who are, in Our signs,﴾ all of them.

﴿believers﴾: believing continuously, without neglecting any of them. In this there is an allusion to them and to their disbelief in the great signs that Moses, peace be upon him, brought, and in what will come after that of clear signs, such as the shading by the cloud, the sending down of manna and quails, and other things.

The repetition of the relative pronoun, although what is intended by it is the very same thing intended by the first relative pronoun, rather than saying "and who believe in Our signs" as a conjunction with "who give zakat," just as the latter was conjoined with "who are mindful," is because of the restriction indicated by placing the prepositional phrase first; that is, they believe in all of Our signs, not in some of them to the exclusion of others.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 157:

﴿Those who follow the Messenger﴾, the one (ﷺ) to whom We reveal a Book specific to him.

﴿the Prophet﴾; that is, the possessor of the miracle (mu'jiza). It has also been said: the title of the message in relation to Him, may He be exalted, and the title of prophethood in relation to the community.

﴿the unlettered﴾, with the hamza pronounced with a damma, a nisba to umm (mother), as if he remains in the state in which his mother bore him; or a nisba to the Arab nation (umma), as he (ﷺ) said: "Indeed we are a nation that neither reckons nor writes"; or a nisba to Umm al-Qura (Mecca). It has also been read with a fatha on the hamza, meaning: the one who did not practise reading and writing, and who nevertheless combined with that the sciences of the first and the last.

The relative clause is either a substitute (badal) for the first relative clause, a substitution of the whole (badal al-kull), or in the accusative by way of praise (nasb 'ala al-madh), or in the nominative by way of praise (raf' 'ala al-madh); that is, "I mean: those who," or "they are those who." As for making it a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is "He commands them," or "those are the successful," this is not sound.

﴿whom they find written﴾ with his name and attributes, such that they have no doubt that he is he; for this reason it is phrased in this way rather than saying "they find his name or his description written."

﴿with them﴾: this is added for the sake of emphasis, and that his (ﷺ) matter is present with them, never absent from them at all.

﴿in the Torah and the Gospel﴾, the two by which the Children of Israel were worshipped, earlier and later. The two adverbial phrases are connected either to "they find him" or to "written." Mentioning the Gospel before its revelation is of the same kind as what we are discussing regarding the mention of the Prophet (ﷺ), and of the noble Qur'an before their coming.

﴿He commands them to do what is right and forbids them from what is wrong﴾: this is a resumed statement (kalam mustan'af) with no place in terms of i'rab, as al-Zajjaj said. It includes a detailing of some of the rulings of the mercy that was promised earlier in summary, for what is explained in it of commanding the right and forbidding the wrong, making lawful the good things and making unlawful the foul things, and removing the burdensome obligations, are all among the effects of His vast mercy.

It has also been said: it is in the accusative position, as a presumed circumstantial clause (hal muqaddara) from the object of "they find him," or from the Prophet, or from the pronoun in "written," or it is an explanation of "written"; that is, of what was written.

﴿and makes lawful for them the good things﴾ which were made unlawful for them because of the evil of their wrongdoing.

﴿and makes unlawful for them the foul things﴾, such as blood, the flesh of swine, usury and bribery.

﴿and relieves them of their burden and the shackles that were upon them﴾; that is, he lightens for them what they were charged with of burdensome obligations, which are of the kind of what was prescribed for them at that time, such as making repentance dependent on killing oneself (qatl al-nafs), prescribing retaliation (qisas) for intentional and accidental killing without the legislation of blood money (diya), cutting off the sinful limbs, scraping the place of impurity from the skin and clothing, burning the spoils of war, and the prohibition of the Sabbath.

It is related from 'Ata': that when the Children of Israel stood to pray, they would wear coarse garments and tie their hands to their necks, and perhaps a man would pierce his collarbone and place in it the end of a chain, and fasten it to a pillar, restricting himself to worship. It has also been read: (āṣārahum), the root of al-asr is the burden that restricts its bearer from movement.

﴿So those who believed in him﴾: an instruction on the manner of following him (ﷺ), and a statement of the high rank of his followers and their seizing the spoils of the vast mercy in both abodes, following the mention of his noble attributes, and an indication of his (ﷺ) guidance to them in commanding the right, forbidding the wrong, making lawful the good things and making unlawful the foul things; that is: those who believed in his prophethood and obeyed him in his commands and prohibitions.

﴿and honoured him﴾; that is, they magnified him and revered him, and assisted him by preventing his enemies from him. It has also been read with lightening (ʿazzarūhu), and its root meaning is prevention, and from it comes ta'zir (discipline).

﴿and supported him﴾ against his enemies in religion.

﴿and followed the light that was sent down with him﴾; that is, with his prophethood, and it is the Qur'an. It is expressed as "light," indicating that it is manifest in itself and makes other things manifest, or that it makes the realities manifest, revealing them, in keeping with the word "following." It is also permissible that "with him" be connected to "followed"; that is, they followed the Qur'an that was sent down along with following him (ﷺ) by acting upon his sunna and what he commanded and forbade, or they followed the Qur'an, accompanying him in following it.

﴿Those﴾: a pointing to those mentioned, in respect of their being characterised by the excellent attributes that have been detailed, to indicate that these attributes are the cause of the ruling; and what it contains of the sense of distance is to announce the exaltedness of their rank and the loftiness of their station in virtue and nobility; that is: those described by those noble attributes.

﴿they are the successful﴾; that is, they are those who attain the sought goal and are saved from distresses, not others among the nations. Thus the people of Musa (peace be upon him) enter into it in the primary sense, since they were not saved from the immense hardship in their repentance. By this the verification is achieved and the harmony and application are made possible between his supplication (peace be upon him) and the response, not merely by what has been said, that he prayed for himself and for the Children of Israel. He was answered with what contains a rebuke of the Children of Israel for their presumption in asking to see God, may He be mighty and majestic, and for their disbelief in His great signs which He brought about by the hand of Musa (peace be upon him), and this is alluded to in His words, may He be exalted: "And those who believe in Our signs."

It is intended that the hearing of the descriptions of their descendants who believed in the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and in what he brought, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and others among the People of the Two Books, should be a kindness to them and an encouragement towards sincere faith and righteous deeds.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 158:

﴿Say: O mankind, indeed I am the Messenger of God to you all﴾ When the attributes of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and the nobility of those from the People of the Book who follow him, and their attainment of the happiness of both abodes, had been related in the two Scriptures, he (peace be upon him) was commanded to make clear that this happiness is not restricted to them, but encompasses everyone who follows him, whoever he may be, by clarifying the universality of his message to both humankind and jinn (al-thaqalan), while the messages of all the other Messengers (peace be upon them) were restricted to their own peoples.

The sending of Moses (peace be upon him) to Pharaoh and his chiefs with the nine signs was only for the purpose of commanding them to worship the Lord of the worlds, may His authority be exalted, and to abandon the great claim that the tyrant was making, which his rebellious faction accepted from him, and for sending the Children of Israel out of captivity and coercion. As for acting upon the rulings of the Torah, it is specific to the Children of Israel.

﴿all﴾ is a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the pronoun in ﴿to you﴾.

﴿Him to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ is in the accusative case, or in the nominative case by way of praise, or in the genitive case as an attribute of the Divine Name (al-jalalah); and even if something that is related to what is attached to it intervenes between them, it is in the position of what precedes it.

His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿There is no god but Him﴾ is an explanation of what precedes it: whoever possesses the world is the God, not anyone else.

His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿He gives life and causes death﴾ is for the purpose of further establishing His divinity.

The fa' in His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿So believe in God and His Messenger﴾ is for deriving the command from what has been established and confirmed regarding his message (ﷺ). Mentioning himself (peace be upon him) with the title of Messenger, in the manner of a shift to the third person (iltifat ila al-ghaybah), is for the sake of emphasizing the obligation to comply with his command.

Describing the Messenger with the words ﴿the Prophet, the Unlettered﴾ is to praise him (peace be upon him) with both of these qualities, and to further establish his matter and confirm that he is the one written about in the two Scriptures.

His description with the words of the Most High: ﴿who believes in God and His words﴾; that is, what was revealed to him and to all the other Messengers (peace be upon them) of His books and revelation, in order to lead the People of the Two Scriptures to comply with what they were commanded. The explicit mention of his belief in God, Most High, is to alert that belief in Him, Most High, is inseparable from belief in His words, and is not realized except through it.

It has been recited as ﴿His word (wa-kalimatihi)﴾, taking it as a generic noun, or as the Qur'an; to draw attention to the fact that what is commanded is belief in him (peace be upon him) insofar as the Qur'an was revealed to him, and not from any other standpoint. Or it is taken to mean Jesus (peace be upon him), as an allusion to the Jews and an alert that whoever does not believe in him has not had his faith counted.

﴿And follow him﴾; that is, in everything he brings and everything he forbids of the matters of religion.

﴿So that you may be guided﴾ is the reason (illah) for the two verbs, or a circumstantial clause (hal) of their doers; that is, hoping that you will be guided to the desired goal, or hoping for it. In attaching it to both of them there is a notice that whoever affirms him but does not follow him by committing to the rulings of his law is far from being guided, remaining persistent in error and misguidance.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 159:

﴿And among the people of Moses is a community that guides by the truth and by it they act justly﴾ is a new sentence (isti'naf) meant to dispel what might be suggested by the restriction of writing mercy, piety and faith in the signs to those who follow the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), namely the deprivation of the forefathers of the people of Moses (peace be upon him) from every good. It also clarifies that they are not all as their conditions were described, but rather among them is ﴿a community that guides﴾, i.e., the people.

﴿By the truth﴾, i.e., connected with it, or they guide them with the word of truth.

﴿And by it﴾, i.e., by the truth.

﴿They act justly﴾, i.e., in the rulings applied among themselves. The imperfect form of the two verbs is for narrating a past state. It has also been said that they are those who believed in the Prophet (ﷺ), but this is contradicted by the fact that they have already been mentioned earlier.

It has been said that when the Children of Israel went to extremes in insolence and tyranny, to the point that they dared to kill the prophets (peace be upon them), a tribe among them disassociated itself from what they had done and made an excuse, and they asked Allah the Exalted to separate them from those tyrants. So Allah the Exalted opened for them a tunnel in the earth, and they travelled through it for a year and a half until they emerged from beyond China, and they are today there, upright Muslims who face our qibla.

It has also been reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that Jibril (peace be upon him) took him on the night of the Isra' toward them, and he spoke with them. Jibril (peace be upon him) said: "Do you know whom you are speaking to?" They said: "No." He said: "This is Muhammad, the unlettered Prophet." So they believed in him and said: "O Messenger of Allah, Musa instructed us: whoever among you attains Ahmad, let him recite my greeting to him (peace be upon him)." So Muhammad returned the greeting to Musa, peace be upon them both. Then he recited to them ten surahs of the Qur'an that had been revealed in Makkah, and no obligation had been revealed at that time other than the prayer and the zakat. He commanded them to establish these where they were, and they used to observe the Sabbath, so he commanded them to gather for worship and to abandon the Sabbath.

Now, you are aware that restricting guidance to them from among his people (peace be upon him), while some of them believed in all the laws, is not free from remoteness.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 160:

﴿And We divided them﴾: that is, the people of Musa, not the nation mentioned among them. It is also read with the lighter form (qati'nahum).

His words, exalted is He, ﴿twelve﴾ are the second object of qatta'a (divided), because it includes the sense of making (tasyir). The feminine form is due to treating the noun as referring to a nation (umma) or a portion (qit'a). That is: We made them twelve nations or twelve portions, each distinguished from the others. Or it is a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of its object: We divided them, counted as this number.

His words, exalted is He, ﴿tribes (asbatan)﴾ are a substitute (badal) for it. It is a plural noun. Or it is a specifier (tamyiz) of it, meaning that each one of the twelve portions was a tribe (asbat), not a single tribe (sibt). It is also read ('ashirata) with a kasra on the shin.

His words, exalted is He, ﴿nations (umaman)﴾: according to the first reading it is a substitute following a substitute, or a qualifier of asbatan. According to the second reading it is a substitute of asbatan.

﴿And We revealed to Musa when his people asked him for water﴾: at the time when thirst overcame them in the wilderness (tih) into which they had fallen through their own misconduct. It was not merely their asking him for water, peace be upon him, but his being asked to bring water for them, as shown by His words, exalted is He: ﴿And when Musa asked for water for his people﴾.

His words, exalted is He, ﴿Strike the rock with your staff﴾ explain the act of revelation (idha'). The matter of the rock has already been explained in the commentary on surah al-Baqara.

﴿Then there gushed forth﴾ is a conjunction (atf) upon an implied clause that the speech carries along with it, which has been omitted because its meaning is fully evident. It is also an indication of how swiftly he hastened to obey, an intimation that striking did not actually cause the effect, and an alert to the extreme speed of the gushing (inbijas), which is bursting forth. It was as if it happened immediately after the command, before the striking was completed, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Strike the sea with your staff, and it split﴾. That is: he struck, and it gushed forth.

﴿from it twelve springs﴾, equal to the number of tribes. As for what has been said, that the intended meaning is "if you strike, then it has gushed forth," this is not worthy of the eloquence of the revealed text. It is also read ('ashirata) with a kasra and a fatha on the shin.

﴿Every people knew their drinking place﴾: every tribe. It was expressed in this way to indicate the large number of each of the tribes.

﴿their drinking place﴾: that is, their own particular spring.

﴿And We shaded them with clouds﴾: that is, We made the clouds such that they cast their shade over them, moving through the wilderness with their movement and settling with their settling. It was also the case that a pillar of fire descended at night, and they travelled by its light.

﴿And We sent down upon them manna and quails﴾: that is, terangabin (a sweet exudation) and quails. It has been said that manna would descend upon them like snow from dawn until sunrise, a sa' for each person, and the south wind would bring quails to them, and a man would slaughter from them what sufficed him.

﴿Eat﴾: that is, and We said to them: Eat.

﴿of the good things We have provided for you﴾: that is, of its delicious things. Whether ma is a relative pronoun or a descriptive term, it refers to the manna and the quails.

﴿And they did not wrong Us﴾ is a return to the pattern of the earlier speech after the report of their address. It is conjoined with an omitted clause for brevity, and to indicate that this is a established matter that needs no explicit statement. That is: so they did wrong, by disbelieving in those magnificent blessings.

And they did not wrong Us by that, ﴿but they were wronging themselves﴾, since its harm does not pass beyond them. The fronting of the object (anfusahum) serves to convey the restriction (qasr) required by the preceding negation. There is in it a kind of mockery of them (tahakkum). The combination of the past and present verb forms indicates their persistence in the wrongdoing and disbelief in which they were.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 161:

﴿And when it was said to them﴾ is in the accusative, governed by a hidden verb addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ). The verb is presented in the passive form while being attributed to Allah, the Exalted, as is made clear by what occurs in Surah al-Baqarah in His words: "And when We said" (﴿وَإذْ قُلْنا﴾), in keeping with the manner of Divine majesty and to indicate that there is no need to state the agent explicitly, since it is determined. The change of arrangement by the command to "remember" is for emphasis in the rebuke; that is: recall to them the time of Allah's saying to their forefathers.

﴿Dwell in this town﴾ is in the accusative as an object (maf'ul bihi), as in the expression "I dwelt in the house" (sakantu al-dar). It is said that it is in the accusative of place (zarfiyyah) by extension. It is Bayt al-Maqdis, and it is said Ariha, which is the town of the giants (al-Jabbarin). In it there were a people from the remnant of 'Ad called al-'Amaliqah, whose leader was 'Uj ibn 'Unuq.

In His words "Dwell" (﴿اسْكُنُوا﴾) there is an indication that what was commanded in Surah al-Baqarah is entering in the manner of settling and residing.

For this reason, "abundantly" (raghadan) is omitted in His words ﴿and eat from it﴾; that is, from its foods and fruits, with "from" (min) being partitive, or "from it" (minha) being for origin.

﴿Wherever you wish﴾; that is, from its various parts, without anyone competing with you over them, for continuous eating in this manner can only be abundant and wide. The conjunction of "eat" (kulu) to "dwell" (uskunu) with "and" (wa) is because the two occur together in time, unlike entering, which precedes eating; for this reason, there it was said: "so eat" (fakulu).

﴿And say: "Hittah"﴾; that is, our request, or your command is "hittah" for our sins. It is a form from "al-hatt" (lowering), like "al-jilsah."

﴿And enter the gate﴾; that is, the gate of the town.

﴿Prostrating﴾; that is, humbling yourselves and submitting, or prostrating in gratitude for their being brought out of the wandering (al-tih). Placing the command to enter before the command to speak, as mentioned in Surah al-Baqarah, does not disrupt this order, because what is commanded is the combining of the two actions without regard to ordering between them.

Then, if by the town is meant Ariha, it has been narrated that they entered it, when Musa (peace be upon him) marched toward it with those of the Children of Israel who remained, or with their offspring, according to the differing narrations, and he conquered it as mentioned in Surah al-Ma'idah. As for if it is Bayt al-Maqdis, it has been narrated that they did not enter it during the lifetime of Musa (peace be upon him); it was said that the meant gate is the gate of the dome toward which they used to pray.

﴿We will forgive you your sins﴾. It was read as "khataya-kum," as in Surah al-Baqarah, and "tughfar lakum khati'atukum," "khataya-kum," and "khati'atukum," in the passive voice.

﴿We will increase the good-doers﴾ is a promise of two things: forgiveness and increase. Dropping the "and" (waw) here does not disturb this, because it is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) following from an implied question arising from the announcement of forgiveness, as if it were said: "What then is for them after forgiveness?" So it was answered: "We will increase." Likewise, "min-hum" (from among them) is an explanatory increase.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 162:

﴿So those who did wrong among them substituted⦁﴾ a saying other than what they had been told, namely, by way of repentance and seeking forgiveness, since they turned away from it and put something else in its place.

﴿a saying﴾ other than that which contained no good. It is related that they entered [the town] crawling on their backsides, and instead of "ḥiṭṭah" (remission/forgiveness) they said "ḥinṭah" (wheat). It was also said that they spoke in Nabataean, "ḥaṭan shamqathan," meaning "red wheat," making light of God's command and mocking Moses, upon him be prayers and peace. (p-284)

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿other than what had been said to them﴾, it is an attribute of "qawlan" (a saying). The difference is stated explicitly, even though substitution already implies it with certainty, for the sake of emphasis and to affirm that the difference is in every respect.

﴿So We sent upon them﴾ immediately after they did what they did, without delay. In Surat al-Baqarah the phrase is ﴿upon those who did wrong﴾, and the meaning is the same. Sending (irsal) is from above, so it is like sending down (inzal).

﴿a plague (rijz) from the heaven﴾, a punishment coming from it. What is meant is the plague (ta'un). It is related that twenty-four thousand of them died in a single hour.

﴿because they used to do wrong﴾ on account of their continuous wrongdoing, both before and after, as indicated by combining the past and present forms of the verb, not on account of the substitution alone, as the sequence of the sending after it with the particle "fa'" might suggest. The explicit statement of this reason is because the ruling here is linked to the pronoun rather than to the relative clause with "wrong," as in Surat al-Baqarah. As for the causation by "transgression" (fisq) after the indication of wrongdoing as cause, its aspect has already been discussed there. And God knows best.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 163:

﴿And ask them﴾ is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to the implied element in "idh" (when). It has been said: that is, "Ask the Jews contemporary with you a question of reproach and affirmation concerning their ancient disbelief and their transgression of the limits of God, the Exalted; and as an informing that this matter, although it is among their hidden sciences, which none attains except one who has studied their books, has been fully known to the Prophet ﷺ. And since that was not by receiving it from their books—for he ﷺ was far removed from that—it is determined that it was, on the part of the source, plain revelation (al-wahy al-sarih)."

﴿concerning the town﴾; that is, concerning its condition and its story, and the great calamity that befell its people. It is Ayla, a town between Madyan and Mount Sinai (al-Tur). It has been said: it is Madyan. It has been said: it is Tiberias. The Arabs call a city "qarya" (town).

﴿which was situated by the sea﴾; that is, close to it, overlooking its shore.

﴿when they transgressed in the Sabbath﴾; that is, they exceeded the limits of God, the Exalted, by hunting on the day of Sabbath (al-sabt). The "idh" (when) is an adverbial clause (zarf) for the omitted noun that was annexed, or a substitute (badal) for it. It has been said: it is an adverbial clause for "kanat" (was), or for "hadirah" (situated), but this is not right, since there is no benefit in restricting the state of being, or of being situated, to the time of transgression.

It was read as "ya'uddun" (they transgress), whose origin is "ya'tadun" (they exceed), and "yu'iddun" (they prepare), from "i'dad" (preparation), since they used to prepare the implements of hunting on the day of Sabbath, though they were forbidden from occupying themselves with anything on it other than worship.

﴿when their fish came to them﴾: this is an adverbial clause for "ya'dun" (transgress), or a substitute after a substitute. The first is the better, because the question about their transgression is more fitting for reproach.

"Hitan" (fish) is the plural of "hut"; the waw was changed to ya' because of the kasra before it, like "nun" and "ninan," in form and meaning. Its attribution to them (their fish) serves to indicate that it is specific to them, since it is distinguished by properties that hardly exist in other members of the species, extraordinary properties beyond the ordinary habit; or because what is meant by it is the fish present in that region, and the coming and not-coming that is mentioned is due to their habit of not being exposed on the day of Sabbath.

﴿on the day of their Sabbath﴾ is an adverbial clause for "ta'tihim" (comes to them); that is, it came to them on the day of their glorifying the matter of the Sabbath. "Sabt" is a verbal noun: "sabatat al-yahud" means when the Jews glorified the Sabbath by devoting themselves to worship. It has been said: it is a name for the day, and the annexation is because they were specified with rulings concerning it. The first meaning is supported by the reading of one who read: "yawma asbatihim" (on the day of their rests).

God, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿their fish being visible﴾ is the plural of "shari'" (approaching), from "shara'a 'alayhi," when he drew near and overlooked. It is a circumstantial state (hal) of "hitanihim" (their fish); that is, it came to them on their day of Sabbath, visible on the surface of the water, close to the shore.

﴿and on the day they did not keep the Sabbath﴾; that is, they did not observe the matter of the Sabbath. But not merely by the non-observance while the day of Sabbath is established, as is the apparent meaning, but with the absence of both together; that is, there is no Sabbath and no observance, as in the saying:

"And you do not see the lizard therein burrowing"

It was read "la yusbitun" (they do not keep the Sabbath) from "asbata," and "la yusbatun" in the passive, meaning: they do not enter upon the Sabbath, the ruling of the Sabbath is not applied to them, and they are not commanded in it with what they were commanded on the day of Sabbath.

﴿it did not come to them﴾, as it used to come to them on the day of Sabbath, out of caution regarding their hunting. The change of construction, where it did not say "and it did not come to them on the day they do not keep the Sabbath," is because the report of its coming on their day of Sabbath is a likely occasion for the question: "Then what is its condition on the day they do not keep the Sabbath?" So it was said: on the day they do not keep the Sabbath, it does not come to them.

﴿Thus We test them﴾; that is, like that wondrous, terrible trial, We deal with them in the manner of one who tests them, so that their transgression becomes manifest and We take them to account for it. The present tense form is for narrating a past state, to bring its image to mind and to express wonder at it.

﴿because they used to transgress﴾; that is, because of their continuous corruption, indicated by combining the forms of the past and the present, but not in that particular matter; for their corruption in it was not the cause of the trial, rather it was because of their continuous corruption in everything they did and everything they neglected.

It has been said: "Thus" is connected to what precedes it; that is, "it does not come to them like what came to them on their day of Sabbath." The sentence after it is then a resumptive clause (isti'naf) answering the question about the wisdom of the variation in the state of the fish, by coming at one time and not coming at another.

﴿And when they said﴾ is coordinated with "when they transgressed" (إذْ يَعْدُونَ), and is brought in to show their persistence in transgression and their refusal to desist from it after the admonitions and warnings.

﴿a community of them﴾; that is, a group of their righteous ones, who went to great lengths in admonishing them, riding the back of every difficult and docile thing, until they despaired of these others accepting the admonition. These others would not give up reminding them, hoping for benefit and effect, exaggerating in presenting an excuse and hoping for the benefit of the warning.

﴿Why do you admonish a people whom Allah is going to destroy﴾; that is, whom He will completely annihilate and cleanse the earth of.

﴿or punish with a severe punishment﴾, short of total destruction. It was also said: "destroy them" means "disgrace them in this world," or "punish them in the Hereafter" because they did not desist from the sinfulness and rebellion they were engaged in. The disjunction (أوْ) is for precluding the absence of both, not for precluding their combination, since they will be destroyed in this world and punished in the Hereafter. The choice of the active participle form (اسم الفاعل) — "destroyer" (مُهْلِكُهم) and "punisher" (مُعَذِّبُهم) — although each of the destruction and the punishment is awaited, serves to indicate their certain realization and settlement, as if they were already occurring. They said this to exaggerate that the admonition does not benefit them, or to frighten the people, or as a question about the wisdom and benefit of admonition. Perhaps they said it in the presence of the people, urging them to take heed, since a categorical statement about their destruction and punishment casts fear and dread into their hearts.

It was also said: the intended meaning is a group from the doomed sect, who answered their admonishers with this, as a rejection of them and in mockery of them. But this is not the case, as you will come to understand.

﴿They said﴾; that is, the admonishers.

﴿As an excuse to your Lord﴾; that is, we admonish them as an excuse before Him, Exalted is He, taking it as an object of purpose (مَفْعُولٌ لَهُ), and this is most suitable given the apparent meaning of their words "Why do you admonish." Or we make an excuse, an excuse, taking it as a verbal noun (مَصْدَرٌ) of a deleted verb. It was also read in the nominative, as the predicate of a deleted subject; that is, "our admonition is an excuse before Him, Exalted is He," so that we will not be attributed to any kind of negligence in forbidding the evil. The addition of "Lord" (الرَّبّ) to the pronoun of the addressees contains a kind of allusion to the questioners.

﴿and perhaps they will be God-fearing﴾ is coordinated with "as an excuse" (مَعْذِرَةً); that is, and in hope that they may fear God to some degree. This is explicit that those who said "Why do you admonish..." etc., were not from the doomed sect, for otherwise the address would have been obligatory.

(p-286)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 165:

﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of﴾; that is, they abandoned what their righteous ones had admonished them with, abandoning it as one abandons something forgotten, and turned away from it entirely, such that none of those admonitions came to their minds at all.

﴿We rescued those who forbade evil﴾, and they are the two groups mentioned, and the presenting of their deliverance in the form of an answer, whose proper structure would be to follow from the condition, namely the forgetting of the transgressors which entails their destruction, is because what falls within the scope of the condition is two matters: forgetting and reminding. It is as if it were said: when the reminders reminded and the transgressors did not heed, We rescued the first group and seized the others. As for beginning the answer with their rescue, it is because of the hastening, which has passed many times, to explain their salvation from the outset, together with the kind of lengthiness found in what is delayed.

﴿And We seized those who did wrong﴾ by transgression and by opposing the command.

﴿with a severe punishment﴾; that is, harsh, in form and in meaning, from "ba's yab'us ba'san" (bu'sa), meaning it became intense. It has been read as "bay'is" on the pattern of "fay'il", with the ayn vowelled with fatha and with kasra, and "bi'is" like "hadhir" with the ayn lightened and its vowel moved to the fa', like "kibd" for "kabd", and "bayiis" with the hamza changed to ya', like "dhiib" for "dhi'b", and "bayyis" like "rayyis" by changing the hamza of "ba'is" to ya' and assimilating the ya' into it, and "bays" on the lightened pattern of "bayyis", like "hayn" for "hayyin". The indefiniteness of "punishment" is for magnification and awe.

﴿because they used to defy﴾; this is connected to "seized" like the first "bi", and there is no harm in it since the two differ in meaning; that is, We seized them with the punishment mentioned because of their persistence in defiance, which is going out of obedience, and it is also wrongdoing and transgression. Applying the ruling to the relative pronoun, although it implies that what is in the clause of the relative is its cause, nevertheless he expressly stated the stated cause to signal that the cause is the continuation in wrongdoing and transgression, with the consideration that this is a departure from the obedience of Allah, mighty and majestic, not the mere act of wrongdoing and transgression; otherwise they would not have been delayed from the beginning of the act even for an hour.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 166:

It may be that God, exalted is He, punished them with a severe punishment short of total annihilation, so they did not desist from what they were engaged in, but rather increased in error, and then He transformed them (masakha-hum) after that. This is because of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when they became arrogant regarding that which they had been forbidden﴾; that is, they rebelled and grew proud, and refused to abandon what they had been forbidden.

﴿We said to them: Be apes, despised⟩ (khasi'in): humbled, abased, distant from people. The intended meaning of the command is the command of creation (al-amr al-takwini), not the command of speech (al-amr al-qawli). The ordering of the transformation upon their arrogance in refraining from what they had been forbidden is to indicate that it was not specific to the characteristics of the fish; rather, the essential matter in this is the violation of the command and the defiance against Him, exalted is He.

It has been said: the intended meaning of "the painful punishment" (al-'adhab al-ba'is) is the transformation, and the second clause is an affirmation of the first. It was narrated that the Jews were commanded to observe the day that we were commanded to observe, which is Friday, but they abandoned it and chose Saturday. This is what is meant by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Sabbath was only prescribed for those who differed concerning it﴾. So they were tested with it: hunting in it was forbidden to them, and they were commanded to honor it. The fish would come to them on Saturday like the shallow waves (al-makhad), so that the surface of the water could not be seen because of their multitude, and they would not come to them on the other days. They remained in this state for a period of time. Then Iblis came to them and said: "You were only forbidden from taking them on Saturday; so make pools that are easy to enter and difficult to exit." They did so, and they began driving the fish into them on Saturday, so the fish could not leave them, and they would take them on Sunday.

A man among them took a fish and tied a thread to its tail, (p-287) and fastened the thread to a piece of wood on the shore. Then he roasted it on Sunday. His neighbor smelled the scent of the fish and looked into his oven, and said to him: "I see that God will punish you." When he was not punished, he (the neighbor) took two fish on the following Saturday. When they saw that the punishment was not hastening upon them, they persisted in this; they hunted, ate, salted, and sold, and they numbered about seventy thousand. So the people of the town became three groups: one third persisted in the prohibition; one third grew weary of the admonition and tired of it, and said to the preachers: "Why do you admonish ..." etc.; and one third engaged in the sin. When they did not desist, the Muslims said: "We will not live with you," so they divided the town with a wall, having a gate for the Muslims and a gate for the transgressors.

Dawud, peace be upon him, cursed them, and one day the forbidders awoke in their assemblies, and none of the transgressors came out. They said: "Surely something has happened to them." They climbed the wall, looked, and behold, they were apes. They opened the gate and entered upon them, and the apes recognized their kin from among men, while those (men) did not recognize them. The ape would come to his relative, sniff his clothes, and weep; his relative would say to him: "Did we not forbid you?" and the ape would nod his head: "Yes." Then they died after three days.

It has been said: the young men became apes and the old men became swine. It was narrated from Mujahid, may God be pleased with him: "Their hearts were transformed." Al-Hasan al-Basri said: "By God, they ate the most calamitous meal that its people ever ate, the heaviest of them in disgrace in this world and the longest of them in punishment in the Hereafter. Hah! By God, a fish that a people took and ate is greater in the sight of God than the killing of a Muslim man. But God has appointed a term, and the Hour is more calamitous and more bitter."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 167:

﴿And [remember] when your Lord proclaimed﴾ is in the accusative as an object, governed by a suppressed verb coordinated with His saying, Exalted is He: "﴿And ask them﴾".

Ta'adhdhana (proclaimed) here means adhana (announced), just as tawa'ada (threatened) means awada (warned). Or it means 'azama (resolved), since one who resolves upon a matter speaks it to himself. It is treated as the verb of an oath, like ﴿Allah knows﴾ and ﴿Allah bears witness﴾.

Therefore it is answered with its answer, where it is said: ﴿He will surely send against them until the Day of Resurrection﴾; that is, mention to them the time when God, Exalted is He, made it binding upon Himself that He would absolutely set over the Jews [someone] ﴿who will afflict them with the worst torment﴾, such as humiliation, the imposition of the jizya (poll tax), and other kinds of torment. God sent against them, after Solomon, peace be upon him, Bukhtnasar (Nebuchadnezzar), who ruined their homes, killed their fighting men, and took captive their women and children, and imposed the jizya upon those of them who remained, and they used to pay it to the Magians. Until the Prophet ﷺ was sent, and he did what he did, then he imposed the jizya upon them, so it continues to be imposed upon them until the end of time.

﴿Indeed your Lord is swift in punishment﴾, He punishes them in this world.

﴿And indeed He is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful﴾ toward those among them who repent and believe.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 168:

﴿And We divided them﴾; that is, We scattered the Children of Israel.

﴿in the earth﴾, and We made each group of them to be in one region of its regions, such that no area of it was free of them, as a completion of their [former] dispersal, so that they would have no strength (shawka).

As for His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿nations (umaman)﴾, it is either a second object of qatta'na (We divided), or a circumstantial state (hal) of its object.

﴿Among them are the righteous﴾: this is a qualifier of umaman, or a substitute (badal) for it, and they are those who believed in Medina and whoever follows their way.

﴿And among them are others less than that﴾; that is, people below that description, that is, deviating from righteousness, and they are their disbelievers and their sinners. (p-288)

﴿And We tested them with good things and bad things﴾: with blessings and afflictions.

﴿that they might return﴾: from what they were in of disbelief and disobedience.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 169:

﴿Then there succeeded them﴾; i.e., after those mentioned.

Khalf (succession): i.e., a bad replacement. It is a verbal noun described by the word, and for this reason it applies to the singular and the plural. It has also been said that it is a plural. It is commonly used for evil, whereas khalaf (with a fatha on the lam) is used for good. The intended meaning is those who lived in the age of the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

﴿who inherited the Book﴾; i.e., the Torah, from their forefathers, reading it and understanding what is in it.

﴿They take the goods of this lower life﴾ is a resumed clause, brought to explain what they do with the Book after inheriting it; i.e., they take the trifling goods of this lesser thing, i.e., the worldly life. It derives from dunuww (nearness) or dana'a (baseness). The intended meaning is what they used to take as bribes in judgments and for distorting speech. It has also been said that it is a circumstantial clause relating to the waw in "inherited".

﴿and say: "It will be forgiven us"﴾, and God the Exalted will not hold us to account for it and will overlook it. The clause may be coordinated or circumstantial, and the verb is attributed to the prepositional phrase, or is a verbal noun of "they take".

﴿And if a similar good comes to them, they will take it﴾ is a circumstantial clause relating to the pronoun in "for us"; i.e., they hope for forgiveness, while they are persisting in the sin, returning to its like, not repenting of it.

﴿Was not the covenant of the Book taken from them﴾; i.e., the covenant stated in the Book.

﴿that they should not say about God except the truth﴾ is an explicative apposition to the covenant, or is dependent upon it; i.e., that they should not say... etc. The intended meaning is the refutation of them and the rebuke for their categorical claim of forgiveness without repentance, and an indication that this is a fabrication against God the Exalted and a departure from the covenant of the Book.

﴿And they studied what is in it﴾ is coordinated with "Was not ... taken" in meaning, for it is an affirmation; or it is coordinated with "inherited", and it is a parenthetical clause.

﴿And the Last Abode is better for those who fear God﴾ than what these people did.

﴿Do you not then understand?﴾ so that you would know this, and not exchange the lower thing that leads to punishment for the everlasting bliss. It is also read with the letter ya', and the shift in address serves to intensify the rebuke.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 170:

﴿Those who hold fast to the Book﴾; i.e., they hold fast in the matters of their religion. It is said: "he held (maska) to the thing" and "he clung (tamassaka) to it." Mujahid said: they are those among the People of the Book who believed, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and his companions, who held fast to the Book that Musa (peace be upon him) brought, so they did not distort it, did not conceal it, and did not take it as a means of gain (ma'kalah). 'Ata' said: they are the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). It was also read as (yumsikuna), from al-imsak (holding).

It was also read as (tamassaku, istamsaku), in agreement with His saying, ﴿and establish prayer﴾. Perhaps the change in the well-known reading is to indicate that holding fast to the Book is a continuous matter at all times, unlike establishing prayer, which is restricted to its times. Its singling out from among the other acts of worship is for its excellence over them. As for the place of the relative clause, it is either in the genitive case by coordination with "those who fear God" (alladhina yattaqun), and His saying, "﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾" is a parenthetical clause confirming what precedes it.

Or it is in the nominative case as a subject (mubtada'), and the predicate is His saying, ﴿Indeed We do not waste the reward of the righteous﴾. The link (rabit) is either the deleted pronoun, as is the opinion of the majority of the Basrans, the implied meaning being: "the reward of the righteous among them"; or the definite article (alif-lam), as is the opinion of the Kufans, for it is in the position of "their righteous ones," as in His saying, ﴿Indeed Paradise is the refuge﴾ (p-289), i.e., "their refuge." Or the generality in "righteous" (muslihin) is the link, as in "what a fine man Zayd is," according to one of the views. It was also said: the predicate is deleted, and the implied meaning is: "those who hold fast to the Book will be rewarded or recompensed," and His saying, "﴿Indeed We do not waste...﴾" etc., is a parenthetical clause confirming what precedes it.

And when We raised the mountain above them, [as though it were] a canopy—that is, We uprooted it from its place and lifted it over them.

﴿كَأنَّهُ ظُلَّةٌ﴾ ("as though it were a canopy"): that is, a shelter, meaning everything that provides shade over you.

﴿وَظَنُّوا﴾ ("and they thought"): that is, they were certain.

﴿أنَّهُ واقِعٌ بِهِمْ﴾ ("that it would fall upon them"): that is, it would drop down on them, because a mountain does not remain suspended in the air. They had been warned of it, and the use of the word "thought" in the narrative is because its object did not actually occur. The reason was that they refused to accept the rulings of the Torah because of their weight, so God Most High raised Mount Tur over them, and they were told: "If you accept what is in it, well and good; otherwise it will indeed fall upon you."

﴿خُذُوا ما آتَيْناكُمْ﴾ ("Take what We have given you"): that is, [We said], or saying: "Take what We have given you of the Book."

﴿بِقُوَّةٍ﴾ ("with strength"): with earnestness and determination to bear its hardships. It is a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) referring to the waw (the plural subject) [in "khudhū"].

﴿واذْكُرُوا ما فِيهِ﴾ ("and remember what is in it"): by acting upon it, and do not abandon it as one who has forgotten.

﴿لَعَلَّكم تَتَّقُونَ﴾ ("so that you may be God-conscious"): through that, [avoiding] ugly deeds and base character; or hoping that you will be included among the ranks of the God-conscious.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 172:**

﴿وَإذْ أخَذَ رَبُّكَ﴾ ﴿And when your Lord took...﴾ is in the accusative (*mansub*) governed by an implied verb (*mudmar*), and it is coordinated with what the phrase *idh nataqna* (﴿when We lifted﴾) is governed by. The passage is directed as an argument against the Jews, by reminding them of the general covenant that encompasses all of humankind, and as a rebuke for their breaking of it, following the argument against them by reminding them of the covenant of Mount Sinai. Linking the remembrance to a time, although the intent is to remind them of the events that occurred in it, has been explained many times before. The meaning is: "And mention to them the taking by your Lord..."

﴿مِن بَنِي آدَمَ﴾ ﴿from the Children of Adam﴾: What is meant by them are those to whom offspring were born, whoever they were, generation after generation, excluding those to whom no offspring was born for some reason among the reasons, such as infertility, not marrying, or dying young. The choice of *al-akhdh* (taking) over *al-ikhraj* (bringing forth) is to signal attention to the matter of those taken, because it contains news of their being chosen and selected. This is also the reason for attributing it to the name of the Lord by way of *iltifat* (shift of grammatical person), together with what it contains of preparing for the question that follows. Its attribution to his pronoun ﷺ (the Prophet's pronoun) is for honour.

﴿مِن ظُهُورِهِمْ﴾ ﴿from their backs﴾ is a substitute (*badal*) for "Children of Adam," a partial substitute (*badal al-ba'd*) with the repetition of the preposition, as in His saying: ﴿لِلَّذِينَ اسْتُضْعِفُوا لِمَن آمَنَ مِنهُمْ﴾ ﴿to those who were deemed weak, to those among them who believed﴾.

The *min* in both places is *ibtida'iyyah* (indicating origin/starting point). In it there is further affirmation of building the matter upon clarification after vagueness, and detail after generality, and an alert that the covenant was taken from them while they were in the loins of their fathers, and not deposited in the wombs of their mothers.

﴿ذُرِّيَّتَهُمْ﴾ ﴿their offspring﴾ is the object of *akhadha*, delayed after the object by means of the preposition, because it contains a pronoun referring back to it, and in observance of its originality and origin, and because of the suspense toward the delayed element that has been mentioned many times. It was also read as *dhurriyyatihim* (plural form). What is meant by them is their descendants in general. Thus the Jews contemporary with the Messenger of God ﷺ are included in them initially, just as their forebears were included among the Children of Adam in the same way. Restricting both to the Jews, past and future, while what is intended to be made clear of the marvellous work of God, the Exalted and Majestic, encompasses all people without exception, would undermine the grandeur of the revelation and the eloquence of the illustration.

﴿وَأشْهَدَهم عَلى أنْفُسِهِمْ﴾ ﴿and made them testify concerning themselves﴾: That is, He made each one of those offspring, taken from the backs of their fathers, testify concerning *itself* and not concerning anything else, as an affirmation to them of His complete lordship and what it entails of worship, exclusively, and other rulings of it.

﴿ألَسْتُ بِرَبِّكُمْ﴾ ﴿"Am I not your Lord?"﴾ is on the assumption of speech: that is, saying: "Am I not your Lord and the Owner of your affairs, and your Sustainer absolutely, without anyone having any part in any of your affairs?" Thus the entitlement to worship is included, and His exclusive right to it, which is the Exalted's, is necessitated.

﴿قالُوا﴾ ﴿They said﴾ is a resumptive statement (*istinaf*) built upon a question arising from the discourse, as if it were said: "What did they say at that time?" So it was said: "They said..."

﴿بَلى شَهِدْنا﴾ ﴿"Yes, we testify."﴾: That is, concerning ourselves, that You are our Lord and our God, and there is no lord for us other than You, as has come in the noble hadith. This is an illustration of His, the Exalted's, creating them all at the beginning of the natural disposition (*fitrah*), prepared to reason by the proofs set up in the horizons and in the souls, which lead to monotheism and submission, as His saying ﷺ indicates: "Every child is born upon the fitrah," and the hadith in full.

The whole is built upon an analogy (*tashbih*) of the mode derived from His, the Exalted's, presenting them with the knowledge of His lordship after enabling them to attain it, by means of the intellects and insights placed within them, and the proofs set up for them in the horizons and the souls with complete enabling, and their complete capacity to reach them, and their strong exposure to them. This is in a mode derived from His carrying them to acknowledge them by way of command, and their hastening to that without any hesitation at all, without there being any actual taking, testifying, question or answer there, as in His saying: ﴿فَقالَ لَها ولِلأرْضِ ائْتِيا طَوْعًا أوْ كَرْهًا قالَتا أتَيْنا طائِعِينَ﴾ ﴿He said to it and to the earth, "Come willingly or unwillingly." They said, "We come willingly."﴾

﴿أنْ تَقُولُوا﴾ ﴿lest you should say﴾ is read with the *ta'* (second person), by way of shifting the address (*talwin al-khitab*) and turning it away from the Messenger of God ﷺ to his contemporaries among the Jews, for intensification in the obligation. Or it is addressed to them and to their predecessors by way of *taghlib* (the dominant form standing for the whole). However, this is not from the standpoint that they are addressed by His saying: "﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾", for that is not part of the reported speech.

It was also read with the *ya'* (third person), on the basis that the pronoun refers to the offspring. In either case it is an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*) for what precedes it, namely the taking and the making to testify. That is: We did what We did out of aversion that you should say, or lest you, O disbelievers, should say, or they should say.

﴿يَوْمَ القِيامَةِ﴾ ﴿on the Day of Resurrection﴾ at the manifestation of the matter.

﴿إنّا كُنّا عَنْ هَذا﴾ ﴿"Indeed we were of this"﴾ — concerning the oneness of lordship and its rulings.

﴿غافِلِينَ﴾ ﴿"unaware."﴾ We were not alerted to it. For they, since they were created upon what has been mentioned of complete readiness to realize the truth, and the near capacity close to actual action, became those who are refuted and unable to offer an excuse by this, since there is no way for anyone to deny what has been mentioned of their creation upon the sound natural disposition.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 173:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Or you should say, "Only our fathers associated partners with God before us, and we were offspring after them."﴾ It is coordinated (ʿaṭf, grammatical coordination) with "say," and "or" (aw) here serves to prevent a void (khuluw, the absence of both options) but not to prevent combination. That is: they themselves invented association and they were the ones who instituted it.

﴿Before [us]﴾; that is, before our time.

﴿And we were﴾, we ourselves,

﴿offspring after them﴾, who could not find the way and could not reason by evidence.

﴿Will You destroy us for what the falsifiers did?﴾ Namely, what our fathers, the misguiders, did after it became clear that they were the criminals. We were incapable of planning and of independent judgment. Or [the meaning is]: "Will You hold us accountable and destroy us…?" The complete preparedness [of their minds] mentioned above closes for them the door of excusing themselves with this as well, for imitation (taqlid) has no valid basis at all when the proofs are present and they have the capacity to reason from them.

Having said this, this dialogue has been taken literally, as is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with him both, that: when God Exalted created Adam, peace be upon him, He wiped his back and brought forth from it every soul that He would create until the Day of Resurrection. Then He said, ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾ They said, "Yes." Then on that day it was proclaimed: the pen has dried over what will be until the Day of Resurrection.

It is also narrated from ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, that he was asked about this noble verse, and he said: I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ being asked about it, and he said: "God Exalted created Adam, then wiped his back with His right hand and drew out from it offspring. He said: I created these for Paradise and they will act with the deeds of the people of Paradise. Then He wiped his back and drew out from it offspring, and said: I created these for the Fire and they will act with the deeds of the people of the Fire."

The meaning is not that God Exalted brought out all of them from the back of Adam, peace be upon him, directly. Rather, He brought out from the back of Adam, peace be upon him, his biological sons, and from their backs their biological sons, and so on to the end of the chain. But since the original locus was the back of Adam, peace be upon him, and since the purpose of the two noble hadiths is to describe the condition of the two groups in general, without any scientific purpose attached to mentioning the intermediaries, the bringing forth of all was attributed to him.

As for the noble verse, since it is directed as an argument against the unbelievers contemporary with the Messenger of God ﷺ, and to show that attributing association to their fathers offers them no excuse, the context required attributing the bringing forth of each one of them to the back of his father, without addressing the bringing forth of Adam's biological sons from his back, which is certainly the case.

The absence of mention of the covenant (mithaq) in the hadith of ʿUmar, may God Exalted be pleased with him, is not a proof of its absence, nor does it imply its absence. As for what some have said, that taking the covenant was for removing the excuse of heedlessness, as indicated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿lest you should say on the Day of Resurrection, "Indeed, we were heedless of this"﴾, and it is known that this does not remove their heedlessness in the abode of obligation, since no individual of mankind recalls that, then this is rejected. However, [it is rejected] not for the reason given, that God Mighty and Majestic has made the proofs of His oneness and the truthfulness of His messengers in what they reported clear, so whoever denies it is a stubborn violator of the covenant and bears the proof against him, and their forgetting and failure to retain it does not cancel the argument after the report of the truthful reporter. Rather, [it is rejected] because His saying, Exalted is He: "﴿lest you should say﴾ …" is not an object of purpose (mafʿul lahu) governed by His saying: "﴿and He made them testify﴾," and what follows from it, His saying: "﴿Yes, we testify﴾," such that it would be necessary that this testimony be preserved for them in its binding force. Rather, it is an object of purpose governed by a hidden verb to which the speech extends.

The meaning is: We did what We did of the command to mention and explain the covenant out of aversion that you should say, or so that you, O unbelievers, would not say on the Day of Resurrection: "Indeed, we were heedless of that covenant; we were not alerted to it in the abode of obligation, and otherwise we would have acted in accordance with its requirement." This is according to the reading of the majority. As for the reading with the letter ya (yaʾ), then it is an object of purpose governed by the hidden verb itself, which governs "when He took" (idh akhadha). The meaning is: Remind them of the covenant taken from them in the past, so that they will not make excuses on the Day of Resurrection by heedlessness of it, or by imitation of their fathers. This is on the assumption that His saying, Exalted is He, "we testify," is part of the speech of the offspring, which is the apparent reading.

As for the assumption that it is part of His own speech, Exalted is He, then it is what governs "that you should say," and there is no objection at all. The meaning is: We testify to this your statement, so that you do not say on the Day of Resurrection … etc., because We will then refute you and declare you liars.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 174:**

﴿Wa-kadhalika﴾ is a demonstrative pointing to the verbal noun (masdar) of the verb mentioned after it, and the distance implied in it serves to signal the exalted rank of what is pointed to and the remoteness of its station. The kaf is an inserted (muqhamah) particle emphasizing the grandeur that the demonstrative noun (ism al-isharah) conveys. Its placement before the verb serves to restrict (qasr) the meaning, and its grammatical position is in the accusative (nasb) by way of being a verbal noun (al-masdariyyah); that is: that eloquent detailing (al-tafsil al-baligh), which brings about (al-mustatbi'), the sublime benefits.

﴿Nufassilu al-ayat﴾ — the aforementioned signs — and not anything other than that.

﴿Wa-la'allahum yarji'un﴾ — and so that they may return from what they are upon of persistence in falsehood and the imitation of their forefathers. We detail the aforementioned explanation, so the two waws are initial (ibtida'iyyah). It is permissible for the second to be conjunctive (ataf) upon an implied element that follows from the detailing; that is: and thus We detail the signs so that they may take note of what they contain of encouragements and warnings, and so that they may return... etc.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 175:

﴿And recite to them﴾ is coordinated (ʿatf) with the implicit pronoun that governs "idh akhadha" (when He took), and it follows the same pattern in reporting the turning from one state of rectitude to deviation, and from guidance to misguidance; that is, "And recite to the Jews."

﴿The news of him to whom We gave Our signs﴾: that is, his account, which has importance and significance. He was one of the scholars of the Children of Israel. It is said that he was Balʿam ibn Baʿura' or Balʿam ibn Baʿir, from the Canaanites, who was given knowledge of some of the Books of God, the Exalted.

It is also said that he was Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt, who had read the books and knew that God, the Exalted, would send a messenger in that era, and he hoped that he himself would be that messenger. When God, the Exalted, sent the Prophet (ﷺ), he envied him and disbelieved in him. The first view is more fitting to the context of rebuking the Jews for their conduct.

﴿Then he withdrew from them﴾: that is, from those signs, like the skin being stripped from the sheep. He did not bring them to mind at all; or he went out from them completely by disbelieving in them and casting them behind his back. Whichever is the case, the expression "withdrawal" (insilakh), which indicates the separation of the encompassing from the encompassed by nature and the permanent absence of contact between them, is used to signal the complete estrangement from the signs after there had been complete connection between them.

﴿So Satan pursued him﴾: that is, he followed him until he overtook and caught up with him, so that he became his companion. This is the meaning according to the reading "fa-ittaba'ahu" (from the iftiʿal form), and it implies that he was more deviated than Satan himself; or [it means] he made Satan's steps follow him.

﴿So he became one of the misguided﴾: that is, he became one of the group of those who went astray and were firmly rooted in error, after having been one of the guided. It is reported that his people asked him to curse Moses, peace be upon him, and he said: "How can I curse one who is accompanied by angels?" But they kept at him until he did so; and they remained in the wandering (al-tih). This is refuted by the fact that the wandering was for Moses, peace be upon him, a comfort and ease, and it was only the Children of Israel who were punished with it, and that happened through his, peace be upon him, supplication against them, as mentioned in Surat al-Ma'ida.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 176:**

﴿And if We had willed﴾ is a resumptive sentence, brought to explain the basis of what was mentioned concerning his having withdrawn from the signs and fallen into the pits of error. The object of the will (mashi'a) is omitted because it occurs as a condition, and because its object is the consequent of the condition, according to the established rule. That is: and if We had willed to raise him.

﴿We would have raised him﴾; that is, to the lofty stations of the righteous, who know those signs and act in accordance with them. But not by a mere act of Our will, without his having any part in it at all, for that would contradict the legislative wisdom founded on linking the recompenses to the voluntary actions of the servants. Rather, it would be with his actually undertaking the deed that leads to the elevation, by directing his choice toward attaining it, as indicated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿by them﴾; that is, by means of those signs, by acting upon what they require. For his choice, although it has no effect in bringing about the attainment nor in the elevation's following from it, both of them being by the creation of God Exalted, nevertheless His creation of them is inseparably bound to that choice, according to the course of the divine custom.

This has been alluded to in the exception, by attributing to him what would lead to the opposite of the consequent, where it is said: ﴿but he clung to the earth﴾. Yet clinging to the earth, too, is something that is not realized when he directs his choice toward it except by God's creation of it, Exalted is He. It is as if it were said: And if We had willed his elevation by his undertaking its cause, We would have raised him by means of those signs, which are the strongest causes of elevation; but We did not will it, because he undertook the cause of its opposite. So in each of the two situations what was mentioned in the other was omitted, relying on the indication of the mentioned by the omitted, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if God touches you with harm, there is none to remove it but He; and if He intends you good, there is none to repel His bounty﴾ (p-293).

The specification of each of the two mentioned matters to its own situation serves to indicate that elevation is willed by Him, Exalted is He, in its essence, and is pure grace upon him, with no part of it in his act in reality. How could it not be so, when all His acts and their origins are among His blessings and graces, Exalted is He?
