And its opposite befell him only through his own evil choice, in accordance with the requirement of the threat, not through the essential will of Him, Glorified is He. This is the reason mentioned concerning the mention of will with good and touching with harm in the aforementioned verse. It is also the secret behind the Qur'anic practice of attributing good to Him, Exalted is He, and ascribing evil to others, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when I am sick, it is He who heals me﴾ and its like.

To cling to a thing (al-ikhlad ila al-shay') is to incline toward it together with being at rest in it. By "the earth" is meant this world; it has also been said to mean baseness and lowliness. The meaning is: he preferred the base world over the lofty stations, or lowliness and baseness over elevation and majesty.

﴿And followed his desire﴾, turning away from those sublime signs, so he sank to the most extreme degradation and was reduced to the lowest of the low.

To this was alluded by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So his likeness is that of the dog﴾, because it is the basest and lowest of animals.

His condition has been illustrated by its basest and most abject state, where it is said: ﴿If you attack him, he pants, or if you leave him, he pants﴾; that is, his condition, which is a proverb for evil, is like his description in its most wretched state, namely the state of constant panting in both conditions of fatigue and rest. It is as if it were said: he descended into a degradation and vileness beyond which there is no end. The choice of the nominal sentence over the verbal one, by saying: "So his likeness has become that of the dog ..." etc., serves to indicate the continuity of his being characterized by that abject state and the full stability and persistence upon it. The address in the conditional verb is to everyone who has a share of address, for it is more effective in spreading the atrocity of his state.

Lahath (panting): the protrusion of the tongue with intense breathing. That is, he is in a constricted and distressed state, constantly panting, whether you stir him up and disturb him with violent driving away, or leave him in his state. For in dogs it is a nature that they cannot easily expel the heated air and draw in cool air, because of the weakness of their hearts and the severance of their hearts; unlike the rest of the animals, which do not need intense breathing and are not afflicted with distress and constriction except when fatigued and exhausted.

The conditional clause together with its sister is an explanation of what was left vague in the simile, a detailing of what was summarized in it, and a clarification of the comparison by stating the aspect of resemblance. It has no place in grammatical analysis (i'rab), following the pattern of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He created him from dust, then said to him, "Be," and he was﴾ after His saying: ﴿Indeed, the likeness of Jesus with God is like the likeness of Adam﴾.

It has also been said that they are in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal) with respect to the dog, on the basis that the two have come out of the true meaning of the conditional and have shifted to the meaning of equivalence, according to the shift of the two contradictory interrogatives into it, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾. It is as if it were said: panting in both states. Whatever the case, the more apparent view is that it is a comparison of the form drawn from what befell him after his withdrawal of bad condition, the inflaming of the heart, the continuance of anxiety and agitation, and not finding rest in any state, with the form drawn from what was mentioned of the condition of the dog.

It has also been said: when Bal'am invoked (evil) upon Musa, peace be upon him, his tongue came out and hung down upon his chest, and he began to pant like a dog until he perished.

﴿That﴾ is a reference to the abject state mentioned, attributed to the dog, or to the one who withdrew; and the demonstrative carries the sense of distance, to indicate the remoteness of its rank in baseness and vileness. That is: that is the evil likeness.

﴿The likeness of the people who denied Our signs﴾, and they are the Jews, since they were given in the Torah what they were given of the descriptions of the Prophet ﷺ and the mention of the inimitable Qur'an and what it contains. They confirmed him and gave the people good news of the imminence of his mission, and they used to seek victory through him. But when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it and withdrew from the ruling of the Torah.

﴿So relate the narratives﴾. Qasas (narratives) is a verbal noun which has been used to name the object, like salb (what is taken). The alif-lam is for prior reference, and the fa' is for the ordering of what follows upon what precedes; that is: when it is established that the mentioned likeness is the likeness of these deniers, then relate it to them as it was revealed to you.

﴿Perhaps they will reflect﴾, so that they may come to know the clear state of affairs, be restrained from what they are upon of disbelief and error, and know that you have learned it through revelation, and so increase in certainty concerning you. The clause is in the accusative position, being either a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun of the addressee, or an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu); that is: so relate the narratives, hoping for their reflection; that is, or hoping for their reflection.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 177:

﴿ساءَ مَثَلا﴾ is a resumptive (istinaf) clause, brought in to explain the complete ugliness of the state of those who deny, after explaining that their state is like that of the dog, or of the one who has stripped himself (of the signs). Sa'a here carries the meaning of bi'sa (an evil or wretched thing, "how evil"), its doer (fa'il) is a pronoun concealed within it, and mathalan is a specifying accusative (tamyiz) that clarifies it.

The thing being censured (al-makhsus bi'l-dhamm) is the words of the Exalted: ﴿the people who denied Our signs﴾. Since there must be agreement (tasadduq) between this and the doer and the tamyiz, it becomes necessary to posit an elided genitive construction (mudaf), either attached to the first (the doer), which is the apparent reading, i.e., "evil is the example of the people ... etc.", or attached to the tamyiz, i.e., "evil are the companions of the example of the people ... etc."

It has also been read as: ﴿sa'a mathalu al-qawm﴾. The repetition of "the people" described by the relative clause, despite the sufficiency of a pronoun (by saying "sa'a mathalan mathaluhum"), is to signal that the basis of the evil is what lies within the scope of the relative clause, and to link to it the words of the Exalted: ﴿and they were wronging themselves﴾. For this (clause) is either conjoined to "they denied" and included with it in the ruling of the relative clause, meaning: they combined the denial of God's signs after the proof had been established against them and their knowledge of them, with their wronging of themselves specifically; or it is disjoined from it, meaning: they did not wrong by denial except themselves, for its harm does not pass beyond them. Whichever it is, in "yazlimun" there is an allusion to the fact that their denial of the signs includes wrongdoing, and that this too is considered in the restriction (qasr) derived from the fronting of the object (taqdim al-maf'ul).

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 178:**

﴿Whomever Allah guides, he is the one who is guided.﴾ When the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to relate the story of the one who cast off the signs (al-munsalikh) to these misguided people, whose likeness is the likeness of that man, so that they would reflect upon it and abandon what they were clinging to of inclination toward error and be guided to the truth, this was followed by affirming that guidance and misguidance come from Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Admonition (al-'izha) and reminder (al-tadhkir) are only among the ordinary means (al-wasa'it al-'adiyya) for attaining guidance (al-ihtida'), without having any effect of their own in it, other than being incitements (dawa'i) that turn the servant's choice (ikhtiyar) toward attaining it, in accordance with what Allah the Exalted has attached to His creation of it, like all other human actions.

The intended meaning of this guidance (al-hidaya) is that which necessarily brings about being guided, but not because its reality is a guidance that definitely reaches the goal. Rather, it is because it is the complete instance (al-fard al-kamil) of the reality of guidance, which is indication (al-dalala) toward what leads to the goal; that is, that which by its nature leads to it, as was previously established in the explanation of His words, Exalted is He: ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾.

The intention is not merely to inform that whoever Allah guides is guided, such that one might suppose it yields no benefit on its face, since it is evident that His guiding someone entails that person's being guided. Rather, the noble phrasing is to be understood as magnifying the status of being guided and drawing attention to the fact that it is, in itself, a great perfection and a mighty benefit, which would suffice even if nothing else were obtained. Indeed, it is a restriction (qasr) of being guided to those whom Allah the Exalted guides, as the definiteness of the predicate (ta'rif al-khabar) requires. So the meaning is: whomever Allah guides, that is, creates guidance in him in the manner mentioned, he alone is the one who is guided, no one else, whoever he may be.

﴿And whomever He leaves astray﴾, by not creating guidance in him, but rather creating misguidance in him to turn his choice toward it.

﴿Those are﴾ the ones described with misguidance in the manner mentioned.

﴿They are the losers﴾; that is, the complete losers, and no others. The singular "the one who is guided" is in view of the wording "whoever" (man), while the plural "the losers" is in view of its meaning, to indicate the unity of the path of guidance and the dispersal (tafarruq) of the paths of misguidance. (p-295)

﴿And We have indeed created﴾: this is a new sentence, confirming the meaning of what precedes it by way of *tadhyil* (a rhetorical device in which a sentence is appended to confirm the preceding meaning). That is, "We created."

﴿for Hell﴾: that is, for entering it and being punished therein.

Its being placed before His saying, ﴿many﴾, that is, a great many creatures, though it is the object, is because its complements contain a kind of length. Placing it between them, or delaying it beyond them, would disturb the eloquence of the noble composition.

His saying, ﴿of the jinn and mankind﴾, is connected to an implied element that serves as a qualifier of "many": that is, "existing from both of them." The jinn are mentioned first because they are more deeply rooted than humankind in the attributes under discussion, more numerous, and created earlier. Those meant are those upon whom the eternal decree of wretchedness has been fulfilled. However, this is not by way of *jabr* (compulsion, the doctrine that human acts are entirely determined without any real choice), as if there were nothing on their part that leads to this. Rather, it is because God, exalted is He, knows that they will never turn their choice toward the truth, but will persist in falsehood with nothing to divert them and no inclination to turn them back from the signs and warnings.

On this basis, their creation was made to end in Hell, just as all of both groups, in view of their complete innate readiness for worship and their full capacity for it, had their creation made to end in worship, as expressed by His saying: ﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me﴾.

His saying, ﴿they have hearts﴾, is in the accusative position as another qualifier of "many."

His saying, ﴿with which they do not understand﴾, is in the nominative position as a qualifier of "hearts." It emphasizes what its indefiniteness and vagueness imply: that they are not familiar, differing from the rest of the members of the species and entirely lacking its perfection. Yet this is not, in reality, by their innate nature, but because of their refusal to direct them toward attaining it. This is a description of them in terms of complete extremity in hardness, for since understanding never came from them in any way, it is as if they were created unable to receive it at all. The same applies to their eyes and ears.

The omission of the object is for generality. That is, they have hearts that are not fit for understanding anything that is fit to be understood, so this includes what is appropriate to the situation of truth and its proofs, by primary inclusion. Restricting it to that would undermine the clarity of what this condition of theirs is.

﴿And they have eyes with which they do not see﴾: the discussion of this is the same as that of what it is conjoined to. The seeing and hearing that are negated refer to the kind of perception specific to rational beings, as is the function of the two weighty ones (humans and jinn), not to mere sensation of a shape or sound, as is the function of cattle. That is, they do not see with them any of the visible things, so it includes the cosmic signs that indicate the truth, by primary inclusion.

﴿And they have ears with which they do not hear﴾: that is, any of the things that are heard, so this covers the revealed signs by primary inclusion. The repetition of the predicate in the two conjoined clauses, though the sentence could have been arranged as "and eyes with which they do not see and ears with which they do not hear," is to affirm the wretchedness of their condition. It also affirms the three faculties as belonging to them.

Then describing these faculties as lacking awareness, rather than negating them from them outright, as one would say, "they have no hearts with which they understand, nor eyes with which they see, nor ears with which they hear," contains, in testimony to their complete entrenchment in ignorance and error, what is not hidden.

﴿Those﴾ is a reference to those mentioned, in view of their being described by the attributes mentioned. The sense of distance in it indicates the distance of their rank in misguidance. That is, "those described by the aforementioned attributes."

﴿like cattle﴾: that is, in lacking awareness in the manner mentioned, or in that their faculties are directed toward the means of livelihood and confined to them.

﴿Nay, they are further astray﴾: for cattle perceive what it is their nature to perceive of benefits and harms, and they strive with all their effort to obtain the one and avoid the other, although they are far from eternity. These people are not like that, since they do not distinguish between benefits and harms, but reverse the matter, leaving behind lasting bliss and rushing toward eternal punishment.

It has been said: cattle recognize their master, remember him, and obey him, whereas these people do not know their Lord, do not remember Him, and do not obey Him. In a report: "Every created thing is more obedient to God than the son of Adam."

﴿Those﴾: those described by what has passed of the likeness to cattle and worse than them.

﴿they are the heedless﴾: those who are complete in heedlessness, deserving that this name be reserved for them and not applied to anyone else. How could it not be so, when they know nothing of the affairs of God, mighty and majestic, nor of the affairs of anything besides Him, so that they associate others with Him, exalted is He, "there is nothing like unto Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing"? They associate with Him their idols, which are among the basest of His creatures, exalted is He.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 180:

﴿And to Allah belong the most beautiful names﴾. This is an admonition to the believers regarding the manner of invoking Him, may He be exalted, and the manner of dealing with those who neglect this and who, heedless of Him, glorified be He, attribute to Him what befits Him and what does not befit Him, following the explanation of their complete heedlessness and their overwhelming misguidance.

Al-husna (the most beautiful) is the feminine form of al-ahsan (the most excellent); that is, the names which are the most excellent of names and the most glorious, because they indicate the most excellent and noblest meanings.

﴿So call upon Him by them﴾; that is, name Him by those names.

﴿And leave those who deviate concerning His names﴾. Al-ilhad (deviation) and al-lahd both mean inclination and deviation. It is said: lahada and alhada, when one inclines away from the right course. It has been recited as (yalhidun) from the triliteral root; that is, they incline concerning them away from the truth towards falsehood, either by naming Him, may He be exalted, with what has no divine warrant, or with what suggests a corrupt meaning, as in the saying of the Bedouin: "O father of generosity, O white-faced one, O bakhil (miser)," and similar expressions.

Thus, the abandonment commanded here means avoiding that, and "His names" means what they have applied to Him, may He be exalted, and named Him by, according to their own supposition, and not His names in reality. On this reading is understood the omission of the pronoun, so that it would be said: "they deviate concerning them." Or it means that they turn away from naming Him, may He be exalted, by some of His noble names, as when they said: "And what is al-Rahman? We know only the Rahman of Yamama."

Thus the abandonment here also means avoidance, and "names" means His names in reality. The meaning is: name Him, may He be exalted, by all His most beautiful names, and avoid excluding any of them from the whole. Or it means that they apply them to other than Him, may He be exalted, as they named their idols "gods," or that they derive from some of them names for their idols, as they derived "al-Lat" from Allah, may He be exalted, and "al-'Uzza" from al-'Aziz.

Thus "names" means His names in reality, as in the second reading, and the explicit noun in place of the pronoun, together with stripping them of any attribute in all cases, is to indicate that their deviation lies in the very names themselves, without regard to any attribute. The abandonment here does not mean avoidance of that, since it is not conceivable that such deviation would proceed from the believers so that they would be commanded to abandon it. Rather it means turning away from them and not caring for what they do, awaiting the descent of punishment upon them soon, as is evident from His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They will be recompensed for what they used to do﴾. For this is a resumptive clause that comes as an answer to a question arising from the command to disregard them and to turn away from retribution, as if it were said: "Why should we not care about their deviation, nor take it upon ourselves to requite them?" It is said: "Because His punishment will descend upon them, and you will be satisfied with that soon." As for the first two readings, the meaning is: avoid their deviation, lest there befall you what befell them, for the punishment of their deviation will surely descend upon them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 181:

﴿And among those We have created is a community who guide by the truth and by it act justly.﴾ This is a general statement about the condition of those other than the two groups mentioned (humankind and jinn), who were described with the misguidance and deviation from the truth mentioned above. The position of the adverbial phrase (al-zarf) is nominative, as it is a subject (mubtada'), either in terms of its meaning or by implying a described noun (al-mawsuf), and what follows it is its predicate (khabar), as was discussed in the explanation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And among mankind ...﴾ etc. That is: and some of those whom We have created, or some of them are a community; that is, a large group who guide people while adhering to the truth, or who guide them with the word of truth and direct them to uprightness, and who judge by truth in the rulings that operate among them and do not deviate in them.

From the Prophet ﷺ, that when he recited it he would say: "This is for you, and a people before you were given the like of it," and ﴿And among the people of Moses is a community ...﴾ to the end of the verse. And from him, peace and blessings be upon him: "Indeed among my community there is a people upon the truth until 'Isa (Jesus) descends." And it is narrated: "A group from my community will not cease to be upon the truth until the command of Allah comes." And it is narrated: "A community from my community will not cease to be standing by the command of Allah; those who forsake them or oppose them will not harm them, until the command of Allah, exalted is He, comes while they are dominant."

In this is a clear indication of the validity of consensus (ijma') to an extent that is evident. Restricting their description to guiding people indicates that their own guidance is a certain matter, well established and needing no explicit mention.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 182:

﴿And those who denied Our signs﴾: This begins the establishment of the truth by which the guiding ones guide, by which the just ones act justly, and by which people are urged to be guided by it in the manner of warning. The place of the relative pronoun (al-ladhina) is in the nominative case, as it is the subject (mubtada') whose predicate (khabar) is what follows it, the conditional sentence (al-jumla al-istiqbaliyya). The attribution of the signs (al-ayat) to the plural of majesty (nun al-'azama) is to honour them and to magnify the enormity of daring to deny them. That is: and those who denied Our signs, which are the criterion of truth and the confirmation of sincerity and justice.

﴿We will gradually lead them﴾; that is, We will draw them step by step, without fail, towards destruction. Al-istidraj (gradual leading) is an verbal noun of the form istif'al from daraja. It may mean: he ascended, and then it was extended so that it is used for every gradual transfer, whether by way of ascent, descent, or moving straight on. Or it may mean: he walked a weak walk. Or it may mean: he folded (tawa).

The first meaning is the most fitting to the intended sense, which is transfer to the highest levels of ruin, so that they reach the furthest degrees of punishment and torment. Then it was borrowed for seeking every gradual transfer from one state to another of the states that suit the one transferred and agree with his desire, such that he supposes that this is an advancement in the ladders of his benefits, while in reality it is a descent into the abysses of his downfall. So God's istidraj of them (the Exalted) is that He continually showers blessings upon them while they are immersed in error, so that they consider them to be kindness from Him, the Exalted, and thus they increase in insolence and transgression. But it is not that what is intended is their gradual advance through degrees of blessings; rather, it is their gradual advance through the paths of sins until the word of punishment is due against them in the most dreadful and vile state. The first is a means to it.

As for His words, exalted is He: ﴿from where they do not know﴾, it is connected to an implied element that stands as a qualifier of the verbal noun of the mentioned verb; that is: We will lead them in a leading that comes from where they do not know that it is so, but rather they suppose it to be a favour from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and a drawing near to Him. It has been said: they do not know what is intended for them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 183:

﴿And I will give them respite﴾ is conjoined to "We will gradually lead them (sanastadrijuhum)" but is not included in the ruling of the sin (al-sin, the letter sin of the future tense). This is because al-imla' (granting respite), which is an expression for giving time and prolonging, is not among the gradual matters, unlike al-istidraj (gradual leading on), which occurs little by little in itself. Rather, it is an act that occurs all at once. What occurs gradually are its effects and rulings, not itself, as the change of expression to the singular pronoun indicates, together with the eloquence it contains which points to greater attention to the content of the speech, because it is based on renewing the intention and resolve. (p-298)

As for the claim that this is to indicate that it is purely by the divine decree, and that the gradual leading on is through the intermediary of the governing angels, its basis is the indication of the plural of majesty (nun al-'azamah) on partnership, and how could that be? Otherwise it would have been avoided in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And let not those who disbelieve suppose that Our giving them respite is good for them. We only give them respite that they may increase in sin...﴾ (the verse). Rather, its occurrence in such contexts is by way of following the customary manner of majesty.

﴿Indeed, My plan is firm﴾ is a confirmation and emphasis of the threat; that is, strong, which cannot be repelled by strength or by stratagem. What is meant by it is either the gradual leading on and respite together with their outcome, which is the severe seizing unawares, so calling it a plan (kayd) is because its outward appearance is kindness while its inward reality is subjugation; or it is that seizing alone, and the naming is due to its preliminaries being so.

As for the claim that the true meaning of kayd is seizing in concealment without considering in it the display of the opposite of what is concealed, this is something on which no reliance can be placed, given its lack of suitability to the context, since it necessarily requires the aforementioned condition to be considered.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 184:

﴿Have they not reflected? There is no madness in their companion.﴾ This is an independent statement brought forth to deny that they have reflected on his condition (ﷺ), and to express their ignorance of the reality of his state, which would necessitate belief in him and in the signs that were sent down upon him, which they denied. The hamza (interrogative particle) here expresses denial, astonishment and reproach, and the waw (conjunction) is for coordination with an implied element that the sequence and context of the noble composition call for.

"Ma" (mā) is either interrogative, expressing denial, in the nominative position as the subject of the nominal sentence, with the predicate being "bi-ṣāḥibihim" (with their companion); or it is negative, its subject being "jinna" (madness) and its predicate "bi-ṣāḥibihim." The word "jinna" is among the verbal nouns that are intended to express a state (hay'a), like "rukba" (a way of riding) and "jilsa" (a way of sitting), and its indefiniteness is for minimization and belittlement.

The clause is dependent on the verb of reflection, since that verb is one of the verbs of the heart, and its position, according to both possibilities, is in the accusative by removal of the preposition; that is: Did they deny them (the signs) and not reflect on any madness whatsoever that was in their companion, who is the greatest of the guiding nation with the truth, and upon whom the signs were sent down? Or (they did not reflect) on whether there was any madness at all in their companion, such that reflection would lead them to ascertain his truthfulness and the soundness of his prophethood, so that they would believe in him and in what was sent down upon him of signs.

It was also said: The speech is complete at His saying, exalted is He, "Have they not reflected?", meaning: Did they deny them and not perform reflection? Then a new sentence begins: "What madness is there in their companion?", in the manner of denial, astonishment and rebuke. Or it was said: "There is no madness in their companion," and the expression of him (ﷺ) as "their companion" is to indicate that the long companionship they had with him (ﷺ) is something that informs them of his purity (ﷺ) from any trace of what has been mentioned. Thus there is in it emphasis of the denial and intensification of it. The mention of the negation of madness from him (ﷺ), despite the obvious impossibility of its occurrence in him (ﷺ), is because speaking what is extraordinary and contrary to the normal course of intellect and custom issues only from one who has a touch of madness, in whatever manner it happens, without there being any basis or meaning in it; or from one who has divine support, who informs about unseen matters. Since there is in him (ﷺ) no trace of the first, it is established that he (ﷺ) is supported from Allah, exalted is He.

It was also said: He (ﷺ) ascended al-Safa at night and began calling the clans of Quraysh clan by clan, warning them of the punishment of Allah, exalted is He. One of them said: "Indeed this companion of yours is surely mad; he spent the night shouting until morning." Then this was revealed. The explicit negation of madness at that time is a response to their hideous calumny, and the expression of him (ﷺ) as "their companion" comes in the form of their own speech, together with the subtlety mentioned.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He is only a clear warner.﴾ is a sentence affirming the content of what precedes it, and clarifying the reality of his (ﷺ) state, following the pattern of His saying, exalted is He, "This is no human," followed by "This is only a noble angel"; that is: he is only one who exaggerates in warning, making it manifest to the utmost degree, displaying complete compassion and exaggeration in giving excuse (warning so that no one has an excuse).

Then His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have they not considered the dominion of the heavens and the earth?﴾ This is another resumptive statement, brought for rebuke and censure, for their neglect of reflection upon the signs of creation set out in the horizons and in themselves, which bear witness to the truth of the revealed signs, following what was said of them regarding their neglect of reflection upon his ﷺ affair. The hamzah (interrogative particle) here carries the sense of denial, astonishment and reproach, and the waw is for conjunction with the implied clause mentioned, or with the negated clause introduced by lam.

Al-malakut means the great dominion. That is: they denied these signs, or they did not reflect upon what has been mentioned, and did not look with a contemplative gaze at what the heavens and the earth indicate of the greatness of dominion and the perfection of power.

﴿And what Allah has created﴾: that is, and what He has created within them, with this being a conjunction with malakut; and its restriction to the two of them is for the full manifestation of the greatness of dominion within them. Or, [it means] "and in the dominion of what He has created," with this being a conjunction with the heavens and the earth, and the generalization is because all share in indicating the greatness of dominion in reality. To this corresponds His exalted saying: ﴿So exalted is He in whose hand is the dominion of everything﴾.

His exalted saying ﴿of any thing﴾ is an explanation of what He created, conveying that the indication mentioned is not restricted to the great created things to the exclusion of their subtle details. The meaning: Have they not looked at the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and at what He created in them, of the great and the minute, of what falls under the name of "thing," so that this would guide them to knowledge of His oneness, exalted is He, and of the rest of His affairs which those signs speak of, so that they would believe in them, since the two are united in what they signify? For each single one of the existences, whether great or small, is a manifest proof of the Maker, the Glorious, and a clear path to the world of monotheism.

His exalted saying ﴿and that perhaps their term has drawn near﴾ is a conjunction with malakut. "An" is the light form of "inna," its noun is the pronoun of the matter, and its predicate is "asa" together with its subject, which is "an yakuna," and the noun of "yakuna" is also the pronoun of the matter, with the predicate being "qad iqtaraba ajaluhum." The meaning: Have they not looked into the matter that perhaps the matter has drawn near, their term?

It has also been permitted that the noun of "yakuna" is "ajaluhum," and its predicate "qad iqtaraba," as a sentence of verb and subject, whose subject is the pronoun of "ajaluhum," due to its being preposed in meaning. Whichever it is, the crux of the denial and rebuke is their delay in looking and reflecting; that is, perhaps they will die soon, so what is wrong with them that they do not hasten to contemplate the created signs which witness to what they denied of the Qur'anic signs? It has also been permitted that the term (ajal) refers to the Hour, and the attribution to the pronoun "hum" is because they are concerned with it through their denial of it and their searching after it.

His exalted saying ﴿then in what discourse after this will they believe?﴾ cuts off the possibility of their believing altogether and negates it entirely, following from what was mentioned of their denial of the signs and their neglect of reflection and contemplation. The ba' is connected to "yu'minun," and the pronoun in "ba'dahu" refers to the signs, by omitting the implied annexed noun understood from "kadhdhabu," and the masculine form is by consideration of their being the Qur'an, or by interpreting them as the mentioned matter.

The placing of the pronoun in the position of the demonstrative: the meaning is, they denied it and did not reflect upon what necessitates its confirmation, from his ﷺ circumstances and the circumstances of created things; so in what discourse will they believe after its denial, and with such strong evidences present? Certainly not, and far from it.

It was said: the pronoun refers to the Qur'an, and the meaning is: then in what discourse after the Qur'an will they believe, if they do not believe in it? This is the utmost in clarity.

It was said: this is a denial and rebuke directed at them, following from their failure to hasten to contemplation of what has been mentioned, as if it were said: perhaps their term has drawn near, so what is wrong with them that they do not hasten to believe in the Qur'an before it is too late, and what do they await after the truth has become clear, and in what discourse more worthy than it do they wish to believe?

It was said: the pronoun refers to their term, and the meaning is: then in what discourse after the ending of their term will they believe? It was said: it refers to the Messenger ﷺ, by omitting a noun: that is, then in what discourse after his discourse will they believe, and he is the most truthful of people.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 186:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Whomever Allah leaves astray, there is none to guide him﴾ is a resumptive (isti'naf) clause that confirms what precedes it, indicating the sealing (al-tab') upon their hearts.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And He leaves them in their transgression﴾ is read with the yā' and with the raf' (nominative), on the basis of istiʾnaf (resumption), meaning: "and He leaves them." It has also been read with the nūn of majesty (nūn al-ʿaẓamah), following the mode of iltifat (shift of grammatical person), meaning: "and We leave them." And it has been read with the yā' and the jazm (jussive), as a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the place (maḥall) of "there is none to guide him," as if it were said: "Whomever Allah leaves astray, no one will guide him, and He will leave them." It is also related that the jazm with the nūn was transmitted from Nafiʿ and Abu ʿAmr as an irregular reading (shadhdh).

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Wandering blindly (yaʿmahun)﴾; that is, they waver and are bewildered. It is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the object of yadhirhum. The singular pronoun in the context of negation is used in view of the wording of "man," while its plural in the context of affirmation is used in view of its meaning, to explicitly indicate that the negation and affirmation apply to all of them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 187:

﴿They ask you about the Hour: when will be its arrival?⌉ This is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf), brought to clarify some of the rulings concerning their misguidance and transgression; that is, [they ask] about the Resurrection (al-qiyamah). It is among the names that have become dominant for it. Its being called "the Hour" is either because it comes suddenly, or because of the swiftness of the reckoning in it, or because it is an "hour" with Allah, the Exalted, despite its length in itself.

It is said that a group of Jews said: "O Muhammad, tell us when the Hour will be, if you are a prophet, for we know when it is." This was a test on their part, while knowing that He, the Exalted, has reserved its knowledge [to Himself]. It is also said that the ones asking were the Quraysh.

As for His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Ayyana mursaha﴾ ("when is its arrival?"), it is with a fatha on the hamza, and it has been read with a kasra. It is an adverb of time containing the meaning of interrogation. It is followed by the subject (mubtada') or the present-tense verb, not the past tense, unlike "mata" (when), which is followed by either of them. It is said that its derivation is from ayy, with the form fa'lan from it, because its meaning is "which time," and that it is from awaytu ila al-shay' (I took refuge in a thing), because the part takes refuge in the whole and leans upon it.

Its place in the i'rab is the nominative, as a predicate preceding (khabar muqaddam), and mursaha is a postponed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar); that is: when is its arrival (irsa'uha), that is, its establishment and fixing. For it is a mimi verbal noun from arsaahu, when he established it and fixed it, and it is hardly used except for a heavy thing, as in His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And the mountains, He set them firmly﴾, and from it: mirsat al-sufun (the anchor of ships).

As for the place of the clause, it is said that it is in the genitive by way of apposition to "the Hour." The verified view is that its place is the accusative by removal of the preposition, because it is an apposition to the prepositional phrase and not only to the genitive noun, as if it were said: ﴿They ask you about the Hour, when will be its arrival﴾. In linking the question first to the Hour itself, and second to the time of its occurrence, there is an indication that the primary aim of the question is the Hour itself, considering its arrival at its appointed time, not its time considered as a place for it. This approach is also followed in the answer that was taught, where knowledge of the object of the question is attributed to its pronoun, so that it is informed that it is exclusive to Him, Mighty and Majestic.

And since it is said: ﴿Say: its knowledge is only﴾; that is, its knowledge in the aforementioned respect,

﴿with my Lord﴾, and He did not say: "the knowledge of the time of its arrival is only." Whoever does not heed this subtle point takes the noble wording to imply an omitted genitive (hadhf al-mudaf). The mention of the title "Lord" together with the attribution to his pronoun, peace be upon him, is to signal that Allah's granting him success in answering in the stated manner is part of training and guidance. The meaning of its being with Him, the Exalted, specifically, is that He, the Exalted, has reserved it in such a way that He has not informed anyone of it, neither a nearest angel nor a sent prophet.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿None but He will reveal it at its time﴾ explains the continuation of that state until its establishment, and a complete despair of disclosing its matter by way of information from Him, the Exalted, or from others, since wisdom in legislation requires that, for it is more conducive to obedience and more restraining from disobedience, just as concealing a person's specific term is likewise.

The meaning is: none will uncover it or make manifest to people its matter about which you ask Me, except Him alone, without any of the created beings perceiving it, so that they might mediate in making it manifest to them. But this does not mean that He will not inform them of its time before its coming, as is what is asked; rather, He will establish it, so they will witness it directly, as the "revealing" (tajliyah) indicates, which suggests complete uncovering that entirely removes ambiguity.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿at its time﴾, that is, at its time, is a restriction on the revealing after the exception has come upon it, not before it. As if it were said: "None but He will reveal it at its time." However, it was placed before the exception to alert from the outset that its revealing is not by way of informing about its time, but by manifesting its very reality at the time about which they ask.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿It has become heavy in the heavens and the earth﴾ is a resumptive sentence, as the one before it, confirming the content of what precedes it; that is, it has become great and burdensome upon their inhabitants, of the angels and the two weighty creatures (humans and jinn), each of whom is concerned by its hiddenness and its departure from the sphere of intellects.

It is said: it has become grave for them, since they fear it and dread its hardships and terrors. It is also said: it has become heavy in them, since none of them or of what is in them can bear it at all.

The first is more appropriate to what precedes it and to what follows it, His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿It will not come upon you except suddenly﴾, for it is a resumptive sentence confirming the content of what precedes it. Therefore the heaviness must be understood in terms of its hiddenness; that is: it will not come upon you except unexpectedly, while you are heedless, as the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "The Hour will come upon people while a man is repairing his pool, and a man is watering his livestock, and a man is displaying his merchandise in his market, and a man is lowering his scale and raising it."

﴿They ask you as if you were well-informed about it⌉ This is a resumptive sentence brought to clarify their error in directing the question to the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, on the basis of their assumption that he, peace be upon him, knows what is asked about, or that knowledge of that is among the obligations of prophethood, following the clarification of their error regarding the very question by indicating the status of what is asked about.

The comparative clause is in the accusative place as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the "kaf" (you). It was brought to explain what prompts them to ask, according to their assumption, and to indicate their error in that; that is: they ask you while your situation in their view is compared to the situation of one who is well-informed about it (hafiyyun 'anha); that is, one who is intensely knowledgeable about it. Hafiyy is a form (fa'il) from hafiya, and its real meaning is: as if you were intensely asking about it, for that is equivalent to intensity in knowing it, since whoever presses hard in asking about a thing and searching for it, his knowledge of it becomes firmly established.

The structure is built on intensity and thoroughness, and from it comes ihfa' al-shari (trimming the moustache thoroughly) and ihtifa' al-baql (uprooting the herbs), that is, eradicating them; and ihfa' in a matter means insistence upon it.

It is said: "'an" (about) is connected to "yas'alunaka" (they ask you), and His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿as if you were well-informed﴾ is a parenthetical clause (mu'tarid), and the complement of hafiyy is omitted; that is, well-informed about it, and it has been read thus.

It is also said: it is from al-hafawa, meaning kindness and compassion, for the Quraysh said to him, peace be upon him: "There is kinship between us and you, so tell us when the Hour is." The meaning: they ask you as if you were being solicitous toward them, singling them out with teaching its time because of kinship, and concealing its matter from others; thus there is a rebuke to them from two angles. It is also said: it is from hafiya bi al-shay', meaning: he was pleased with it; the meaning: as if you were pleased with the question about it, which you love while you dislike it, since it is an encroachment upon the sanctuary of the unseen which Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has reserved the knowledge of for Himself.

﴿Say: its knowledge is only with Allah⌉ He, peace be upon him, was commanded to repeat the first answer, to affirm the ruling, to establish it, and to indicate its cause by way of demonstration, by mentioning the name of the Essence, which indicates its entailing the attributes of perfection, among which is knowledge, (p-302)

and as a preparation for a veiled rebuke of their ignorance by His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿But most people do not know⌉; that is, they do not know what has been mentioned of the exclusiveness of its knowledge to Him, the Exalted. Some of them deny it outright, so they know nothing of what has been mentioned, with certainty. Some of them know that it will definitely occur, and they claim that you know the time of its occurrence, so they ask you about it out of ignorance. Some of them claim that knowledge of that is among the obligations of prophethood, so they take asking about it as a pretext to discredit your prophethood. The exception from these are the believers who are aware of the true state of affairs. As for those among the Jews who ask about it as a test, they are included among the ignorant, since they did not act upon their knowledge.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 188:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: I have no power over benefit or harm for myself﴾, is the beginning of the answer to the question, by explaining his inability to know it (the Hour), following the explanation of the inability of all others regarding it, and the refutation of their assumption upon which they based their question, that he ﷺ is among those who know it; and the repetition of the matter serves to show the complete concern with the subject of the answer, and to draw attention to its independence and its difference from the first. The mention of his inability regarding what was mentioned of benefit and harm serves to establish his inability to know it by way of demonstrative proof.

The lam (in "li-nafsi") is either connected to ama{l}ik (I have power), or to a omitted word that occurs as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of nafʿan (benefit); meaning: I am not able, for my own sake, to bring about any benefit nor to ward off any harm.

﴿Except what Allah wills﴾: that I should possess any of that by Him inspiring it to me, enabling me to it and empowering me over it; or, rather, whatever Allah wills of that exists. So the exception is disjunctive (munqati'), and this is more eloquent in showing inability.

﴿And had I known the unseen﴾; that is, the kind of the unseen, of which is what is between things of the relations that normally make causation and being caused valid, and of the oppositions that entail prevention and repulsion.

﴿I would have acquired much good﴾; that is, I would have attained much of the good whose attainment is tied to the voluntary actions of humans, by arranging its causes and removing its obstacles.

﴿And harm would not have touched me﴾; that is, the harm from which one can escape by guarding against its causes and repelling it with its preventives, not any harm whatsoever, for among it is that which has no repelling.

﴿I am but a warner and a bringer of good tidings﴾; that is, I am but a servant sent for warning and good tidings; my role is to possess what relates to these two of religious and worldly knowledge, not to stand over the unseen matters that have no connection with the rulings and laws. And I have revealed of the matter of the Hour what relates to warning: its inevitable coming and its nearness. As for specifying its time, it is not what warning requires; rather it is of what undermines it, because of what has passed, that keeping it ambiguous is more conducive to restraint from sins. And the placing of the warner before the bringer of good tidings is because the context is one of warning.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿for a people who believe﴾ is either connected to both of them together, because they benefit from the warning just as they benefit from the good tidings; or to the bringer of good tidings alone, and what relates to the warner is omitted; meaning: a warner to the unbelievers, that is, those who remain upon disbelief, and a bringer of good tidings to a people who believe; that is, at whatever time it may be. In this there is an encouragement for the disbelievers to bring about faith, and a warning against persisting in disbelief and transgression.

(p-303) He it is Who created you from a single soul: this is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) brought to show the full enormity of the disbelievers' offence in their audacity to associate partners (with God), by reminding them of the beginnings of their own condition, which is incompatible with such association. The placing of the relative clause as a predicate serves to magnify the status of the subject. The meaning is: He is that Majestic One Who created you all, alone, without anyone else having any share in that in any way whatsoever.

﴿مِن نَفْسٍ واحِدَةٍ﴾ "from a single soul" refers to Adam, peace be upon him. This is a kind of elaboration of what was alluded to at the beginning of the blessed surah in a general way, namely their creation and formation within the creation and formation of Adam, and it explains how that happened.

﴿وَجَعَلَ﴾ "and He made" is a conjunction with "created you" and falls under the same grammatical role as the relative clause. There is no objection to its being prior to it in existence, because the conjunction "wa" does not require sequential order in existence.

﴿مِنها﴾ "from it" means: of its kind (jins), as in His saying: ﴿He made for you spouses from among yourselves﴾, or from its body, according to what is narrated: that God created Hawwa' from a rib of Adam, peace be upon him. The first is the more fitting, since kinship of kind is what leads to the stated end, not partiality.

The verb "made" (ja'ala) is either in the sense of "rendered" (taṣyīr), so that His saying ﴿zawjahā﴾ ("its spouse") is its first object and the second is the preposed adverbial phrase; or in the sense of "brought into being" (inshā'), with the adverbial phrase depending on ja'ala, placed before the explicit object because of the concern with what is preposed and the arousing of suspense for what is postponed, as has been noted many times; or it depends on an omitted element which is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) of the object. The first is the preferable.

His saying ﴿li-yaskuna ilayhā﴾ ("that he might find rest in her") is a final cause for the making, in terms of its connection to its second object; that is, that he might find companionship with her and be at peace with her with a peace that validates the marriage, as is hinted at by the masculine form of the pronoun.

This is made explicit by His saying ﴿fa-lammā taghashshāhā﴾, i.e., he had intercourse with her.

﴿ḥamalat ḥamlan khafīfan﴾ "she bore a light burden" at the beginning of the matter, for when it is a drop (nuṭfa), or a clot (ʿalaqa), or a lump of flesh (muḍgha), it is lighter for her compared with the stages that come after that. The mention of its lightness serves to point to His blessing upon them in His bringing them into being gradually through the stages of creation, from non-existence to existence, and from weakness to strength.

﴿famarrat bihi﴾ "so she carried on with it", i.e., she continued with it as she had been before, going about, standing and sitting, taking and leaving. This is the reading of Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both. It was also read as (famarat) with a light pronunciation, and (fa-mārat), from al-mawr, which is coming and going, or from al-miryah, meaning she suspected the pregnancy and doubted it.

As for what has been said, that the meaning is: she bore a burden which was light upon her, and she did not suffer from it what some pregnant women suffer from their pregnancies of distress and harm, and she did not find it heavy as they find it heavy, so she carried on with it, i.e., she went on with it until its birth without miscarriage or premature delivery; this is refuted by His saying ﴿fa-lammā athqalat﴾ ("when she became heavy"), for its meaning is: when she became one with heaviness due to the size of the child in her womb. There is no doubt that heaviness in this sense is not the opposite of lightness in the sense mentioned; what is opposed to it is the distress that affects some of them from the beginning of pregnancy to its end, not others at all. It was also read as (uthqilat) in the passive voice, i.e., her pregnancy burdened her.

﴿da'awā Allāha﴾ "they both called upon God", i.e., Adam and Hawwa', peace be upon them both, when a matter befell them which they had not known and did not know its outcome, so they were anxious about it and humbly entreated Him, mighty and majestic.

His saying ﴿rabbahumā﴾ "their Lord", i.e., the Owner of their affair, the one truly deserving that the supplication be addressed to Him exclusively, is an indication that they began their supplication with it, as in their words: ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves...﴾ and so on. The object of the supplication is omitted, relying on the testimony of the oath-clause that follows it; that is, their claim that God would grant them a righteous child, and they promised, in return for it, to give thanks, by way of emphatic oath.

﴿la'in ātaytanā ṣāliḥan﴾ "If You give us a righteous one", i.e., a child of our kind, sound.

﴿la-nakūnanna﴾ "we shall surely be", we and whoever descends from our offspring,

﴿min al-shākirīn﴾ "among the grateful", the steadfast in gratitude for Your blessings, of which this blessing is one. The ordering of this answer upon the stated condition is because they knew that what they had made their supplication dependent upon is a model for all individuals of the kind and a criterion for them in essence; the existence of him entails the existence of them, and his righteousness entails their righteousness. So the supplication concerning him includes and entails the supplication concerning all, as if they had said: "If You give us and our offspring righteous children."

It was also said that the pronoun in ﴿ātaytanā﴾ refers to both of them and to everyone who descends from their offspring. The reading is apparent, but you know that placing all of them primarily within the scope of the supplication is contrary to the context of emphasis on the matter they were concerned with. As for making the pronoun in ﴿la-nakūnanna﴾ refer to all, there is no objection to it, because widening the circle of gratitude does not detract from the stated concern, but rather reinforces it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 190:

Whichever view is taken, the meaning of His words ﴿When He gave them a righteous (child)﴾ is: when He gave them what they asked for, both directly and by extension to the offspring and their descendants through the generations. So His words ﴿they made (others) partners﴾ mean: their offspring made partners ﴿for Him﴾, may He be exalted.

﴿Partners﴾ (shuraka') is an instance of ellipsis (hadhf al-mudaf), in which the genitive noun (al-mudaf ilayhi) is placed in the position of the omitted construct noun. This is because the matter is clear, and because the explanation that follows is relied upon.

The same applies to His words ﴿in what He gave them﴾, meaning: in what their offspring were given of children, when they named them ʿAbd Manaf, ʿAbd al-ʿUzza, and similar names. The specific mention of this form of association in a context of reproach, although associating others in worship is graver in sin and earlier in occurrence, is because the thrust of the noble composition is to explain their failure to be grateful for the gift of a righteous child, and the first of their disbelief regarding him was naming him with what has been mentioned.

It is also read as "shirkan" (شِرْكًا), meaning "a partnership", or "dhawi shirkatin" (ذَوِي شِرْكَةٍ), meaning "possessors of a partnership", that is, "partners". This applies if it is said that the aforementioned ellipsis of the construct noun and the substitution of the genitive noun in its place is only admissible where the verb has some connection to the genitive noun as well, through its extension to it either literally or by ruling, and where attributing it to it includes a distinction required by the context. An example is His words ﴿And when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh...﴾, where the deliverance from them, although its connection is literally only to the ancestors of the Jews, is attributed to their descendants by the ruling of its extension to them, in order to fulfil the requirement of the context of favour. Likewise is His words ﴿Say: why then do you kill the prophets of God...﴾, where the killing, although it was the crime of their forefathers, is attributed to them by the ruling of their approval of it, in order to fulfil the requirement of the context of reproach and rebuke.

There is no doubt that both of them, upon them be peace, are free of any extension of the aforementioned making (of partners) to them in any way. So what is the reason for attributing it to them in appearance? We say: its reason is to indicate that they abandoned what was better, since they proceeded to place their offspring alongside themselves, and committed themselves to thanking them along with thanking themselves. They also swore to this before knowing their circumstances, which shows that the failure of their offspring to give thanks, which He promised them with a firm promise confirmed by oath, is equivalent to their own failure in person in incurring breach and violation of the oath. This carries the implication that their wrongdoing is multiplied, since by their making (of partners) mentioned, they placed the two of them in the predicament of breaking the oath, and made them as though they had done it themselves. Thus they combined wrongdoing against God, exalted is He, with wrongdoing against them, upon them be peace.

﴿Exalted is God above what they associate (with Him).﴾ This is a declaration of His transcendence, containing a sense of wonder. The "fa'" (فاء) is for the sequence of this after what has been detailed of the rulings of His power and the effects of His favour, which deter from association and call to monotheism. The plural form (of the verb) is for what has been indicated regarding the specification of the agent, and for exonerating Adam and Eve from this.

The "ma" (ما) in ﴿ʿammā﴾ is either a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyya), meaning "from their association", or a relative pronoun (mawsula) or a descriptive (mawsufa), meaning "from what they associate with Him, glorified is He". The intended meaning of their association is either the aforementioned naming, or the general association which encompasses it primarily.

It is also read as "tushrikūna" (تُشْرِكُونَ) with the second-person prefix, by way of shift (iltifat). It is said that the address is to the family of Qusayy from Quraysh, and that the intended "single soul" is the soul of Qusayy, since they were created from him, and he had a spouse of his own kind, an Arab Qurashi woman. They asked God, exalted is He, for a righteous child, and He gave them four sons, whom they named ʿAbd Manaf, ʿAbd Shams, ʿAbd Qusayy, and ʿAbd al-Dar.

The pronoun in "yushrikūna" (يُشْرِكُونَ) refers to the two of them and to their descendants who followed them. As for what has been said, that when Eve became pregnant, Iblis came to her in the form of a man and said to her: "What do you know of what is in your womb? Perhaps it is an animal, or a dog, or a pig. And what do you know of where it will come out from?" She was frightened by this and mentioned it to Adam, and this troubled them both. Then he returned to her and said: "I have a standing with God, exalted is He. If you ask Him to make it a creature like you and make its emergence easy for you, you should name it ʿAbd al-Harith." His name among the angels was Harith. So she agreed. When she gave birth to him, she named him ʿAbd al-Harith. This is among what cannot be relied upon. How could it be otherwise, when he (ﷺ) was the one who was taught the names of all things? For his not knowing Iblis, his name, and his following him in such a grave matter would be close to impossible. God, exalted is He, knows best the reality of the matter.

﴿Do they associate with Him⁠﴾ is a resumptive clause (*istiʾnaf*, a new sentence that resumes the discourse), brought to rebuke the polytheists and to condemn their associating partners with God in general and to nullify it completely. This is done by explaining the state of what they associated with Him, glorified is He, and detailing its conditions, which necessitate the falsity of what they believed about Him. That is: ﴿Do they associate with Him, exalted is He?⁠﴾

﴿that which creates nothing⁠﴾: that is, it has no power to create anything of things at all. It is necessary for the one worshipped to be a creator of its worshipper, without fail.

The statement of God, exalted is He: ﴿while they themselves are created⁠﴾ is coordinated (*ʿatf*) with ﴿that creates nothing⁠﴾. The use of the two pronouns in the plural form of rational beings, while they refer back to *mā* (that which), by which the idols are expressed, is only according to their belief concerning them, and their treating them as rational beings, and their naming them gods. The same applies to the state of the other pronouns that follow. Describing them as created after describing them as lacking the power of creation is to make clear the complete incompatibility of their condition with what they believed about them, and to show the utmost of their ignorance. For associating with the Creator of all things that which has no power to create anything is something that no person of sound intellect at all could justify. The omission of mention of their Creator is to indicate that He is definite and needs no mention.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 192:

﴿And they have no power to help them﴾; that is, to their worshippers when a serious matter befalls them and a grave calamity strikes.

﴿help﴾; that is, any help whatsoever, either by bringing about a benefit or by averting a harm.

﴿Nor can they help themselves﴾ when some misfortune of the misfortunes befalls them; that is, they cannot ward it off from themselves. The mention of "help" (nasr) here is for the sake of parallelism (al-mushakala). This is an explanation of their incapacity to bring any benefit, of any kind whatsoever, whether existential or privative, to their worshippers and to themselves, after the explanation of their incapacity to bring the benefit of existence to them and to themselves. Except that they were described there as created (al-makhluqiyya), because they are fit for it, whereas here they are not described as being helped (al-mansuriyya), because they are not fit for it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 193:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if you call them to guidance﴾ is an explanation of their inability with regard to what is lesser than the help denied to them and easier, namely mere indication of the sought-after goal and guidance to the path of attaining it, without the seeker himself attaining it. The address is to the polytheists by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person), which indicates greater attention to the matter of rebuke and reproach; that is: if you call them, O polytheists, to guide you to that by which you attain your aims or are saved from what is disliked.

﴿They will not follow you﴾ to your desired purpose and your objective. It is also read with the lightened pronunciation (tukhfif).

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It is the same for you whether you call them or you are silent﴾ is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) affirming the content of what precedes it and explaining the manner of their not following; that is: your calling them is equally without benefit as your pure silence is, for your condition does not change in either of the two states, just as their condition does not change by the ruling of their being inanimate.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Or are you silent?﴾ is a nominal sentence in the sense of a verbal sentence, conjoined to the verbal sentence; for it is in the force of "or you have been silent," and it was turned away from that form for the sake of emphasis on the lack of benefit in calling, (p-306) by showing its equivalence to constant, continuous silence.

As for what has been said, that the address is to the Muslims, and the meaning is: if you call the polytheists to guidance, that is Islam, they will not follow you... etc., this is not supported by the context of the noble composition and its context at all; moreover, if it were so, it would have said "upon them" instead of "upon you," as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾; for the equality of calling and not calling is only with respect to the polytheists, not with respect to the callers, for they are successful by the grace of the call.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 194:

﴿Indeed, those whom you invoke besides Allah﴾ is a confirmation of what precedes it, namely that they do not follow them; i.e., indeed those whom you worship besides Him, the idols, and whom you call gods.

﴿Are servants like you﴾; i.e., they are similar to you, but not in every respect, rather in that they are owned by Allah, Mighty and Majestic, subjugated to His command, and powerless to benefit or harm. Their being compared to you in this, while their powerlessness in these two matters is more manifest and greater than yours, is only because of your acknowledgment of your own powerlessness and your claim that they have power over you; for it is this that calls you to worship them and to seek their help.

And the words of the Exalted: ﴿So call upon them, and let them respond to you﴾ are a verification of the content of what precedes, by rendering them powerless and rebuking them; i.e., call upon them to bring about some benefit or to remove some harm.

﴿If you are truthful﴾ in your claim that they are able to do what you are unable to do.

The commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 195:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do they have feet with which they walk?﴾ and so on, is a rebuke following upon a rebuke, confirming what is conveyed by the challenging command, namely their inability to respond, by demonstrating that their instruments are wholly lacking. For a response from bodily frames is only conceivable if they have life and motive, perceptive powers; and whatever has none of that is entirely remote from acts. It is as if it were said: Do they have these instruments by which a response is realized, so that their responding to you could be possible?

The denial has been directed at each of these four limbs individually, as a repetition of the rebuke and a doubling of the reproach, indicating that the absence of each one by itself is sufficient to show the impossibility of response.

The attribution of walking to the feet is for signaling that the focus of the denial is the attribute. The denial was directed at the feet rather than at the attribute, so that one would not say: "Do they walk with their feet?", in order to establish that, since nothing of what appears from the feet of other feet appears from them, they are not in reality feet. The same applies to what follows concerning the remaining three organs.

The word "am" in His saying: ﴿Or do they have hands with which they seize?﴾ is disjunctive (munqati'ah), and the interrogative particle within it is for the rebuke and obligation mentioned earlier. "Bal" (rather) is for a turning away (idrab) that indicates a transition from one kind of rebuke, once complete, to another kind of it, for the reasons mentioned. Al-batsh (seizing) means taking with strength.

It has also been read as (yabtushun) with a damma on the ta', and this is a dialect form of it. The meaning: Rather, do they have hands with which they take what they wish to take? The placing of this after what precedes it is because walking is their state in themselves, while seizing is their state in relation to others.

As for placing it before His saying: ﴿Or do they have eyes with which they see? Or do they have ears with which they hear?﴾ (p-307), although all are alike in being among their states in relation to others, this is for the sake of matching the pairing of hands and feet, and because the absence of walking and seizing is more evident, and the rebuke by it is stronger. As for placing the eyes first, it is because they are more well-known than the ears, and more evident in their effect and trace.

Furthermore, it has been read: ﴿Indeed those whom you invoke besides Allah are servants like you﴾ with the negative "in" operating as the Hijazi "ma" operates; meaning: "What those whom you invoke besides Him, the Exalted, are servants like you, but rather lower than you." Then His saying, "Do they have..." and so on, is a confirmation of the negation of likeness by affirming deficiency and lack.

﴿Say: Call upon your associates⦆ after it has been made clear that their associates have no power over anything at all, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was commanded to confront them in argument and to repeat the rebuke and the silencing proof against them; that is: Call upon your associates and seek their help against me.

﴿Then plot against me⦆ all of you together, you and your associates, and exert yourselves in arranging whatever you are able of the beginnings of scheming and deceit.

﴿Then give me no respite⦆; that is: do not delay me for an hour after arranging the preliminaries of the scheme, for I do not care about you at all.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 196:

﴿Indeed, my guardian is Allah, who sent down the Book﴾ This is a justification for the indifference that is understood clearly from the context of the driving (of the sacrificial animals?). His, exalted is He, description as the One who sent down the Book serves to indicate the evidence of guardianship, and to point to another cause for the indifference. It is as if it were said: "I am not concerned about you and your partners, because my guardian is Allah, who sent down the Book that declares that He is my guardian and helper, and that your partners cannot help themselves, let alone help you."

As for His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And He takes care of the righteous﴾, it is a concluding statement that confirms the content of what precedes it; that is: it is His custom to take care of the righteous among His servants, to help them, and not to forsake them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 197:

﴿Those whom you invoke﴾; that is, you worship them.

﴿Besides Him﴾ (exalted is He), or you invoke them for assistance against me, as I have commanded you.

﴿Are not able to help you﴾; that is, in any matter whatsoever, or in the specific matter mentioned.

﴿Nor can they help themselves﴾ when some calamity befalls them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 198:

﴿And if you call them to guidance﴾ — until they guide you to that by which you attain your aims absolutely, or in particular the specific scheme that is known.

﴿They do not hear﴾; that is, your call, let alone assist or aid you. This is more emphatic than negating following.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you see them looking at you, while they do not see﴾, it is an explanation of their inability to see after the explanation of their inability to hear, and by it the reasoning is completed, so there is no repetition at all. The seeing is visual.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿looking at you﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the object, and the nominal clause is a circumstantial clause from the subject of "yanẓurūn"; that is: and you see the idols with your own eyes, resembling those who look at you, and it appears to you that they see you, because they fashioned for them eyes set with shining, glittering jewels, and shaped them in the form of one who turns his pupil toward a thing to look at it, while in fact they are unable to see.

The singular pronoun in "tarāhum" (you see them), though it refers to the polytheists, is for directing the address to each one of them individually, not to all of them as a whole as in the preceding addresses; this is a warning that seeing the idols in the stated form is not possible for all of them together, but only for each one who confronts them.

It has been said: the subject pronoun in "tarāhum" refers to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and the object pronoun remains as it is. It has also been said: it refers to the polytheists, on the basis that the reasoning was already complete at His saying, exalted is He: "﴿They do not hear﴾"; that is: and you see the polytheists looking at you, while in fact they do not see you as you are.

From al-Hasan: the address in His saying, exalted is He: "And if you call them to the believers" is on the basis that the reasoning was complete at His saying, exalted is He: "they are helped"; that is: and if you, O believers, call the polytheists to Islam, they will not pay attention to you. Then the Prophet (ﷺ) was addressed by way of abstraction (tajrīd), saying: you see them looking at you, while in fact they do not see you truly; this is a warning that the signs of prophethood and the proofs of the message present in him (ﷺ) are so manifest that they hardly remain hidden from the one who looks.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 199:

﴿Take what is given freely﴾ after what is considered, from the falsehoods and ugly deeds of the polytheists, is something that cannot be borne. He (ﷺ) was commanded to adopt the comprehensive noble characteristics (makarim al-akhlaq), among which is overlooking them. That is: take what comes to you easily from people's actions and make things easy, and do not burden them with what is hard for them of 'afw (pardon), which is the opposite of effort (jahd). Or it means: take the 'afw (pardon) from the wrongdoers, or the surplus (al-fadl) of their charities, and that was before the obligation of zakat (zakat, obligatory almsgiving).

﴿And enjoin what is customary﴾, meaning the good and approved of deeds, for they are close to people's acceptance without objection.

﴿And turn away from the ignorant﴾ without disputation or retaliation. It is said: when this was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked Jibril (peace be upon him), and he said: "I do not know until I ask," then he returned and said: "O Muhammad, your Lord commands you to join ties with the one who cuts you off, to give to the one who withholds from you, and to pardon the one who wronged you." And from Ja'far al-Sadiq: God Most High's command to His Prophet was with the noble characteristics of conduct (makarim al-akhlaq).

It is related that when this noble verse was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "How, O Lord, [can I do that] when anger is certain?" Then there was revealed His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if an incitement from Satan should stir you,﴾ "al-nazgh" (incitement), "al-nasʿ" (driving), and "al-nakhs" (prodding) all mean "goading." His whispering to people and his urging them to commit sins is likened to the goading of a driver against what he drives. Attributing the act to the incitement (al-nazgh) is of the type of "jadda jidduhu" (its fortune has come to its fortune), meaning: if a whispering from him should bring you from his direction something that goes against what you were commanded to do, such as the onset of anger or the like.

﴿So seek refuge in Allah﴾: so turn to Him, exalted is He, for protection from his evil.

﴿Indeed, He is Hearing﴾: He hears your seeking refuge in Him, in words.

﴿Knowing﴾: He knows your humble entreaty to Him in the heart, within speech or without it, so He will protect you from his evil. It has also been permitted that the incitement of Satan may mean the onset of anger, in the manner of metaphor (istiʿara), as in the saying of al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him): "Indeed, I have a devil that besets me." In this there is an added warning against it and an intense caution against acting upon its dictates.

In the command to seek refuge in Allah, exalted is He, there is an emphasis on the gravity of the matter, and an alert that it is among the difficult perils from whose harm one cannot be freed except by taking refuge in the sanctuary of His protection, mighty and majestic is He. It has also been said: He knows what is good for your affair and so He will guide you to it; or He is Hearing of the words of those who harm you and Knowing of their deeds, so He will recompense them for them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 201:

﴿Indeed, those who have taqwa﴾ is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) that confirms what precedes it, by clarifying that what the Prophet ﷺ was commanded regarding seeking refuge in God Most High is a practice followed by the God-fearing (al-muttaqun), while neglecting it is the habit of the deviators (al-ghawun). That is: indeed, those who have attained the state of safeguarding their souls from what harms them.

﴿When a passing thought (taif) from Satan touches them﴾: the least (adna) whisper (lamma) from him. The nunation of the word is for diminution (lil-tahqir). It is an active participle from tafa, yatufu, as if it circles around them and revolves about them in order to strike them; or it is from "taafa bihi al-khayal, yutifu taifan," meaning: it came upon him (alamma).

It was also read as ﴿taif﴾, either as a verbal noun (masdar), or as a lightened form of tayyif, from the waw-type or ya-type root, like hayyin and layyin. The word "Satan" here denotes the species (al-jins), and for this reason its pronoun is made plural in what follows.

﴿They remember﴾: that is, seeking refuge in Him, Exalted is He, and relying upon Him.

﴿Then behold, they﴾ by means of that remembrance,

﴿are seeing clearly﴾ the places of error and the snares of Satan, so they guard against them and do not follow him.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 202:**
