﴿And their brothers﴾; that is, the brothers of the devils, namely those who are immersed in error (al-ghayy), turning away from protecting themselves against harms.

﴿They extend them in error﴾; that is, the devils serve as a supply (madad) for them in it, reinforcing them by adorning it for them and urging them toward it. It is also read as "yumiddūnahum" (from al-imdad) and "yumadduhum," as if they assist them through facilitation and enticement, while these (the others) respond through following and obedience.

﴿Then they do not desist﴾; that is, they do not hold back from misleading until they have entirely turned them away. It is also permissible that the pronoun refers to the brothers; that is, they do not refrain from error and do not desist, unlike the God-fearing (al-muttaqun). It is also permissible that "the brothers" means the devils, and the pronoun returns to the ignorant (al-jahilun), so the statement applies to the one to whom it pertains.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 203:

﴿وَإذا لَمْ تَأْتِهِمْ بِآيَةٍ﴾ "And when you do not bring them a sign" — a verse from the Qur'an, when revelation is delayed, or a sign of what they have proposed.

﴿قالُوا لَوْلا اجْتَبَيْتَها﴾ "They say: Why do you not fabricate it?" The verb ijtaba (to choose, to select) means jaba al-shay' li-nafsihi, i.e., he gathered the thing for himself. The sense is: "Why did you not gather it from your own accord, as an invention (taqawwul)?" By this they mean that all the other verses are likewise [of your own invention]. Or: "Why did you not receive it from your Lord by request (istid'a')?"

﴿قُلْ﴾ "Say," in reply to them.

﴿إنَّما أتَّبِعُ ما يُوحى إلَيَّ مِن رَبِّي﴾ "I only follow what is revealed to me from my Lord," without any part of my own being in it at all. The meaning is the restriction of his ﷺ conduct to following what is revealed to him, by directing the restriction (qasr) conveyed by the word innama ("only") to the act itself in relation to its opposite, which they had imposed upon him ﷺ, and not to the sense of restricting his ﷺ following to what is revealed to him by directing the restriction to the object in comparison with another object, as is common in the usages of the language.

This has already been verified in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿إنْ أتَّبِعُ إلا ما يُوحى إلَيَّ﴾ ("I follow only what is revealed to me"), as if it were said: "I do nothing but follow what is revealed to me from Him, exalted is He." In the mention of the attribute of lordship (rububiyya), which indicates ownership and conveyance to its fitting perfection, together with its attribution to his pronoun ﷺ, there is an honouring of him ﷺ, and an alert to his being supported, which is not hidden.

﴿هَذا﴾ "This" is a reference to the noble Qur'an, indicated by what is revealed to me.

﴿بَصائِرُ مِن رَبِّكُمْ﴾ "are insights from your Lord," in the position of insights for the hearts, by which one sees the truth and perceives what is right. It is also said: clear proofs and luminous demonstrations.

The "min" is connected to an omitted element which is an attribute of "baṣā'ir," conveying its grandeur; that is: insights existing from Him, exalted is He. The mention of the title of lordship together with its attribution to their pronoun is for the emphasis of the obligation of belief in them.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿وَهُدًى ورَحْمَةٌ﴾ "and guidance and mercy," it is conjoined to "baṣā'ir." The placing of the adverbial phrase before them both, and their being followed by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿لِقَوْمٍ يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾ "for a people who believe," serves to indicate that the Qur'an's being in the position of insights for the hearts is established with respect to all, and by it the proof is established against everyone. As for its being guidance and mercy, it is specific to those who believe in it, since they are the ones who receive a share of its lights and benefit from its effects. The sentence is part of the speech that was commanded.(p-310)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 7, verse 204:

﴿And when the Qur'an is recited, then listen to it﴾ is a direction to the path of success in the great benefits alluded to, which the Qur'an contains. That is: when the Qur'an whose grand matters have been mentioned is recited, then listen to it with attentive reflection (istima' tahqiq) and acceptance (istima' qabul).

﴿And be silent﴾; that is: keep silent during the recitation and observe it until its conclusion, in glorification of it and to complete the listening.

﴿That you may receive mercy﴾; that is: that you may attain the mercy, which is its furthest fruit. The apparent sense of this noble structure requires the obligation of listening and remaining silent when the Qur'an is recited in prayer and otherwise.

It is said: its meaning is: when the Messenger recites the Qur'an to you at the time of its revelation, then listen to it. The majority of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, held that it refers to the listening of the one following the imam (in prayer).

It has been narrated that they used to speak during prayer, so they were commanded to listen to the recitation of the imam and to be silent for him. And from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that "the Prophet (ﷺ) recited in the obligatory prayer, and his companions recited behind him; so this was revealed."

As for outside of prayer, the general body of scholars hold that both (listening and silence) are recommended (mustahabb). The verse is either part of the speech commanded, or a new statement from Him, exalted is He.

Then His saying, ﴿And mention your Lord within yourself﴾: according to the first view it is a conjunction with "say" (qul); according to the second, there is in it a turning of the address away from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and it is general concerning all remembrances, for concealment is more inward to sincerity (ikhlas) and closer to being answered.

﴿Humbly and with fear﴾: that is, humbly submissive and fearful.

﴿And without loudness in speech﴾: that is, speaking words that are below loud voice, for that is closer to fine contemplation.

﴿In the mornings and the evenings﴾ is connected to "mention" (udhkur): that is, mention Him at the times of mornings and evenings. It was also read as "wal-iysal" (والإيصال), which is the verbal noun of "asala", meaning he entered the time of late afternoon (asil), and it agrees with "ghuduww" (morning).

﴿And do not be among the heedless﴾ of the remembrance of God Most High.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 7, verse 206:**

﴿Indeed, those who are with your Lord﴾: they are the angels, peace be upon them. The meaning of their being with Him, glorified and exalted is He, is their nearness to His mercy and bounty, because they are devoted to His obedience, exalted is He.

﴿They do not disdain His worship﴾: rather, they perform it as they were commanded.

﴿And they glorify Him﴾: that is, they declare Him far above everything that does not befit the majesty (kibriya') of His presence.

﴿And to Him they prostrate﴾: that is, they reserve for Him the utmost degree of servitude (ubudiyyah) and humility, associating nothing with Him. This is an implicit reproach to the rest of those who are legally responsible (mukallafin). For this reason, prostration (sujud) was prescribed during its recitation.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "When the son of Adam recites a verse of prostration (sajdah) and prostrates, Satan withdraws weeping, saying, 'Woe to him! This one was commanded to prostrate and prostrated, so he has Paradise; I was commanded to prostrate and disobeyed, so I have the Fire.'"

And from him (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah al-A'raf, Allah the Exalted will place between him and Iblis a screen on the Day of Resurrection, and Adam (peace be upon him) will be his intercessor on the Day of Resurrection."
